case20v1-legal.surveillance:
Rasoi Basket: The Line Between Helpful and Creepy

A teaching case on personalisation, consent and surveillance

1. Opening

At 9:30 pm on Tuesday 20 October 2026, Chandrabali Jyotishi opened a video call from her flat in Bengaluru. She was chief product officer of Rasoi Basket, a grocery and household delivery app, and she had until Friday 23 October to tell her colleagues which version of a new personalisation engine would go live on Wednesday 28 October, eleven days before Diwali. On the screen were six faces, a spreadsheet of pilot results, and a screenshot that a designer in Berlin had pasted into the team chat that morning.

The screenshot showed a push notification: "Because your household may be managing diabetes, here are 14 sugar-free picks." The user had never told Rasoi Basket anything about her health.

2. Company background

Rasoi Basket was founded in 2019 by two former e-commerce operators. It sells groceries, dairy, fresh produce and household staples across nine cities, with Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad and Kolkata its largest. It had about 30 lakh monthly active users in September 2026 and a gross merchandise value (GMV) run-rate near ₹1,400 crore a year. Its rivals are formidable: BigBasket and JioMart on scale, Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart on speed, DMart on price. Rasoi Basket competed on being the app a family opened every week and trusted with the household list.

That list was now a data asset. Seven years of baskets told the company what each home ate, which medicines it bought from the pharmacy aisle, and when a household changed. The festive season was when its investors expected the asset to pay.

3. The situation

In July the data team proposed an engine with three layers. The first used only what a customer did inside the app: past orders, searches and the time of day. The second added inferred life-stage and health tags, such as "expecting parent", "diabetic household" or "senior at home", derived from basket patterns (sugar-free staples, prenatal vitamins, adult diapers) and from how long a phone dwelt near clinics. The third was the notification layer that acted on those tags.

From 1 September to 12 October, a six-week window of 42 days, the company tested it on 1,20,000 randomly chosen users who had ordered in the previous 90 days. Each of three arms held 40,000 users: A, the existing category-based recommendations; B, in-app history only; C, history plus inferred tags and tag-driven notifications. Exhibit 1 gives the results.

Arm C lifted orders per user by 21.2 per cent over control (3.15 against 2.60), and Arm B by 11.5 per cent. The step from B to C was 8.6 per cent. But Arm C also lifted complaints from 20 to 612 and lost 800 more users to uninstalls than control. Exhibit 2 splits Arm C by whether a user had been tagged.

Of the 612 complaints, 548 (89.5 per cent) came from the 23.0 per cent of users who had been tagged. Chetna Jajori, who runs customer success from Singapore, forwarded a sample of those tickets. Most were unsettled: "Did you read my pharmacy orders?" "Why does the app think my mother is sick?"

The global team saw the same data differently. In Berlin, the designer was uncomfortable on principle. In Toronto, the data scientist who built the tags noted that they were statistical guesses, right perhaps three times in four, and that a wrong guess about illness is worse than a wrong guess about biscuits. Outside counsel in Mumbai pointed at the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Its consent standard requires consent to be free, specific, informed and given by a clear affirmative action, for a stated purpose. Its Rules, notified in November 2025, bring the main duties into force by May 2027, with penalties of up to ₹250 crore. The Central Consumer Protection Authority's dark-pattern guidelines already apply today.

4. The people

  • Chandrabali Jyotishi, chief product officer, Bengaluru. Joined in 2022. She owns the recommendation and must make the call; she wants a launch she could explain to a customer's face.
  • Chiranjib Joarder, head of growth, Pune. His festive target assumes the full engine. He wants Arm C live and argues that competitors infer far more.
  • Camille Jalui, senior designer, Berlin. She wants no inferred health claims shown to anyone.
  • Chetna Jajori, customer success lead, Singapore. She hears the tickets first and wants a quantified limit on how many unsettled customers the company will tolerate.

The call was held at 21:30 IST, which is 18:00 in Berlin (3.5 hours behind until 25 October), noon in Toronto (9.5 hours behind until 1 November) and midnight in Singapore.

6. The options

Option A: ship Arm C everywhere on 28 October. Inference runs by default, covered by an updated privacy notice. It captures the full uplift. It also takes the complaints, the uninstalls and the legal exposure, and it rests on a consent that customers did not knowingly give.

Option B: ship Arm B only. The company draws the line itself: recommendations may use what customers did in the app, and no health or life-stage tag is created at all. It is simple to defend, at the cost of the extra uplift.

Option C: ship Arm B for everyone, plus an opt-in. The user draws the line. A screen asks customers to say which of the household tags they want, such as "someone at home is diabetic", and only those who tick it receive tag-driven notifications. The cost is that only part of the base will opt in.

Exhibit 3 scales the pilot to 15 lakh users, for one hypothetical six-week window, at the pilot's rates. Fifteen lakh is the number of users resembling the pilot sample (those who ordered in the previous 90 days), not the 30 lakh monthly actives.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, where do the benefits and the complaints of Arm C sit, and what can and cannot be concluded about the tagged users from this pilot?
  2. Who draws the line between helpful and creepy in each of the three options, and what does each choice assume about what customers expect?
  3. How does the consent standard of the DPDP Act bear on the default-on design, and which of Camille's, Chiranjib's and Chetna's concerns would a regulator share?
  4. Which option would you take to the chief executive on Friday, what would you ask the team to measure after launch, and what result would make you change course?

8. A note for the learner

This topic reframes the decision. Personalisation and surveillance use the same data; what separates them is whether the customer would be surprised to learn how a suggestion was produced. The test is expectation, not legality alone, and the question of who draws the line has three possible answers: the model, the company or the customer. Consent law is the floor under that choice. A well-reasoned answer separates what the pilot measured from what it did not, and prices both sides of the trade.

One defensible path is Option C. Arm B already delivers a little over half of Arm C's gain in orders per user (0.30 of 0.55 extra orders), with 24 extra complaints per 40,000 users against 592. The remaining difference between A and C is about ₹2.2 crore of contribution in a six-week window (6.48 − 4.31), set against Option A's 30,000 extra uninstalls and an exposure the company cannot yet size. Because the complaints cluster in tagged users, letting those users choose targets the harm directly. Opt-in also meets the specific, informed, affirmative standard the law is moving toward.

The path has weak points. The 30 per cent opt-in rate is a guess; the tagged users' lift has no control group; and the engineering effort is an estimate. A sound plan therefore launches C with a measured opt-in rate, reviews it after Diwali, and states in advance the opt-in level below which the company would revisit Option B.
case40v1-legal.surveillance:
Sanjaal Technologies and the Sahayak Engine

A case on personalisation, consent and a joined customer record. Sanjaal Technologies and its named customers and partners are fictional; the Indian market, brands and regulators around them are real.

1. Sunday night in Kalyani Nagar

At 10:40 pm on Sunday 15 November 2026, Durba Kanungo sat at the dining table of her flat in Kalyani Nagar, Pune, with four printed options and a screenshot she had read thirty times. She was chief product officer of Sanjaal Technologies, the chemist-led health and household commerce company, and at 9:30 next morning she had thirty minutes with the board.

The screenshot had reached her on Friday 9 October. A customer in Nagpur had opened the app on the family's shared handset and been greeted by Sahayak, the in-app assistant: "Time to reorder? Your last refill was 26 days ago — tap to repeat." Underneath sat the medicine, by name, bought at a counter three kilometres away on the same mobile number by the customer's father-in-law. The engine had written that sentence by joining a counter purchase to an app session.

The team call had run from 9:05 pm — 4:35 pm in Berlin, 10:35 am in Toronto, 11:35 pm in Singapore — to 9:50, and had not converged. Durba had the pilot numbers, a memo from her data protection officer, a Dubai contract with a January milestone, and a distribution agreement expiring in six weeks.

2. The company, and the decision of January 2023

Sanjaal was founded in Pune in August 2017 by Debashish Kolay, still its chief executive, on one idea: the neighbourhood chemist was the most trusted and least digitised node in Indian retail. Sanjaal gave chemists free listing and, from March 2019, a point-of-sale product called Sanjaal Counter. By September 2026 Counter ran at 14,200 partner counters in 38 cities, and the app served about 62 lakh transacting users a month.

The decision that constrains November 2026 was taken in January 2023. Debashish signed a bundling agreement with a handset distribution group: Sanjaal Lite, a cut-down build carrying an SDK of Sanjaal's design, pre-installed on devices sold through six regional chains. Its consent flow was a single bundled checkbox — personalisation, analytics and partner offers — and the agreement specified that flow, so Sanjaal could not change it mid-term. It was renewed in January 2025 for twenty-four months and expires on 31 December 2026.

Lite worked. Of 3.10 crore registered accounts at 30 September 2026, 1.89 crore came through it (Exhibit 5, Panel A). All sit in one identity graph keyed on mobile number (Figure 2), joining app behaviour to counter purchase lines and device signals — the join that wrote the Nagpur sentence, and the join Sanjaal Signals, its brand audience product, rests on.

Figure 2. The identity graph, its three sources and the products that read it. Each source box names the notice its data was collected under.

3. The industry

Sanjaal competes in India's hardest consumer category. Tata 1mg, Apollo 24|7, PharmEasy, Netmeds and Flipkart Health+ fight for the medicine order; Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart have pulled wellness and staples into ten-minute delivery; Nykaa owns beauty. Reliance Retail and Tata hold distribution Sanjaal cannot match, and ONDC has made catalogue presence cheap. Sanjaal's claim is the counter: a chemist who knows the household, and a record of what it buys.

That record is what regulators now look at. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires consent that is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by clear affirmative action against an itemised notice; its Rules were notified in November 2025, the core duties bind from May 2027, and the Data Protection Board can levy up to ₹250 crore. The Central Consumer Protection Authority's dark-pattern guidelines bind today, and health data has no separate statutory tier in India.

Exposure is not only Indian. On 3 March 2026 Sanjaal signed a 36-month licence with Suroor Retail Group, a pharmacy and beauty chain in Dubai, at ₹9.4 crore a year — ₹28.2 crore over the term — for the Sahayak engine in Suroor's stores, the household-inference features live by 31 January 2027.

4. The situation in detail: beliefs by date, evidence by date

In February 2026 Sanjaal shipped Sahayak v2, an assistant drawing only on app behaviour. The plan recorded in June 2026 held three beliefs: that the counter join was covered by the notices then live; that the device layer was the larger prize; and that the Lite notice had been cleared by outside counsel in 2023.

On 1 July 2026 the data team enrolled 4,50,000 accounts in three arms of 1,50,000, drawn at random from the 39 lakh June 2026 transactors that carried the Lite build — 58 lakh transacted in all — so every arm carried the device signals Arm C needed, and measured them for 90 days to 28 September 2026. Arm A used app behaviour only; Arm B added counter purchase lines held in Counter under the same mobile number; Arm C added Lite device signals — coarse location dwell and installed-app inventory — and surfaced inferred health and life-stage tags in Sahayak prompts. Exhibit 1 gives the arms; Exhibit 2 splits Arm C by tag status.

Three facts arrived later. On 5–12 October the Toronto team hand-reviewed 2,400 of Arm C's tagged accounts: 1,704 of the 2,400 reviewed accounts (71.0 per cent) carried a tag a human agreed with, and 608 of the 950 health tags (64.0 per cent) were agreed. The 28 October memo recorded that the 2023 counsel opinion covered the pre-install flow and not the installed-app inventory, added by a Lite release in June 2024. A retrospective on 20 October applied a counter-only tag rule to Arm B, where no tag had been surfaced (Exhibit 3).

Between 1 and 10 October the company showed an itemised re-consent prompt to Lite accounts (Exhibit 5, Panel B); between 22 and 30 September a research firm surveyed Sanjaal users (Exhibit 6). Figure 1 sets the dates against the deadlines.

Figure 1. Scale: 1 July 2026 at the left tick, one day = 2.0 units of width, so 15 November 2026 sits 137 days along. From the product calendar of 2 November 2026 and the contract schedules.

5. The people

Durba Kanungo, chief product officer, Pune, since January 2021. She owns the recommendation, and her 2027 product headcount was approved on a plan that assumes Arm C. She will not, she says, ship a sentence she could not defend to the customer it was about. She has not told the board she approved the June 2024 release that added installed-app inventory.

Debashish Kolay, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. His position: the join stays, the notice gets fixed. A Series D term sheet is in diligence at ₹7,100 crore. He has not circulated the lead investor's question of 6 November, which asks Sanjaal to warrant valid consent for every account in the graph.

Dwaipayan Kashyap, head of growth, Bengaluru, since April 2022. Half his variable pay rides on the January–March quarter and he wants Arm C live before the Sankranti and Pongal push. He has not mentioned that in August his own team switched tag-driven prompts off for internal test handsets.

Devleena Kaviraj, data protection officer, Pune, appointed February 2026; she signs the DPDP filings in her own name. Her position: the graph must be split into consent-scoped stores before anything ships. She has not told the board the notice cannot be re-papered before 31 December.

Diptanu Khastagir, principal data scientist, Toronto, since November 2021; he built the tag model and his Toronto team is funded from it. His position: tags are probabilistic and should be treated so. He published the 71.0 per cent precision on 14 October but not the health-tag figure, and nobody has asked.

Doyeeta Kataky, design lead, Berlin, since June 2024; the Suroor rollout is her first director-track brief. She found the Nagpur screenshot in a support thread and escalated it. Her position: no inferred health claim should be shown to anyone, in any market, at any confidence. She has drafted a resignation letter, unsent.

Debaditya Kabiraj, customer success lead, Singapore, account owner for Suroor. His position: Sanjaal ships what it sold. Suroor's compliance head asked him on 6 November whether the inference features would be lawful in the UAE; he has not escalated it.

Dibyashree Kundoo, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey, hired August 2025 for a North American Signals pipeline. Her position: a privacy-first Sanjaal sells in her market and a joined-graph Sanjaal does not. Two prospects asked in writing for the device SDK to be removed; she has not reported it.

7. Voices

"Arm C gives us close to a fifth more orders per user than control, over ninety real days. And forty-two per cent of the people we asked said yes to the full thing. People do not mind being personalised. They mind being surprised."

Dwaipayan Kashyap, growth review, 2 November 2026

"Forty-two per cent of the two lakh sixty-one thousand who answered. Not of the four lakh we showed it to, and not of the one crore eighty-nine lakh in Panel A. The denominator is the whole argument, and you have used the smallest one available."

Devleena Kaviraj, replying in the same meeting

"The model is a guess with a number attached. When the guess is biscuits, a wrong guess costs a scroll. When it is a medicine, it costs a conversation inside somebody's family that we started and will not be present for."

Diptanu Khastagir, chat thread, 14 October 2026

"We keep arguing about which columns feed the model. The consent happened at a counter in Nagpur, where a chemist took a phone number to send a bill. Nobody has asked what that chemist thinks he agreed to, and he is the only one of us who was in the room."

Doyeeta Kataky, chat thread, 12 November 2026

"Field note, Nagpur, 11 November: the chemist says he tells customers the number is for the bill and for reminders. Asked whether he tells them the app will show the medicine, he said the app is Sanjaal's side of it."

Research note circulated by Debaditya Kabiraj

8. The options as Durba sees them

Each revenue figure below is the pilot's per-user gap annualised at 365 ÷ 90 over the 39 lakh Lite-carrying accounts that transacted in June 2026 — the base the arms were drawn from — at the 9.0 per cent take rate in Exhibit 4, assuming the arms' behaviour holds across that base.

Option 1 — Ship Arm C with a shared-handset suppression. Tags are still computed and surfaced, except on accounts flagged as shared devices, and the app-created base gets an itemised notice. Against Arm A this is ₹845.9 crore of GMV and ₹76.1 crore of commission a year, and about four engineer-months for the flag. It leaves the Lite notice as the agreement specifies until 31 December 2026, and the eleven Signals contracts untouched.

Option 2 — Ship Arm B and switch the device layer off. The counter join stays; location dwell and installed-app inventory stop at the SDK. The agreement requires Lite to be pre-installed but does not specify which signals the SDK collects, so collection stops with a server flag. Against Arm A this is ₹492.7 crore of GMV and ₹44.3 crore of commission a year, forgoing the ₹353.2 crore of GMV and ₹31.8 crore of commission the device step carries. The four Signals contracts worth ₹23 crore would be rebuilt. It leaves the counter join in place.

Option 3 — Split the graph first, ship second. The graph is divided into three consent-scoped stores, and the Lite base re-consented from January 2027, when the notice can be rewritten; the engine then runs on whatever consent returns. Engineering estimates 14 engineer-months. An SMS and in-app campaign across 1.89 crore Lite accounts at ₹0.12 a message, two attempts each, is ₹45.36 lakh. It leaves the Suroor milestone of 31 January 2027 where it is, owed by the same nine engineers.

Option 4 — Move the inference to the counter. The chemist asks a short declared-preference question at the till and records the answer in Counter; Sahayak then uses declared facts rather than inferred tags. A ₹140 monthly incentive across 14,200 counters is ₹2.39 crore a year; retraining cost is not estimated. No coverage figure exists; the pilot did not test this route. It leaves the Lite SDK and the device layer untouched.

All four sheets describe which columns feed the engine. Doyeeta's thread of 12 November and the Nagpur field note describe something else.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Dates. The bundling agreement requires 30 days' notice, so the renewal decision is due 1 December 2026; it ends 31 December. Suroor's household-inference milestone is 31 January 2027, and missing it triggers a service credit of ₹1.175 crore, one-eighth of the annual fee. Seven Signals contracts worth ₹45 crore renew on 31 March 2027.

People. Nine platform engineers. Releases are frozen from 5 December to 2 January for the chemist audit season, leaving 16 November to 4 December and 3 January to 31 January — 48 calendar days, or 6.9 weeks, so 61.7 engineer-weeks, about 14.3 engineer-months at 4.33 weeks to the month. The split is estimated at 14, and the same window owes Suroor.

Money and paper. Cash of ₹212 crore at 30 September 2026 against a burn of ₹14.5 crore a month, or 14.6 months. Sanjaal's counsel has given no written view on whether UAE operation of the inference features is covered by the Suroor licence.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 reports three arms over the same 90 days. What is each arm's per-user figure a figure of — which accounts, enrolled when, measured how — and what must be assumed to carry it to the whole transacting base?
  2. Exhibit 5, Panel B reports a prompt shown to 4,00,000 Lite accounts. Which denominators could a "consent rate" use, which does Panel B support, and what does Panel A say about the rest of the Lite base?
  3. Exhibits 2 and 3 each split a pilot arm by tag status, under differently defined tag rules. What comparison does each exhibit license on its own, and what can be said from the two together?
  4. Exhibit 6 records what 1,240 surveyed users say would trouble them; Exhibit 5, Panel B records what 2,61,000 prompted accounts did. When the two point different ways, which should price a decision, and what measurement would settle it?
  5. The January 2025 renewal fixed Lite's notice until 31 December 2026; the Suroor licence fixed a milestone for 31 January 2027. Who inside Sanjaal should have owned the interaction between those dates, and what would that ownership look like in writing?
  6. What should Durba Kanungo do on Monday morning, 16 November, and what exactly would she say to the board — including what she would tell them she does not know?

11. Eleven fifty

The flat was quiet. Durba laid the four sheets side by side and, because they had stopped telling her anything new, turned them over. On the back of one she had copied two dates, 1 December and 31 January, and drawn a line between them she could not label.

Her phone lit twice. Debashish: "Tomorrow we go in with one number and one ask. Which number?" Then Doyeeta, four and a half hours behind in Berlin: "Did you read the field note?"

Durba opened the Nagpur screenshot again. Twenty-six days since the last refill. A name, a dosage, a tap target. Somewhere in the graph were 3.10 crore mobile numbers, and behind one a family who had not complained, might never, and whose conversation she had started. She typed a reply to Debashish, read it, deleted it.
exp40v2-legal.surveillance:
Ethics, Trust & Compliance · Privacy, Legal, Compliance & Accessibility · Exp40

Personalisation vs Surveillance

Where the line sits, who has standing to draw it, and how expert practitioners price the crossing before they make it rather than after.

1. Two rooms, one week

On 2 March 2026, in a converted mill building in Lower Parel, Sarika Menon, Chief Product Officer of Khirki, reviewed the first month of data from a feature shipped quietly to 5% of users. Khirki was an AI shopping assistant with 2.8 million monthly actives, mostly urban buyers who used it to compare, remember and re-order across Indian e-commerce. The feature was persistent memory: the assistant retained what a customer had told it across sessions, and also what it had worked out. A customer who had asked, in January, about cotton kurtas that would not aggravate eczema was, by March, in a segment labelled sensitive-skin, likely dermatological condition. Nobody had typed that label. The assistant had inferred it, stored it, and was using it to re-rank results. Paid conversion in the treatment cell ran 0.8 percentage points above control. Khirki's Series B close was six weeks out.

Eleven hundred kilometres away, on 5 March, Devendra Iyer, head of product at Qaafila Telematics in Gurugram, faced a structurally identical question with a different set of people in the room. Qaafila sold fleet telematics to 610 long-haul operators covering 41,000 trucks. Its new driver-monitoring unit used an in-cab camera to detect drowsiness and distraction. Driver-facing, the cab chimed and footage was deleted after 30 days, seen by nobody. Fleet-facing, the same footage surfaced on a supervisor's dashboard ranked by "risk score". Six operators had made the second configuration a condition of renewal, worth ₹7.4 crore of annual recurring revenue. The drivers, subjects of every frame, had signed nothing and bought nothing.

 Khirki (consumer, AI-native)Qaafila (B2B, hardware + software)
SubjectThe paying customerThe driver — who is neither buyer nor user
Data in questionInferred health-adjacent attribute from chatContinuous video of a person at work
Who benefitsCustomer and company, jointlyFleet owner and insurer; driver, partially
Measured upside+0.8 pp paid conversion₹7.4 crore ARR at renewal
DeadlineSeries B, 13 April 2026Renewal cycle, 30 April 2026

Exhibit 1. The same question in two product shapes. The damaging row is the second: in Qaafila's column, the person whose data flows agreed to nothing.

Both executives had been given the standard answer and both had noticed it did not fit. The standard answer is that personalisation becomes surveillance when data leaves the context in which it was given. That sentence is correct, and it is where working knowledge stops. It does not tell Sarika whether an inference the customer never supplied is inside or outside the context, and it does not tell Devendra whose context governs when the subject and the buyer are different people.

2. The idea, and the five camps that disagree about it

The intellectual history runs through four moves. Warren and Brandeis, in 1890, framed privacy as a right to be let alone — a boundary around the person. Alan Westin, in Privacy and Freedom (1967), replaced the boundary with a dial: privacy is the claim of individuals to determine when, how and to what extent information about them is communicated. That reframing — privacy as control — is the direct ancestor of every consent screen in existence, including the notice-and-consent architecture of India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Richard Posner, in 1978, attacked it from economics: information about a person is often information others legitimately need, concealment transfers costs onto counterparties, and privacy is an allocation of property rights in facts rather than a dignity interest. Helen Nissenbaum's contextual integrity (2004, 2010) answered a question neither camp could: why identical data feels fine in one hand and violating in another. Information flows carry the norms of the context they occur in — banking, medicine, employment, friendship — and appropriateness is a property of the flow, described by five variables: subject, sender, recipient, information type, transmission principle.

Contextual integrity is the working vocabulary, but it is not a consensus. Five identifiable camps hold different propositions, and an expert can say which sentence each would sign.

Exhibit 2. Five positions, placed by what each takes the harm to be and whether consent machinery can cure it. Practitioners usually hold one without knowing it has a name or an opposition.

The control camp signs: a person should decide what is collected and for what, and a well-built consent flow discharges the obligation. It will not sign that consent obtained is consent understood. The contextual camp signs: a flow can violate norms even with impeccable consent; it will not sign that aggregate agreement cures a context breach. The welfare camp signs: disclosure frequently raises total surplus, concealment has victims too, and a claimed harm with no measurable loss deserves scepticism; it will not sign that discomfort is itself an injury. The structural camp signs: the harm is accumulated predictive power over populations, so individual consent is beside the point; it will not sign that a better toggle helps. The taxonomy camp, following Daniel Solove, signs that "privacy" names a family of distinct injuries — aggregation, secondary use, exclusion, distortion, increased accessibility — and refuses the premise that there is one line at all. That refusal is the most useful thing in the literature for a working PM: the question is never "is this creepy" but "which of the named injuries is this, to whom, and how large."

3. Mechanics: what the work actually is

Expert practice has four moves that a competent practitioner performs in the wrong order or not at all.

Enumerate flows, not features. The unit of analysis is a tuple of the five variables, not a screen. Khirki's memory feature is at least four flows: stated preference used in-session; stated preference persisted across sessions; inferred attribute persisted; inferred attribute joined to the merchandising warehouse where a category manager can query it. The first two sit comfortably inside a shopping relationship. The fourth introduces a recipient the customer never pictured, and it is the one nobody wrote down, because it was not a feature — it was a nightly table sync.

Grade the data by provenance. Declared (typed by the customer for this purpose), observed (behaviour inside the product), inferred (attributes the customer never stated), acquired (bought or joined from outside). Violations cluster heavily in the last two, and inference is the pivot: the moment a system asserts something about a person that the person did not say, it has taken a position they cannot correct and did not authorise. India's regulators reached the same instinct from another direction — the Reserve Bank's digital-lending guidelines bar lending apps from reaching into phone contacts, media and call logs, not because those fields are secret but because the inferences drawn from them sit nowhere near a lending relationship.

Measure the expectation gap. The operational proxy for a norm is a survey. Describe the flow in plain language — "Khirki remembers that you mentioned a skin condition and uses it to choose which brands to show you" — and ask customers whether they expected it and how comfortable they are, on a five-point scale. Khirki's numbers: for persisted stated preferences, 71% expected it, mean discomfort 1.4. For persisted inferred health attributes, 19% expected it, mean discomfort 3.9. That 52-point expectation gap is the measurement corresponding to the theory.

Price the margin, not the average. This step separates the two levels, and it requires an ablation, not an A/B test. An A/B test tells you personalisation works. An ablation tells you which features carry the lift. Khirki's team retrained the ranker with the inferred-sensitive features removed, and got Exhibit 3.

VariantPaid conversionLift vs controlAdded revenue / yrDiscomfort delta₹ crore per discomfort point
Control (no memory)4.1%————
A: declared memory only4.6%+0.5 pp₹2.10 cr+0.37.00
B: A + inferred attributes4.9%+0.8 pp₹3.36 cr+1.62.10

Exhibit 3. 2.8m MAU, paid tier ₹1,499/yr. Variant B's average exchange rate (₹2.10 crore per discomfort point) flatters it. At the margin the inferred layer buys revenue at ₹0.97 crore per point — one-seventh the efficiency of the declared layer it sits on.

The arithmetic reverses the usual intuition. Teams defend sensitive inference on the grounds that it works. It does work. It also works worst per unit of norm violation, because the declared and observed layers have already captured most of the signal and the inferred layer competes with them for the same residual. A practitioner who runs the ablation habitually finds the objectionable 10% of the feature set producing 15–25% of the lift while carrying 80% of the exposure — a bad trade at almost any price, and invisible unless the decomposition is run.

Three second-order effects follow, and none appear in the first spreadsheet. Trust decay across features: the cost of a violation is rarely borne by the feature that caused it, but by the opt-in rate of the next four launches. Adverse selection in opt-outs: the customers who find and use the control are the higher-value, higher-literacy cohort, so a setting used by 3% of users can remove 9% of revenue-weighted signal, quietly degrading the model for everyone. The feedback loop: a ranker that narrows what a customer sees also narrows the behaviour it observes, so confidence in a stale inference rises even as accuracy falls — Khirki's eczema label would keep strengthening for a customer whose condition cleared in February, because she would stop being shown the alternatives that would have revealed the change.

4. The conditions, stated so they can be falsified

Contextual integrity is a strong tool inside its range and actively misleading outside it. Five conditions define the range, each testable.

ConditionKhirkiQaafila
C1. A nameable context with settled norms exists.Holds — retail commerce.Contested — road safety, or employment supervision?
C2. The subject is a party to the relationship.Holds.Fails. The driver is subject, not party.
C3. The subject can learn of the flow.Only via a help article — weak.Holds — the camera is visible.
C4. Norms are stable over the product's horizon.Unstable — AI memory norms are forming now.Stable — workplace monitoring norms are old.
C5. The violation, if any, is reversible.Partly — stored inferences can be deleted.Poorly — a dismissal cannot be undone.

Exhibit 4. Khirki fails on stability, Qaafila on party status — different failures needing different instruments.

Where C2 fails, contextual integrity gives the wrong answer, because the norms of the buyer's context — fleet management, where monitoring vehicles is entirely ordinary — get cited to license a flow about a person. Devendra's mistake, for three weeks, was arguing about whether fleet operators expected dashboards. They plainly did. The governing norm was never theirs. Where C4 fails — and it fails for every AI-native product right now — the tool measures a norm still congealing, and a March 2026 survey about conversational memory has an unknown shelf life. The honest response is not to abandon the tool but to shorten the commitment: ship with a stated review date, and design the flow so withdrawal does not read as a confession.

5. Edge cases and organisational seams

Most real violations are not decisions. They are seams. A consumer app with three business units has a warehouse all three query; the growth team's join of the inference table to the merchandising table is not a product decision, has no design review, and never appears in a privacy impact assessment because no external party is involved. Yet secondary internal use is the most common way contextual integrity breaks in mature companies. The tell is the gap between what a firm says — "we never sell data" — and what it does, which is to let any team with warehouse credentials use any table for any purpose. Firms that genuinely fixed this did one thing: attach a purpose tag to the column at collection and make the warehouse refuse cross-purpose joins without an approval record. It is an engineering control, not a policy, which is why it works.

Two-sided markets create a second seam: a flow appropriate for one side violates the other. A marketplace telling sellers "buyers in your category also viewed X" is inside seller norms and, at fine enough granularity, outside buyer norms — and the granularity is set by an engineer choosing a cohort threshold, not by anyone who understands the norm. Regulated contexts create a third: in health, finance and children's products the norm is written into law, and the DPDP Act's treatment of children's data and of Significant Data Fiduciaries converts a judgement call into a compliance artefact. Hardware adds a fourth that software people underrate: a device in a physical space captures non-users — Qaafila's camera sees the loader who climbs in at Nashik, the mechanic, the driver's brother riding along on a Sunday, none party to any contract. AI-native products add the fifth: the model is both recipient and discloser. A system that has inferred something will eventually say it out loud, so discovery happens at the moment of maximum surprise, mid-conversation, with no framing.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

The marginal exchange rate, not the average

The tell is a growth deck that reports the lift of "personalisation" as one number. The expert asks for the ablation immediately, because the average conflates a cheap, uncontroversial layer with an expensive one stacked on top. The obvious reading — the feature is net-positive, so ship it — is wrong because the decision on the table is not the feature, it is the increment. Khirki's increment cost seven times more discomfort per rupee than the base it sat on, and nobody in that room would have defended it had it ever been presented alone.

Accuracy makes the violation worse, not better

The tell is a team defending an inference by citing its precision: "we're 92% accurate on life-stage." An expert hears an aggravating factor. A wrong guess is annoying; a correct guess about something the person never disclosed demonstrates, unmistakably, that the system knows more than the relationship licensed. The obvious reading treats accuracy as a proxy for legitimacy — better models, better product. In the sensitive quadrant the relationship inverts: complaint volume rises with model quality, because only an accurate model produces the experience of being read.

Opt-out rates measure interface design, not consent

The tell is a slide reporting that only 1.8% of users disabled the setting. The expert asks what fraction ever saw the screen. If 4% reached the settings page, a 1.8% overall opt-out means roughly 45% of those who saw the control used it — the opposite conclusion. The obvious reading treats low opt-out as revealed preference. It is usually revealed navigation depth. The diagnostic: compute opt-out conditional on exposure, and run a one-off in-line prompt to a 1% cell for an unconditional estimate.

When the customer learns is part of the flow

The transmission principle has a time coordinate the five-variable framing leaves implicit. Disclosure at collection, at first use, and in a help-centre article are three different flows with the same data. The tell is a feature whose explanation exists only in documentation nobody reads. The obvious reading — disclosure is binary, done or not done — misses that late disclosure is experienced as concealment, a distinct injury from the original collection and frequently the larger one.

The product's own output is the disclosure channel

The tell lives in support tickets, in the phrase "how did it know that." An expert reads free-text volume for that exact string: it is the highest-fidelity signal that a flow has crossed a line, and it arrives weeks before anything shows in churn or NPS. The obvious reading treats these tickets as confusion to be resolved with a better explanation. They are not confusion. They are the surprise measurement, arriving unbidden and for free.

"It's aggregated" is a claim about a number, and the number is usually small

The tell is aggregation asserted without a threshold. Cohorts of eight are not anonymous to a category manager who knows the category. The expert asks for the minimum cell size, whether it is enforced at query time or by convention, and whether repeated queries with shifting filters can be differenced to isolate an individual — the elementary attack on any aggregate interface. The obvious reading treats aggregation as a category of safety. It is a continuum with a parameter, and the parameter is usually unset.

Withdrawal is harder than launch, so design the exit first

The tell is legal counsel advising against removing a feature because removal signals fault. The advice is rational, and it is how creepy features become permanent. The expert's counter is a sunset clause written at launch: this inference layer expires on a stated date unless re-approved, which converts removal from an admission into a schedule. The obvious reading assumes decisions are symmetric — what you can ship you can unship. Reputationally and legally, they are not.

The line is market-wide, and it moves in both directions

The tell is a team citing a competitor's practice as evidence of acceptability. Norms do drift toward acceptance through habituation — location personalisation made that journey between 2011 and 2020 — but drift is not monotonic. One enforcement action or leak can re-sensitise a whole data category across a market, for every firm in it, including firms that behaved well. The obvious reading is that yesterday's tolerance predicts tomorrow's. Norm capital is borrowed from a market-wide pool, and it can be called in by someone else's failure.

7. How the shape of the product changes the answer

In consumer products the context is singular and named at signup, so violations are legible and the main risk is narrative — one screenshot travels. In B2B and enterprise the split between buyer and subject is the whole problem; governing norms come from employment, not the purchase, and the instrument is not consent but structural limitation: aggregation thresholds, no individual drill-down, retention caps, consultation with worker representatives. Platforms and marketplaces carry two norm sets on one pipe, and the operative decision is a granularity parameter that usually has no owner. Hardware captures bystanders party to nothing, which is why device teams need a physical-space analysis software teams can skip. AI products differ in two genuinely new ways: inference is continuous rather than a discrete feature decision, and the system discloses its own inferences conversationally, without a design review, at a moment of the customer's choosing rather than the company's.

Stage changes exposure, not the norm. A 50,000-user startup can ship Khirki's variant B, learn, and reverse it in a week with no press. At 2.8 million users and a Series B in progress, the identical flow is a diligence question and a headline. Where stage genuinely changes the analysis is capacity: a pre-Series-A company cannot run an expectation survey and an ablation for every feature, and pretending otherwise produces theatre. The version that survives contact with a ten-person team is one question in the spec template — "describe this flow in one sentence a customer would recognise" — plus a standing rule that inferred sensitive attributes require a named approver. Not rigour; the cheapest available substitute, and it catches most of what matters.

8. Three worked cases, including one that broke

Tamasha Play, a regional streaming service with 9.1 million subscribers, faced the household problem: one account, five viewers, wildly different tastes. The tempting solution was device-level behavioural fingerprinting to separate viewers invisibly. The team instead shipped explicit profiles with a short prompt, accepting that some households would not bother. Adoption reached 58% of households in four months; within those, completion rose 11.4% and monthly churn fell from 3.9% to 3.1%, worth roughly ₹19 crore in retained annual revenue. The declared mechanism captured most of the available value because the customer's own interest was aligned; the inference would have added perhaps a fifth more at a cost the team never had to pay.

Kasturi Pharmacies, a 480-store chain with a 6.2 million-member loyalty programme, is the failure. In 2024 it built a retail-media network and let brand partners target cohorts derived from purchase history, including cohorts that were chronic-condition inferences in all but name — "high-frequency metformin basket", "cardiac-adjacent". Media revenue reached ₹44 crore annualised within three quarters. In August 2025 a customer received a diabetes-management campaign at a home address where her diagnosis was not known, and wrote about it. Loyalty enrolment at point of sale fell from 34% to 21% of transactions within six weeks and stayed down. Recovery took seven months: deleting the derived health cohorts entirely, rebuilding targeting on declared categories plus an opt-in "care reminders" programme, and publishing the cohort taxonomy. Media revenue returned to ₹27 crore — 61% of peak — at a third of the 2025 complaint volume. The instructive number is not the ₹17 crore of lost media revenue; it is the enrolment rate, which had nothing to do with media and was the company's most valuable long-run asset.

Daftar Work Cloud, an enterprise collaboration-analytics vendor, made the opposite trade deliberately. It refused individual drill-down, enforcing a minimum cohort of ten at the query layer, and lost an estimated 18% of deals to rivals offering manager-level views. It won longer contracts — average tenure 3.4 years against a category norm near 2.1 — and cleared procurement at two European multinationals that had rejected every competitor. Net revenue retention of 128% more than covered the lost deals. The constraint was the product.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Legal sign-off read as ethical sign-off"Privacy reviewed it" replaces a description of the flowWhat did they review — exposure, or expectation?Discovery happens in public, not in a review
Silent internal secondary useAn unowned warehouse table appears in a new dashboardWho can query this column, for what stated purpose?Years of undocumented flows to unwind under deadline
Inference creep in an AI productTickets containing "how did it know"What is the system asserting that no one told it?Stored inferences propagate into every downstream model
Consent theatreOpt-out reported unconditionallyWhat share of users ever saw this control?A consent record regulators discount and customers disown

Norm borrowed from a competitor"X does this too" is the justification of recordWhat did our onboarding copy promise?Exposure to a market-wide re-sensitising event

Exhibit 5. Each warning sign is observable without new instrumentation.

The pattern across the six: early signals are qualitative, late signals are quantitative — exactly backwards from how most product organisations allocate attention. By the time a privacy failure is visible in a metric, the cheap window has closed. The organisations that catch these early are the ones where someone reads support free-text weekly and has standing to stop a launch.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Position one: consent, done properly, is sufficient. The strongest form is not the weak version about checkboxes. It is that preferences differ enormously — some customers actively want aggressive personalisation — and any framework that overrides stated preference substitutes the designer's taste for the customer's autonomy. The evidence is real variance in willingness to trade data for value, and the success of granular controls where they are genuinely offered. For this to be wrong, preference as expressed in an interface would have to be so construction-dependent that it cannot be recovered at all — and the privacy-paradox literature, where stated and revealed preferences diverge sharply under trivial framing changes, points that way without settling it.

Position two: norms govern, consent is secondary. Markets for privacy fail structurally — no individual can price a flow whose consequences are aggregate and deferred — so appropriateness must be set by the context's norms and, where necessary, by regulation. The evidence is the observed uselessness of notice at scale, and the fact that the flows people object to most are usually ones they formally agreed to. For it to be wrong, norms would have to be too unstable or contested to measure — precisely the objection in AI-native categories, where the norm is being manufactured by the products themselves in real time.

Position three: the frame is individual, the harm is collective. Zuboff's argument at its strongest is that debating any single flow concedes the point, because the harm is accumulated capacity to predict and shape behaviour at population scale, which no per-flow analysis can see. The evidence is the concentration of predictive infrastructure. For this to be wrong, the aggregate would have to be decomposable — controlling individual flows would have to control it. Practitioners mostly act as though it is, partly because the alternative leaves them nothing to do on a Tuesday.

The disagreement is not academic: position one produces a consent-flow roadmap, position two a norm-measurement practice, position three a case for not building the feature at all. No committee reconciles them.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this can name the five variables. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They ask for the ablation before the lift number, so the conversation starts at the margin. They describe flows in one plain sentence and watch a real customer's face rather than circulating a policy. They treat the warehouse and the model as recipients as seriously as an external vendor, because that is where violations actually live. And they hold a position they can name — control, context or structure — so that a disagreement with a competent colleague can be located as a dispute about which harm counts rather than about who cares more. That last is the real marker. Novices argue about whether something is creepy. Experts argue about which injury is alleged, to whom, at what magnitude, and on whose authority the line gets drawn — and they say plainly when the answer is that nobody has standing yet and the company is making the norm rather than following it.

12. Decisions, and questions for the room

Sarika shipped variant A. Her reasoning to the board was the exchange rate: the increment bought ₹1.26 crore at seven times the norm cost of the base layer, and the stored health-adjacent inferences would have propagated into every downstream model Khirki built for three years. She kept variant B alive as a design problem rather than killing it — specifically, whether a customer could be shown what the assistant had concluded about her and correct it, which converts an inference into a declaration and moves the flow back inside the context.

Devendra did not choose between his two configurations. He built a third: fleet-facing dashboards restricted to aggregated safety events over a minimum of twelve trips, no video, no individual ranking, raw footage staying driver-facing and auto-deleted at 30 days, releasable to a supervisor only on a specific incident and with the driver notified. Four of six operators accepted; two did not renew, costing ₹2.6 crore of the ₹7.4 crore at stake. His internal argument was that C2 could not be repaired by consent, because drivers had no leverage to refuse, so the only instrument left was structural limitation — and that Qaafila's long-run position depended on drivers not disabling the cameras, which 19% in the fleet-facing pilot had already found ways to do.

For discussion:

1. Khirki's inference was accurate and the customer benefited. If both hold, what is the injury — and does naming it aggregation, secondary use or distortion change the remedy?

2. Devendra's two lost operators will buy fleet-facing monitoring elsewhere and those drivers will be watched anyway. Does Qaafila's restraint accomplish anything? Is "someone else will do it" an argument or an evasion?

3. Where norms are still forming, first movers write the norm the survey will later measure. Who has standing to set it, and what obligations does that authorship create?

13. Going deeper

  • Data, consent and the DPDP Act — the statutory floor; purpose limitation and consent managers are where a context judgement becomes a legal obligation.
  • Personalisation strategy — the other half of the trade: building lift from declared and observed data so the inferred layer is never the interesting one.
  • Privacy expectations in consumer products — measuring the norm rather than asserting it, including survey design that does not manufacture the answer.
  • Memory and personalisation in LLM products — where inference becomes continuous and the system discloses itself; the fastest-moving edge of this topic.
  • Privacy by design — purpose tagging and minimum-cell enforcement: the controls that turn a policy into something that binds.
  • GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes — legitimate-interest and sale-of-data doctrines give different answers to the same flow across markets.
  • Consent flows and cookie UX — where the control school's promises are kept or broken, and where opt-out conditional on exposure is measured.
  • Security compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001 — what makes an enterprise claim about restricted access auditable rather than aspirational.
  • Terms of service, SLAs and contracts — where the transmission principle gets written down, and how a contract binds a buyer's use of a subject's data.
  • IP, patents and trademarks for PMs — derived data raises ownership questions the privacy frame does not answer.

Personalisation vs Surveillance

Where is the line between helpful personalisation and creepy surveillance — and whose job is it to draw it?

A Thursday in Bengaluru

On 10 September 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Vittam Money, sat in a glass-walled conference room on the ninth floor of an office park in Bellandur, looking at a feature her team had spent four months building. Vittam Money was a personal-finance app with 4.2 million monthly active users, most of them salaried professionals in their twenties and thirties who used it to track spending across bank accounts and UPI apps. The feature, internally called Vittam Nudge, would open with a message like: “You’ve spent 34% more on food delivery this month than your three-month average — want to set a weekly cap?” It was built on two layers of data. The first layer was data customers had knowingly typed or tagged themselves: transaction categories, monthly budgets, savings goals. The second layer, added six weeks earlier by the growth team, was inferred: the list of other apps installed on a user’s phone, pulled through a standard Android package-visibility permission, cross-referenced against a purchased taxonomy to guess “financial life stage” — newly employed, wedding-planning, first-home, new-parent.

Karthik Nair, Vittam’s product-legal counsel, had flagged the second layer the week before. His objection wasn’t that it was illegal in a narrow sense — the installed-app-list permission was granted at install time, buried in a standard OS dialog. His objection was that customers had agreed to share transaction data so Vittam could help them budget, and nothing in that relationship implied Vittam would also profile the other apps on their phone to infer whether they were expecting a baby. Vittam’s board review was in nine days. The growth team’s model projected the richer version of Nudge would lift paid conversion meaningfully; the leaner, declared-data-only version would lift it less. Ananya had to decide which version shipped, and defend the decision to a board that had, until that morning, only ever asked her about growth.

The idea: contextual integrity

The analytic tool Ananya reached for did not come from a privacy lawyer’s checklist. It came from the philosopher and computer scientist Helen Nissenbaum, who published it as contextual integrity in a 2004 paper and a fuller 2010 book, after a decade of watching two dominant ideas fail to explain how people actually feel about data. The first idea, “public versus private,” couldn’t explain why a customer is fine with a bank knowing their salary but furious when the same bank tells their employer. The second idea, “notice and consent,” couldn’t explain why a customer who clicked “agree” on a sixty-page terms document still feels violated when that agreement gets used in a way they never pictured. Nissenbaum’s answer was that every exchange of personal information happens inside a specific social context — banking, healthcare, friendship, employment — and each context carries its own norms about who may know what, and how it may move. Information flow is appropriate when it matches those norms and inappropriate when it doesn’t, regardless of how much data is involved or whether a box was ticked.

The sentence Ananya could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: personalisation stays helpful exactly as long as the data keeps moving inside the norms of the relationship the customer believes they’re in; the moment it crosses into a use, an audience, or a purpose that relationship never implied, the identical data makes the product feel like surveillance. Nothing about the data itself changes. What changes is whether the flow matches the story the customer has in their head about who they’re dealing with.

Exhibit 1. Contextual integrity names five variables in every information flow. Change the recipient or the transmission principle — even while the subject and the raw data stay identical — and the same flow can flip from expected to violating.

How the check actually runs

In practice, a product team applying contextual integrity works through four steps, and the two that get skipped under deadline pressure are the ones that matter most. First, name the context precisely: not “fintech app” but the specific relationship the customer signed up for — here, a budgeting and savings tool, which carries banking-adjacent norms of confidentiality. Second, name the actual recipient, including every internal team and any vendor the data will touch, not just the customer-facing feature. Third — the step most often skipped — state the transmission principle in words a customer would recognise, such as “used only to power the nudge you see in this screen” versus “used to build a profile that may inform other products.” Fourth, check the resulting flow against the norms of the named context, not against what is technically permitted by the OS or the fine print.

Run Vittam Nudge through this. For the first data layer — a customer’s own transaction tags and stated budgets, used only to power a nudge inside the app — the subject, sender, recipient, information type and transmission principle all sit inside the banking-adjacent context the customer signed up for. Nothing about it would surprise a reasonable Vittam user. For the second layer, the recipient is the same model, but the information type (installed-app list, used to infer pregnancy, job change or debt distress) and the transmission principle (repurposing a phone-level signal collected for something else, unstated at the point of collection) sit outside any context the onboarding flow described. That is the entire mechanical test: not how much data, not whether a permission dialog was technically shown, but whether the flow as executed matches the flow the customer would say they agreed to if you asked them in plain language.

The arithmetic Ananya’s team actually ran

Before the board meeting, Ananya asked the growth and legal teams to price both versions of Nudge, not just describe them. The baseline: of Vittam’s 4.2 million MAU, 6% converted to the paid tier, Vittam Plus, at ₹999 a year — 252,000 payers, ₹25.17 crore in annual subscription revenue. The team modelled two scenarios for Nudge, shown in Exhibit 2.

Modelled churn cost / yr
(3.1% of MAU × ₹410 blended ARPU, Scenario B only)		–₹0–₹5.34 crore
Net, as modelled+₹5.40 crore+₹4.69 crore

Exhibit 2. Both scenarios clear as net-positive on the spreadsheet the growth team brought into the room. Scenario B looks almost as good as Scenario A once churn is netted out — which is exactly the trap: the churn line only prices the customers who noticed and left within the model’s window.

Run the second pass, changing one input: replace the modelled churn rate with what actually happened at a comparable Indian lending app in 2025, where a similar installed-app-based inference leaked into a press report. Complaint volume did not rise by 3.1% — it rose sharply within one product cycle, and the effect showed up not as a spike in that quarter’s churn but as a persistently lower opt-in rate on every subsequent feature for the following three quarters, because customers who did not leave nonetheless stopped trusting new asks for data. Model that drag conservatively at even half a percentage point of lost conversion on Vittam’s next four feature launches, each roughly the size of Nudge, and Scenario B’s ₹4.69 crore “net positive” turns into a multi-year loss before accounting for the separate, non-probabilistic exposure under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: using data collected for one stated purpose to build an undisclosed inference is a purpose-limitation breach the Data Protection Board of India does not average into anyone’s spreadsheet.

The spreadsheet cannot tell the difference between a customer who left and a customer who stayed but stopped trusting you — and the second group is always larger, and always shows up later, in a different feature’s numbers.

Seven distinctions worth sitting with

Personalisation is not targeting

Personalising an experience a customer already invited you into — showing budgeting nudges inside a budgeting app — is a different act from targeting them elsewhere with an inference drawn from that data, such as serving an ad on a different app because Vittam guessed they’re job-hunting. Teams routinely defend the second by pointing to comfort with the first.

Volume is not the variable

A single, well-placed inference — correctly guessing a customer is pregnant before she has told her own parents — can violate context far more sharply than a large volume of mundane transaction history ever would. Contextual integrity asks about fit, not bytes; a small amount of out-of-context data can feel like more surveillance than a large amount of in-context data.

Consent collected is not consent understood

DPDP’s notice-and-consent architecture, built around specified purposes and consent managers, produces a defensible audit trail. It does not prove the customer connected the dots between an install-time OS permission and a life-stage profile built six months later. A signature is evidence of process, not evidence that the norm was actually accepted.

Matching a norm is not the same as the norm being fair

Contextual integrity is descriptive, not moral: it tells you whether a flow matches existing expectations, not whether those expectations are themselves defensible. Insurers have historically “expected” to ask questions that function as proxies for protected categories. “This matches what people expect” is a data point for a product team, never the end of the ethical conversation.

The line moves — in both directions

Location-based recommendations felt invasive in 2011 and unremarkable by 2020; habituation genuinely shifts norms. But the same drift can reverse overnight: one high-profile leak or regulatory action can make an entire data category feel like surveillance again for an entire market, not just the company involved. Build as if the norm you’re relying on could snap back.

It prices no downstream trust decay

Contextual integrity tells you a flow violates a norm. It does not tell you what that violation costs in the following four quarters, spread thinly across every future opt-in rate. That number has to be modelled separately, with humility about how bad the estimate probably is, and modelled before shipping, not discovered after.

The sharpest violations are usually about the recipient, not the depth

A first-party team knowing a customer more deeply, inside the relationship the customer signed up for, is rarely the trigger. A previously unpictured recipient — an ad network, a data broker, an affiliated lender — receiving accurate data is what breaks contextual integrity fastest, because the subject never modelled that party as part of the relationship at all.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace, and scale

Exhibit 3. The five variables stay the same across product types; what changes is which one is hardest to pin down — the recipient in B2B, the subject’s awareness in marketplaces.

In consumer products like Vittam Money, the context is usually singular and named at signup, which makes violations relatively easy for a customer to spot and articulate. In B2B and enterprise tools — imagine Vittam later selling a spending-pattern analytics layer to employers for expense-policy design — the person whose data flows (the employee) is not the person who agreed to the deal (the employer), and the relevant norms come from employment law and workplace expectations, not consumer banking. In marketplaces, two contexts sit on one data pipe: a flow that is perfectly normal from the seller’s side (seeing aggregated buyer demand patterns) can be a surveillance violation from the buyer’s side if they never pictured a seller seeing their individual browsing. Stage matters too: an early-stage Vittam with 50,000 users could have shipped Scenario B quietly, with no press attention and easy reversal; at 4.2 million users and ahead of a Series C, the identical practice is a headline waiting to happen. The norm hasn’t moved. The visibility and the stakes have.

Four mistakes, and how to catch them cheaply

Treating legal sign-off as ethical sign-off. The symptom is a team saying “privacy reviewed this, we’re fine,” when what was reviewed was regulatory exposure, not customer expectation. The cheapest catch: have a support agent read the feature’s plain-language description to five real customers cold, and watch their faces.

Benchmarking against competitors instead of your own promise. The symptom is “X app does this too.” The underlying error treats context as generic to an industry rather than specific to what your own onboarding copy promised. Pull that copy and check the data use against it directly.

Mistaking a buried toggle for informed consent. The symptom is shipping a sensitive inference behind an opt-out three screens deep and calling it optional. Check the number of users who have ever visited that settings screen — it is almost always under 2%, which tells you what the toggle really is.

Measuring lift without measuring the backlash it produces. The symptom is a dashboard that tracks conversion but not complaint or unsubscribe rate for the same cohort, on the same chart. Put both lines on one graph before shipping; if they rise together, that is the line being crossed in real time.

What good looked like, eighteen months earlier

Vittam had already done this correctly once. In early 2024 the team launched Spend Alerts, a feature that told customers, at the moment they overspent a self-set category budget, exactly why: “Because you tagged this ₹640 order as Dining on 14 March.” Every input was something the customer had typed themselves; the transmission principle was stated at the point of use, not buried in onboarding; and the alert carried a one-tap “stop showing me this” control that worked instantly, not a settings-menu toggle. Unsubscribe from the alert itself ran near 9% — unremarkable — while a follow-up trust survey put Vittam at 4.4 out of 5 on “this app explains itself,” the highest of any feature the company had shipped. Nothing about Spend Alerts required inference beyond what the customer had already told Vittam, and nothing about it needed a customer to imagine a use they hadn’t pictured. That was the version of personalisation contextual integrity predicts will hold up, and it did.

What Ananya decided

Ananya took Scenario A into the board meeting and shelved Scenario B, not indefinitely, but pending a redesigned consent flow that named the installed-app signal and its purpose explicitly at the moment of collection, and a review against DPDP’s purpose-limitation requirement with Karthik’s team. Her reasoning to the board was arithmetic before it was ethical: Scenario A’s ₹5.40 crore net was smaller than Scenario B’s ₹4.69 crore but real and durable, while Scenario B’s number depended on a churn model that, by the team’s own admission, could only price the customers who left loudly, not the much larger number who would quietly trust Vittam less with every feature that followed. The next things on Ananya’s reading list were the DPDP Act’s consent-manager provisions in detail, since Vittam would need one regardless, and memory and personalisation design in AI copilots, since Vittam’s own roadmap included a conversational assistant that would make dozens of these context judgments per day, silently, unless someone designed it not to.

Two questions worth sitting with:

When a company and its customers genuinely disagree about what a relationship implies, whose expectation should govern — and does that answer change once the data volume gets large enough to move a stock price?

If a data flow is fully legal but still violates contextual integrity, who inside a product organisation is supposed to be the one who says no — and what happens to that person’s incentives the quarter growth misses target?
