Gochara Technologies: One Profile, Many Purposes

A case for discussion. Gochara Technologies Private Limited is fictional; the brands, regulators and institutions around it are not.

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

At 10.40 p.m. on Sunday, 25 October 2026, Nandana Yashopadhyay had four documents open and could not get them to agree. The board of Gochara Technologies met at 11 the next morning in Bengaluru, two floors above the desk that would spend the week loading Diwali offers for 41,000 outlets. Diwali fell on 8 November and the freeze ran from 1 to 23 November, so whatever the board decided, nothing would be built for three weeks.

The first was a letter from Gaveshan Finserve Private Limited, dated 12 October, seeking written confirmation, by 6 November, of the lawful basis on which Gochara supplied its monthly audience segments. The renewal behind it was worth ₹32.0 crore over twenty-four months from 1 January 2027, against ₹14.6 crore in the year just closed.

The second was a note from the Data Protection Board of India, received 2 October, seeking information about a complaint from a user in Pune who had asked on 11 August for erasure, been told it was done, and seen her number go out again in the segment refresh of 1 September. The third was a memo from Toronto, four pages long, about a hash.

The fourth was her own deck, with four options on slide nine and a slide ten she had written and deleted twice. As chief product officer she owned the consent screen, the identity graph and the data product on top of it; she had joined in 2019 and had argued for three of the decisions now constraining her.

2. The company, and the decision of October 2021

Gochara was founded in Bengaluru in March 2017 to run loyalty programmes for retailers who could not build their own. By 2026 it ran white-label programmes for eleven mid-market chains — supermarkets, a pharmacy chain, a fashion retailer, a fuel-station network — and a consumer app in which a shopper saw all her programmes in one place. Revenue reached ₹286.0 crore in the year to 31 March 2026 (Exhibit 1).

The decision that shaped everything else was taken on 1 October 2021, when Gochara shipped "One Profile". Before it, a chain record and an app account were separate rows in separate stores; after it both resolved to one identity keyed to her mobile number, under a single consent covering programme delivery, personalisation and partner offers. Nirmalya Yoganandi, the co-founder who built it, called the merge a removal of duplication. It also removed the boundary between the data Gochara holds for the chains, as their agreements describe it, and the data it holds for itself under its own notice. Three years of events now sit in one append-only store in Singapore, authorised by the 2021 text.

3. The industry

Loyalty in India divides on who can afford to own it. Tata Neu, Reliance Retail and Flipkart run their estates in-house, Zepto and Swiggy theirs inside their apps, and PhonePe and Paytm see spend without the basket. The mid-market cannot build any of it, and that is Gochara's market: SKU-level baskets from 41,000 outlets resolved to one identity, in a country where UPI has made a mobile number the practical primary key for commerce.

Two forces press on that position. The first is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, whose Rules were notified in November 2025 with a phased runway; Gochara's external counsel reads the notice, consent and rights obligations as biting from mid-May 2027 and has declined to put the reading in writing. The second is ONDC, which lets a chain reach shoppers without an intermediary holding the graph at all. Gulfline Group FZ-LLC, a Dubai supermarket operator, is the largest single programme, contracted at ₹24.0 crore over the thirty-six months from 1 January 2027; on 14 October its legal team asked for a UAE-resident copy of its programme data.

4. The situation in detail: what was written down, and when

Figure 1 gives the dates.

On 1 August 2023 Gochara opened a separate register, Gochara Teen, for shoppers aged 13 to 17, verified by a parent's mobile number, and on 1 March 2024 added an optional date-of-birth field to ordinary signup; 61.0 lakh of the 113.0 lakh accounts opened since have filled it (Exhibit 2). There is no age field for the 186.0 lakh opened between October 2021 and February 2024, nor for the 42.0 lakh opened before them.

In February 2026 the growth team circulated a note stating that 92.0 per cent of users had consented to partner offers. On 5 October external counsel recomputed it on the registered base, and on 6 October Nilratan Yugdhar recomputed it on a stricter test. Exhibit 3 holds all three.

Between 14 March and 11 June 2026 — ninety days — a crash-reporting SDK in the Android app transmitted screen titles, the retailer name and an unsalted SHA-256 hash of the mobile number to the vendor's servers in the United States. The request log retains thirty days, so only 13 May to 11 June can be reconstructed: 2.14 crore screen events from 58.3 lakh devices, 3.67 per device. On 18 June the internal assessment logged no personal data, on the ground that the number was hashed. The Toronto memo of 9 October observes that Indian mobile numbers begin with 6, 7, 8 or 9, so an unsalted hash of a ten-digit number has 400 crore candidates, and that Neelabja Yotibarua's team enumerated it against 50,000 sample hashes in four hours on one machine.

The Pune request of 11 August was closed on 19 August; closing means a tombstone in the serving layer (Exhibit 4). The Singapore store is append-only with thirty-six-month retention, the Toronto snapshots are kept eighteen months, and the 1 September segment refresh is generated from a snapshot.

5. The people

Nandana Yashopadhyay, 41, chief product officer, Bengaluru. Position: the board needs one answer on Monday, not a programme. Incentive: her FY27 bonus is weighted 40 per cent to Signal revenue. Not saying: she signed off the February note without asking which base it used.

Nirmalya Yoganandi, 47, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune, who built One Profile. Position: re-consent is a screen problem; the real problem is the data model. Incentive: a rebuild he lacks the people for would be led by someone else. Not saying: he has known since a 2023 spike failed that the event store cannot delete at row level.

Nilratan Yugdhar, 52, general counsel and data protection officer, Mumbai, joined February 2025. Position: consent for one purpose cannot be stretched to another, and grandfathering will not survive a question from the Board. Incentive: he is the named officer. Not saying: counsel gave him two readings of the runway; he circulated the later one.

Nikhilesh Yatinath, 44, president of partnerships, Jersey City, carrying Gaveshan, Gulfline and the brand subscriptions. Position: the Gaveshan covenant is met on the pilot's own numbers. Incentive: his commission on the renewal is the largest item in his FY27 plan. Not saying: Gaveshan's procurement head told him on 15 October that a cohort-only feed would price forty per cent lower.

Neelabja Yotibarua, 36, principal data scientist, Toronto. Position: the company argues about a screen while its snapshots hold erased users and an unknown number of minors. Incentive: Signal pays for her team. Not saying: two production models were trained on a snapshot holding devices from the SDK window up to that snapshot’s own date.

Navonil Yamidutta, 39, customer success lead, Singapore, who owns the chains and Gulfline. Position: the chains must be told before anything changes. Incentive: four chain renewals fall in Q4 FY27. Not saying: two chains have asked in writing whether Gochara is processor or fiduciary; he has answered neither.

Nirav Yuvasen, 33, design lead, Berlin, four and a half hours behind IST since the clocks went back that morning, and author of the July pilot. Position: it measured tolerance for an interruption, not a preference about data. Incentive: a granular screen is his team's largest work this year. Not saying: its dismiss control was styled as the primary button for six days.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 3 is one quantity measured three ways, each naming its population and the date it was counted.

The pilot in Exhibit 5 was run to price Option A. It produced two retention figures from the same hundred thousand accounts, and Nikhilesh Yatinath and Nilratan Yugdhar quote different ones.

7. Voices

“The covenant needs 180.0 lakh. Take the 37,800 who kept it over the 61,400 who answered, apply that to 298.6 lakh, and you get 183.8. We clear it by nearly four lakh records and I would sign that letter tomorrow.”

Nikhilesh Yatinath, e-mail to Nandana, 13 October, 21.14 IST

“On the other reading it is 112.9 lakh. You cannot count a person who swiped a card away as having agreed. And the letter Gaveshan wants is about basis, not volume.”

Nilratan Yugdhar, reply on the same thread, 14 October, 07.02 IST

“Four options and all four end at a screen. C touches the data model, at the wrong end. Nobody has priced what it costs to make the store forget.”

Nirmalya Yoganandi, comment on slide nine, 23 October

“Two production models were trained on the May snapshot. I can tell you how many of the devices in it fall inside the SDK window up to its date. I cannot tell you how many are thirteen-year-olds: the field arrived in March 2024 and we never asked the 228 lakh who registered before it.”

Neelabja Yotibarua, memo of 9 October 2026

“Two of my chains have written to ask whether you are their processor or your own fiduciary. They ask because their lawyers cannot tell from your notice, and mine cannot either.”

Navonil Yamidutta, call with Nandana, 20 October, 09.30 SGT

8. The options as Nandana sees them

Option A. A purpose-wise consent screen to all 341.0 lakh accounts: build in December and January, waves through February and March, complete by 20 March 2027, direct cost ₹8.76 crore. It does not change what the event store retains and creates no age field for the 186.0 lakh accounts without one.

Option B. The same screen to new signups only, from February 2027, leaving the existing base on the 2021 and 2019 notices: ₹3.00 crore over 29.0 lakh signups. Counsel has two readings of whether a notice in force at signup still supports a purpose after the Rules commence; Nilratan has circulated one.

Option C. Supply nothing addressable to an individual: Signal becomes cohort statistics with a floor of 5,000 members, built in ten weeks, effect in the window ₹15.34 crore of which ₹13.44 crore is revenue. It leaves the consent text, the identity graph, the Teen register and the snapshots as they are.

Option D. Rebuild consent as artefacts a registered consent manager can read and revoke: nine months from 1 December 2026, the whole fourteen-person squad plus four contractors, finishing 31 August 2027, effect in the window ₹15.20 crore. The Gulfline rollout moves to 1 July 2027, and the UAE-resident copy requested on 14 October is outside the scope as drafted.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at 11 a.m. on Monday, 26 October 2026, and Gaveshan wants its letter by 6 November. The freeze runs 1 to 23 November, leaving ten clear engineering months inside the twelve-month window, so nothing starts before 1 December. The data-platform squad is fourteen engineers across Bengaluru and Pune, and Gochara has never recruited more than six in a quarter. Cash at 30 September was ₹118.0 crore and the FY27 plan carries ₹9.0 crore of unallocated change budget, which covers the direct cost of A, B or C but not D's ₹11.20 crore. The eleven chain agreements name Gochara as processor for programme data and are silent on the merged graph. Counsel's later reading puts the notice, consent and rights obligations at mid-May 2027. Nilratan's memo of 6 October states that the Act's schedule of penalties runs to ₹250 crore for a failure of security safeguards and ₹200 crore for obligations concerning children, and that both are ceilings rather than tariffs.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 3 states one quantity three ways. For each reading, say what question it answers and what it cannot answer; then say which you would put before the board, and what you would say about the other two.
  2. Exhibit 2 holds a date of birth for 61.0 lakh of the 113.0 lakh accounts opened since 1 March 2024, none for the 186.0 lakh opened between October 2021 and February 2024, and none for the 42.0 lakh before October 2021, the Teen register apart. What can Gochara establish today about the ages of those cohorts, and what would it have to do to establish more?
  3. Exhibit 5 yields two retention figures from the same 1,00,000 accounts. What measurement would separate them, and what in the pilot's design prevents it being made now?
  4. The chains' agreements call Gochara their processor; Gochara's notice treats app users as its own; and Figure 2 puts both in one identity graph. Work through Exhibit 6: which options change that, which do not, and what does each leave the chains and Gulfline carrying?
  5. Exhibit 6 prices four responses over one window. Which exposures described elsewhere does it not price, and how would you put a number on the two you judge most material?
  6. It is Monday morning. What do you do, in what order, in the first week; what do you say to the board; and what do you tell them you do not know?

11. Later that night

At 1.20 a.m. Nandana reopened the February note and set the two later recomputations beside it. She wrote three sentences for slide ten, deleted two, and could not decide which two. Toronto was still working; Neelabja's status line said re-running the enumeration against a fresh sample. The deck was due with the company secretary at nine, and outside the operations floor was lit, loading Diwali offers against a notice written in 2021.

Gochara, Gaveshan Finserve, Gulfline Group and all individuals named here are fictional. Brands, regulators and institutions named as market context are real and are not parties to these events.

Data, Consent and the DPDP Act

What India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 actually obliges a product to do — the seams where competent teams get it wrong, and the questions the law has not settled.

Two decisions, three weeks apart

On 4 September 2026, Aparna Godbole, chief product officer of Pukaar Voice Cloud, sat in a Bengaluru meeting room with a slide her head of machine learning had titled, without irony, "The corpus is right there." Pukaar transcribes and scores about 2.4 crore contact-centre calls a month for forty enterprise clients — two private banks, a general insurer, a large e-commerce operator, a tail of BPOs. Fine-tuning Pukaar's own Indic speech model on that traffic would cut word-error rate on Hindi–English code-switching from 22% to roughly 14%, worth a costed ₹40 crore a year.

The obstacle was not technical. For every one of those calls Pukaar was a Data Processor, working on its clients' instructions, for its clients' purposes, under a master services agreement; the callers were the banks' customers. Training Pukaar's own model was a new purpose, chosen by Pukaar for Pukaar — and for that purpose Pukaar would be a Data Fiduciary, needing a lawful basis it did not have and could not easily get, having no relationship with the several crore people in the corpus. Thirty-seven of forty contracts permitted use of "de-identified data to improve the services"; the three that did not were the largest. The board met on 30 September.

Five days later in Pune, Rustom Daruwala, head of product at Jugnu Home Systems, faced a harder version with less room. Jugnu makes connected air and water purifiers: 6.8 lakh installed units, a companion app, a filter subscription. The next model, frozen for manufacture on 20 October, carried an always-on particulate sensor and a wake word. Three uses were on the roadmap — streaming room telemetry to predict filter life, selling a neighbourhood air-quality index to a property portal, and keeping the device working after the app was uninstalled. Consent would be captured once, on one phone, by whoever did the setup. The device would then sense a room holding that person's spouse, parents, staff and children, none of whom had been asked anything, and it had no screen on which any of them could withdraw.

Both decisions turn on the same statute, and neither is answered by reading the consent screen.

The idea, stated precisely

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 received assent on 11 August 2023. It is a short, duty-imposing statute built on four roles. Personal data is any data about an individual identifiable by or in relation to it — no carve-out for "non-sensitive" data, no special-category regime. Processing is a wholly or partly automated operation on digital personal data; paper enters only once digitised. A Data Principal is the individual. A Data Fiduciary determines purpose and means; the word comes from trust law and Jack Balkin's "information fiduciaries," and its consequence is that its duties survive delegation. A Data Processor works on instructions under contract.

Section 4 states the rule: process only for a lawful purpose, and only with consent or under a "certain legitimate use" listed in Section 7. Section 3 sets the reach — processing in India, and processing abroad connected with offering goods or services to Data Principals in India. That limb is narrower than the GDPR's, which also catches monitoring of behaviour; a foreign firm profiling Indians without offering them anything sits, on the text, outside Section 3(b).

The Act exists because its predecessor did almost nothing: Section 43A of the IT Act, 2000 and the 2011 SPDI Rules reached only "sensitive" data, were contractual, created no erasure or access right, and were barely enforced. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) held informational privacy a fundamental right; the Srikrishna Committee's 2018 report supplied the fiduciary framing; a 2019 Bill went to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, which in 2021 returned a longer text reaching non-personal data; that was withdrawn; a shorter draft introduced "deemed consent"; and the 2023 Act replaced it with the closed Section 7 list.

Four schools, and what each will actually sign

Disagreement here is less about the text than about whether consent is the right organising idea at all.

Table 1 — The four camps, as propositions each would and would not endorse.
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Consent and control (Srikrishna report)"A revocable, freely given authorisation is the only legitimate default for commercial processing.""Consent fatigue means consent should give way to accountability."
Accountability and harms (Matthan, Beyond Consent)"At scale consent shifts risk to the party least able to price it; hold fiduciaries answerable for outcomes.""Data should be saleable as property."
Techno-legal (DEPA, Account Aggregator)"Consent becomes real when machine-readable, granular and revocable through a Section 6(7) Consent Manager.""Consent is unfixable."
Civil-liberties critique"An executive-appointed Board, wide Section 17(2) exemptions and the Section 44(3) RTI amendment discipline firms, not the State.""The Act's brevity is a virtue."

Aparna's ML lead belongs unwittingly to the second camp: nobody is harmed by a better acoustic model, so consent is ceremony. Rustom's general counsel is a first-camp purist. The statute adopts neither cleanly.

Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice does not begin at the consent screen. It begins with a matrix — one row per data element, one column per purpose — because every obligation is expressed per-purpose and none can be discharged without knowing which purpose a field serves. Section 5 requires an itemised notice of the data and the specific purpose, how to exercise the Section 11–13 rights, and how to complain to the Board. Section 6 requires consent free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, by clear affirmative action, limited to data necessary for that purpose. Section 8(7) requires erasure on withdrawal or once the purpose is served, unless another law compels retention. "Specific purpose" is the pivot for all three.

Drawing the map produces a second-order effect teams rarely anticipate: purpose granularity has an interior optimum. Coarse purposes — "to improve our services" — collect easily and cannot survive a necessity test. Fine purposes are defensible but multiply the consent surface, and fourteen toggles yield consent specific in form and uninformed in substance, failing Section 6 on another limb. The working rule is to name the smallest set of purposes a user would answer differently.

The second move is to cost the exposure rather than fear it. The Schedule caps penalties per contravention: up to ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards, ₹200 crore for failing to notify a breach, ₹200 crore for breaching the children's obligations in Section 9, ₹150 crore for the extra Significant Data Fiduciary duties, and up to ₹50 crore residually. These are ceilings, not tariffs: Section 33(2) directs the Board to weigh gravity, duration, repetition, gain made or loss avoided, and mitigation.

Table 2 — Jugnu's annualised exposure model, built before the October freeze. The probabilities are the team's own estimates, documented as such.
FailureP(surfaces)P(adverse)PenaltyExpected/yr
Telemetry breached at the cloud tier0.080.55₹22 cr₹0.97 cr
Breach not notified in the prescribed window0.080.70₹14 cr₹0.78 cr
Air index re-identified to a household0.150.45₹9 cr₹0.61 cr
Wake word captures a child; §9 claim0.050.60₹30 cr₹0.90 cr
No withdrawal path on a screenless device0.300.50₹4 cr₹0.60 cr

What changed Rustom's mind was the arithmetic under the first row, not the penalty column. One reading a minute from 6.8 lakh devices is 6,80,000 × 1,440 ≈ 9.79 crore rows a day, every one personal data because every one carries a device identifier tied to an account. Computing filter-life features on-device and sending one summary every six hours gives 27.2 lakh rows a day, a 97.2% reduction. What mattered was not the storage saving but that the erasure surface for a Section 12 request fell from eleven systems to three, dropping the table's first two rows by an order of magnitude for nine engineer-weeks of firmware work.

On the Rules. The Act is in force; its operative detail sits in subordinate rules. MeitY published a draft on 3 January 2025, and rules were subsequently notified with a phased commencement over roughly eighteen months, so as this is written in September 2026 some obligations are live and others are approaching. Read the notified text and the commencement schedule, not a summary. A figure such as the 72-hour window for detailed breach intimation to the Board is the draft's, cited for the shape of the obligation rather than as operative text.

When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Five claims settle whether an activity sits inside this statute, and each can be tested rather than argued. First: is it digital personal data about an identifiable individual? For Pukaar, yes — a voice identifies even after names are redacted, which is why the embedding in Figure 1 is not derived-and-therefore-safe. For Jugnu the answer is more instructive: a particulate reading is not personal data, but one carrying a device identifier bound to an account holder is. The claim is about the record, not the measurement.

Second: for this purpose, do you determine means and ends? Role is per-purpose, not per-company: Pukaar is a Processor on four edges and a Fiduciary on two, simultaneously, for the same bytes. Third: does Section 3 reach it? Jugnu's pipeline ran in a Singapore region, which Section 16 permits unless that destination is notified as restricted — but Section 16(2) preserves any stricter Indian rule, which is where a lender, not Jugnu, meets the Reserve Bank's 2018 payment-data storage directive.

Fourth: does an exemption apply? Section 17(2)(b) exempts processing for research, archiving or statistical purposes where no decision specific to a Principal is taken and prescribed standards are met. Aparna's team wanted this to cover model training. It is a poor fit: building a commercial model for sale is not comfortably "research," and an exemption that would render the statute inoperative if generalised is one you are misreading. Fifth: does a Section 7 legitimate use cover it? Section 7 is a closed list — data voluntarily provided for an evident purpose, State functions, legal obligations and court orders, medical emergencies, disasters, and employment purposes. It is not a balancing test: India has no analogue of the GDPR's "legitimate interests," so "the benefit outweighs the intrusion" imports a test Parliament declined to enact.

The frame misleads in three situations: when a team treats anonymisation as a safe harbour, which the Act neither defines nor grants; when it treats the Act as a security standard, so that an ISO 27001 certificate is read as evidence of lawful basis; and when it assumes symmetry with the GDPR and expects a private right of action. There is none. Individuals complain to the Data Protection Board, penalties go to the Consolidated Fund, appeals lie to the Appellate Tribunal. Exposure is regulatory and reputational, not a class action — which changes how the risk is priced and explains why some boards under-invest.

The hard cases, and what mature companies actually do

The genuinely difficult questions appear at organisational seams rather than inside features. In a multi-product group, consent collected by one entity does not travel to a sibling that sets its own purposes, and the Section 17(1)(d) exemption for a court-approved merger is narrower than corporate development hopes. In a two-sided marketplace, the platform must decide, purpose by purpose, whether it is Fiduciary for the buyer's address disclosed to a seller or merely the channel through which the buyer consents to that seller. In regulated sectors, rules stack: a lender's Section 8(7) erasure duty collides with the Reserve Bank's retention norms, and the resolution is to document which rule compels which column for how long.

Hardware plus software produced the problem Rustom could not design away. Consent from one household member cannot be free, specific or informed for the others in the room, and the Act offers no household-agent doctrine. No consent architecture fixes this; only minimisation does. AI-native products add a problem the statute does not address: erasing personal data from a training corpus is straightforward, erasing it from model weights is not, and machine unlearning is a research area rather than a deployable control. Mature teams keep the corpus separately deletable, retrain on a fixed cadence so deletions propagate within a stated window, and tell users that window instead of implying instant forgetting.

Internal seams are where damage usually starts: an advertising pixel firing on a page that also carries KYC fields, a notebook holding a six-month-old copy of production, a support agent pasting a customer's chat into a public chatbot. What mature companies say they do is annual privacy training. What the good ones do is narrower: tag every warehouse column with its justifying purpose and fail the build on an untagged column, keep an egress allowlist so a new SDK cannot ship unreviewed, and sample live records quarterly, asking which notice line authorises each field.

Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1"Free" is a claim about the counterfactual, not the wording. The tell-tale is an opt-out that exists on the screen but not in the product: switch it off and the app refuses to work. Section 6 judges necessity against the service provided, not the business model, so a separate toggle does not cure bundling if declining it still costs the user what they came for.

2Withdrawal does not oblige you to keep serving the withdrawn purpose. Section 6(5) puts the consequences of withdrawal on the Principal. Teams read this backwards, conclude that anyone who withdraws must still get the whole product, and then resist building withdrawal at all. The correct design degrades precisely: what depended on the withdrawn processing stops, the rest continues, and the user is told which.

3A client's instruction cannot manufacture a basis the client never had. The tell-tale is a clause warranting that the customer "has obtained all necessary consents." It allocates commercial risk between two companies and does nothing for the Data Principal or for the question of who chose the purpose. Pukaar's thirty-seven permissive contracts were worth something in a dispute and nothing on whether the callers had agreed.

4Anonymisation is an evidentiary burden, not a status. The Act grants no safe harbour and prescribes no technique, so the expert asks for the re-identification test result rather than for the word "aggregated" in a design document. Jugnu ran the test: at 250-metre cells and hourly buckets, 61% of populated cells held fewer than five devices. The index died on that number, not on an opinion.

5The children's provisions are prohibitions, not defaults you can consent past. Section 9 requires verifiable parental consent under eighteen and separately forbids tracking, behavioural monitoring and advertising targeted at children. The tell-tale is "we have parental consent, so retargeting is fine": that answers the first limb and is irrelevant to the second. The Government may exempt classes by notification, so the boundary moves by notification, not interpretation.

6Significant Data Fiduciary status is conferred, not crossed. Section 10's criteria include volume and sensitivity of data, risk to Principals, and risk to India's sovereignty and to electoral democracy, so a modest platform with political salience can be designated before a larger, duller one. The tell-tale is "we're not an SDF yet" used to skip impact assessments; a DPO and an audit trail take months, the notification none.

7Notice language is a compliance surface, not a localisation nicety. Section 5(3) entitles the Principal to the notice in English or any Eighth Schedule language. The tell-tale is an English-only consent flow in a product whose analytics show seventy per cent of sessions in Hindi or Tamil: cheap to fix, and evidence that nobody read Section 5 past its first sub-section.

8The consent record and consent enforcement are different systems, and usually only one is built. The tell-tale is that marketing can pull an audience from the warehouse without joining the consent table, meaning the record exists, is accurate, and governs nothing. An expert's first diagnostic at a new company is therefore not "show me the consent screen" but "show me a query that would fail if a user withdrew."

How the practice differs by product and by stage

Some variation here is real and some is folklore. The notice obligation and the security duty do not scale down: a seed-stage app owes the same Section 5 notice and the same reasonable safeguards as a listed company. Section 17(4) does empower the Government to notify classes of Fiduciaries, expressly including startups, to whom Sections 5, 8(3), 8(7), 10 and 11 will not apply — but that is an enabling power exercised by notification, so the founder's question is whether their class has actually been notified, not whether they feel small.

Table 3 — Where the obligation really changes shape, and where the difference is asserted more than it is real.
Product typeWhere it really differsWhere it does not
Consumer appOwns the consent UX, rights desk and grievance channel; opt-in rate is a product metricSecurity duty, breach notification, erasure discipline
B2B / enterprise SaaSUsually a Processor; burden shifts to the processing agreement and audit rightsFlips to Fiduciary once it processes for its own purpose
Platform / marketplaceAllocates Fiduciary status per purpose across independent businessesCannot contract away what it determined
Hardware + appWithdrawal must work without a screen or an appPersonal data is personal data on a device or in a region
AI-nativeCorpus provenance; erasure propagating through retrainingSection 7 still has no "we needed the data" ground

Stage changes three things. A pre-product-market-fit company can hold its purpose map in a spreadsheet and should, because tagging an empty schema costs nothing while retrofitting an undifferentiated user table at five lakh accounts costs quarters. A scaling company's binding constraint is the vendor estate. A designated Significant Data Fiduciary's constraint is evidentiary: it must demonstrate compliance to an independent auditor on demand, which almost nobody can retrofit quickly.

Three worked cases

Pukaar: buying the corpus rather than assuming it

Aparna abandoned the de-identification argument and built a contributing-tenant tier: a 12% discount on the per-minute rate for opting into model contribution, on condition that the client obtained its own customers' consent. Two banks could, their onboarding already naming service improvement as a separately-toggled purpose; most could not. Three of forty joined in the first quarter, contributing 94 lakh calls a month against the 2.4 crore on the original slide. Word-error rate fell from 22% to 16.5%, not 14%, and sales re-costed the opportunity at ₹31 crore. Seven engineer-weeks enforced a per-tenant eligibility flag at ingestion rather than at query time, so ineligible audio never entered the training bucket; the discount cost ₹2.4 crore a year. Pukaar bought roughly 65% of the gain for a fraction of the exposure.

Jugnu: minimisation as the cheaper control

Rustom shipped the on-device design, killed the neighbourhood index, and asked manufacturing for eleven extra days to add a recessed button that clears local state and disables the sensor — a withdrawal mechanism that works for the grandmother who never installed the app. He also had the notice printed inside the box lid, with a QR code to Marathi, Hindi and English versions, because Section 5 requires notice at or before collection and the device begins sensing at first power-on, not at app install. Cost: ₹38 a unit, eleven days, ₹6 crore of foregone index revenue.

Khelghar Learning: where it went wrong, and what recovery cost

Khelghar Learning, a Hyderabad learning-games app with 18 lakh monthly actives and a median user age of nine, did what the consent school recommends and still failed, because consent was never the operative rule for its users. Growth ran on a refer-a-friend mechanic that uploaded the child's contact list; revenue ran on a third-party advertising SDK doing behavioural targeting, worth ₹7.2 crore a year, 61% of total. The parental-consent screen cured nothing: Section 9's prohibition on behavioural monitoring and advertising directed at children is not consent-able, the age gate was self-declared, and the SDK's own collection had never been inventoried.

Three warnings were visible for months — parents asking why their child saw advertisements for things the parent had browsed, a referral conversion rate implausible for a children's product, and a diligence pack listing four vendors where the binary contained eleven. Recovery took fourteen weeks: the SDK went, taking the ₹7.2 crore with it; monetisation moved to a paid family plan plus school-district licensing; referral was rebuilt on shareable codes; verifiable parental consent replaced self-declaration; and all 18 lakh accounts were re-noticed. Of those, 4.1 lakh parents responded and 3.3 lakh confirmed; the rest were suspended and deleted at the notice window's end, taking reported monthly actives to 5.9 lakh. Revenue fell 48% for two quarters, survivable only on sixteen months of runway. Against a Schedule exposure of up to ₹200 crore on the Section 9 limb, ₹7.2 crore had never been worth defending — but nobody had put those two numbers on one slide.

Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Table 4 — Recurring failures, the signal preceding each, and the cost of noticing late.
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Purpose driftA PRD saying "we already collect this"Which notice line authorises this use?Retrospective notice, a re-consent campaign, a shipped feature switched off
Processor becomes FiduciaryA roadmap item that benefits you, not the clientWho chose this purpose?A model with unusable provenance; renegotiation with every client
Anonymisation theatreA dashboard that filters down to n=3What is the smallest cell in the output?A launched product killed, as Jugnu's index nearly was
Consent recorded, not enforcedGrowth builds audiences without the consent tableShow me a query that fails when a user withdrawsEvery campaign sent since the record diverged
Unmapped vendor estateThe data map lists fewer vendors than the binary holdsWhat leaves the device, measured not documented?Breach duties for data you did not know you held
Erasure that deletes only the visible rowDeletion is one call to one serviceWhich systems still hold this person after 30 days?A rights request you cannot honour, in writing

In every row the early sign is cheap to observe and belongs to someone other than the legal team: purpose drift to whoever reviews PRDs, the vendor gap to whoever builds the app bundle, unenforced consent to whoever writes the marketing query. A programme routing these through an annual legal review sees none until they compound.

Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether consent works at population scale. The accountability school's evidence is strong: opt-in rates for anything genuinely optional cluster in the thirties, comprehension of notices is low in every study that has measured it, and Europe's cookie banners suggest granular consent at scale produces clicking rather than choosing. The consent school replies that outcome standards let firms decide what counts as harm — the delegation the fiduciary framing was meant to prevent — and that low opt-in rates show consent working. The first position fails if well-timed asks produce stable, informed opt-in; the second fails if withdrawal stays near zero even where surveyed users say they object.

Whether the negative-list transfer model protects Indians. Defenders say an adequacy regime would have bottlenecked every Indian startup behind a bureaucratic assessment of foreign jurisdictions, and that Section 16(2) lets sector regulators localise where it matters. Critics say the default is therefore free flow to jurisdictions with weaker protection and no onward-transfer discipline. Defenders would be wrong if data were routinely transferred where Indian Principals have no effective remedy; critics would be wrong if the notification power were used actively.

Whether the State exemptions are fatal. Section 17(2)(a) lets the Government exempt notified State instrumentalities from most of the Act, and Section 44(3) narrowed the RTI Act's personal-information exception. Critics read a law that binds companies and releases the country's largest data collector. Defenders answer that such exemptions exist in comparable regimes, are exercised by notification and therefore reviewable, and that Puttaswamy's proportionality test still constrains State action. The practical consequence is narrow but real: a government-linked data-sharing request is not automatically lawful.

Whether de-identified data may be used for model training. This is Aparna's question, and it is genuinely unsettled in India. One camp holds that a corpus stripped of direct identifiers is no longer personal data. The other holds that voice, text and behavioural traces are re-identifying by nature, that the Act's silence on anonymisation gives the first camp no foothold, and that Section 7 offers no training-data ground. There is as yet no Indian decision, guidance note or Board order resolving it. An expert states the uncertainty plainly and then decides how much of the company to stake on the optimistic reading — which, in practice, is the whole skill.

What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a consent screen and a policy document and can recite the four roles. Someone who has internalised it differs in four observable ways. They ask "for which purpose?" before anything else, because every duty is indexed to purpose. They treat the data map as a product artefact updated in the same pull request as the schema change, not a document legal refreshes annually. They price exposure rather than fearing it, putting the Schedule's caps and the revenue at stake on one slide, as Khelghar never did. And they are precise about uncertainty: where the Rules are still settling or no Indian authority has ruled, they say so, build to the stricter plausible reading, and record the reasoning so an auditor later sees a judgement made rather than a question avoided.

What they decided

On 30 September, Aparna recommended the contributing-tenant design and the board approved it with one amendment she had not proposed: the training-eligibility flag was to be auditable by any client on request, defensibility being now a sales asset rather than a cost. Rustom got his eleven days from manufacturing on 15 October, shipped the button and the box-lid notice, and told the property portal Jugnu would sell it nothing. Both cost real money — ₹9 crore of forecast revenue in one case, ₹6 crore and a schedule slip in the other. Neither was primarily a moral decision. Both rested on the conclusion that the cheapest control is to hold less data, and that a lawful basis you cannot state in one sentence is a basis you do not have.

For discussion

1. Pukaar's thirty-seven permissive contracts were worthless for the purpose the company most wanted. What would it have taken, when they were signed, for them to be worth something — and is that within a vendor's power?

2. Jugnu's reset button lets a household member who never consented stop the sensing. Does that discharge the obligation to that person, or merely mitigate a design that should not have shipped?

3. Khelghar's board saw the ₹7.2 crore of advertising revenue and never the ₹200 crore exposure. Whose job was it to put those on one slide, and what mechanism would have done it without a crisis?

Going deeper

Privacy by design — the discipline that makes these duties cheap rather than expensive; minimisation moved both protagonists' risk more than wording did.

Personalisation vs surveillance — once consent is clean: how much a product may infer before inference is itself the harm.

GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes — DPDP by contrast: legitimate interests, adequacy and private rights of action exist there, not here.

Consent flows and cookie UX — where Section 6 meets interface design, and where dark-pattern findings abroad preview "as easy to withdraw as to give."

Security compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001 — the evidence base for "reasonable security safeguards": necessary, insufficient for lawfulness.

Terms of service, SLAs and contracts — where Fiduciary and Processor duties are really allocated, years before the roadmap exists.

IP, patents and trademarks for PMs — who owns a model trained on someone else's data.

Open-source licences — obligations that travel with an artefact and cannot be cured after release.

Data, Consent and the DPDP Act

What India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act actually requires of a product — and why the checkbox is the least of it.

On the second Monday of September 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Bhrigu Finance, a Bengaluru-based digital lending app with 1.1 million active borrowers, sat with the company's newly hired data protection officer and a printed copy of the loan-onboarding screen. The screen had one checkbox: "I agree to Bhrigu's Terms, KYC verification, credit assessment, and to receive offers from Bhrigu and its lending partners." Ninety-six percent of applicants ticked it, mostly because there was no way to get the loan without ticking it. The DPO's question was simple: under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (the DPDP Act), was that one checkbox actually four separate acts of consent, bundled in a way the law does not allow? Bhrigu was two weeks from a board review of its Q3 numbers, and the marketing team's cross-sell pipeline — leads passed to partner insurers and wealth platforms — ran entirely off that checkbox. If Ananya unbundled it, the pipeline would shrink. If she didn't, and a regulator or an aggrieved borrower later complained, Bhrigu was looking at a law that lets the Data Protection Board of India impose penalties running into hundreds of crores of rupees for the wrong kind of mistake. She had until the board meeting to decide what the checkbox should say.

The idea

The DPDP Act, passed by Parliament and given presidential assent on 11 August 2023, is India's first comprehensive law governing how organisations may collect and use the personal data of individuals. It replaces a thin, decade-old set of IT Rules with a dedicated statute built around a small set of roles and a small set of obligations. The person whose data it is, is the Data Principal. The organisation that decides why and how that data is processed is the Data Fiduciary — a deliberate word choice: the Act treats holding someone's personal data as a position of trust, not simple ownership. A Data Processor is anyone the Fiduciary hires to process data on its behalf, under contract; the Fiduciary remains legally accountable regardless of who does the actual processing. The Act's core mechanism is that a Data Fiduciary may process personal data only for a lawful purpose, and lawful purpose almost always means one of two things: the Data Principal gave free, specific, informed consent for a stated purpose, or the processing falls within a short, enumerated list of "certain legitimate uses" that Parliament wrote into Section 7 (things like voluntarily provided data for an obvious purpose, employment-related processing, medical emergencies, or state functions). The problem this was invented to solve is the one every Indian product team already knew from experience: personal data — a name, a phone number, a PAN, a bank statement — moved through apps, aggregators and marketers with no consistent rule about whether the person had actually agreed, and no working mechanism for them to say no later. The single sentence Ananya could say in the board meeting without sounding glib: "Under the DPDP Act, consent is not a checkbox — it is a specific, informed, revocable authorisation tied to one stated purpose, and every use of a customer's data has to trace back to that purpose or to one of the law's narrow listed exceptions."

How it actually works

The mechanics start before any data is collected. Section 5 requires a Data Fiduciary to give the Data Principal an itemised notice, in clear language, stating what personal data will be collected and for what specific purpose, at or before the point of collection — not buried three screens deep in a privacy policy the person never opens. A serious product team writes two layers: a short, plain notice on the screen itself, and a longer policy one tap away. Only after notice comes consent, and the Act is specific about what counts: free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given through a clear affirmative action, and limited to the data necessary for the stated purpose. A proviso practitioners often skip matters most in practice: a request for consent cannot be made conditional on accepting processing that is not actually necessary for the goods or service being provided. That is the rule Ananya's checkbox was breaking: KYC and credit-assessment data are necessary to give someone a loan; passing their profile to insurance partners for marketing is not, so it cannot ride on the same tick mark. Once given, consent keeps processing inside the purpose it was given for — purpose limitation — and the Fiduciary must stop processing, and generally erase the data, once that purpose is served or consent withdrawn, subject to any longer retention a specific law requires. Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent was, through a comparably convenient means; it does not undo processing already done, only what comes next. The Act also creates an optional new institution, the Consent Manager — a registered, interoperable intermediary through which a person can see and manage every consent they've given across Fiduciaries in one place, modelled loosely on the RBI's Account Aggregator framework. At the time of Bhrigu's board meeting, that ecosystem existed but was still thin outside a few regulated financial-data use cases, so most consumer apps, Bhrigu included, were still collecting consent directly rather than through a Consent Manager.

A worked example

Ananya's team ran the numbers on two designs. The current, bundled flow produces near-universal but not-genuinely-free consent; a corrected, unbundled flow separates the mandatory KYC/credit-assessment consent from the optional marketing consent, defaulted to off. The immediate effect on the monthly marketing-eligible pool, out of 40,000 applications, is a straightforward multiplication.

Table 1 — Effect of unbundling consent on Bhrigu's monthly marketing pool (40,000 applications/month)
DesignMarketing opt-in rateMarketing-eligible recordsNote
Bundled checkbox (current)96%38,40040,000 × 0.96 — largely forced, not "free" consent under §6
Unbundled, default-off, at onboarding34%13,60040,000 × 0.34 — a genuine, separately-ticked opt-in
Unbundled, asked after first repayment52%14,56028,000 repayers (70% of 40,000) × 0.52

The first pass looks brutal: unbundling at onboarding cuts the eligible pool from 38,400 to 13,600, a drop of 24,800 records a month, or 64.6%. That is the number the marketing team led with. The second pass changes one input — timing, not wording. If the consent ask for marketing moves from the moment of loan approval, when the applicant is anxious and clicking through, to the moment after their first successful repayment, when 70% of the original cohort (28,000 people) are still active and have had a good experience with Bhrigu, the opt-in rate on that smaller, later base rises to 52%: 28,000 × 0.52 = 14,560 records — slightly more than the onboarding-unbundled figure, still well below the old bundled number, but composed entirely of people who chose it. The arithmetic told Ananya two things at once: the bundled number was never real demand, and a well-timed, honestly-asked consent recovers most of the addressable audience without breaking the law.

The nuances

1Consent is not the only lawful basis. Section 7's "certain legitimate uses" cover a specific, closed list — data voluntarily given for an obvious purpose, employment necessities, medical emergencies, disaster response, state functions, compliance with a court order, among others. It is not a general "legitimate interest" balancing test the way GDPR's Article 6(1)(f) is; a product manager cannot invoke it for something merely convenient, only for something the section actually names.

2Purpose limitation outlives the transaction. Consent for KYC is not a standing licence. Once the loan is disbursed or rejected and the purpose served, the default obligation is to stop processing and erase — a real tension for lenders, since RBI's own record-keeping norms require certain loan records be retained for years. A sector regulator's retention rule can override the default erasure duty, but every retained field then needs its own documented legal basis, not just "we might need it later."

3This is not GDPR with an Indian accent. The two laws share vocabulary but diverge in structure: DPDP uses a government-notified blacklist for cross-border transfer (data may leave India unless the destination is specifically restricted) rather than GDPR's adequacy regime; it has no separate "special category" data regime with its own stricter rules, though children's data gets distinct, stronger protection; and its lawful-basis list is shorter and more literal than GDPR's six grounds. Reading DPDP as "India's GDPR" leads people to assume protections the text does not contain, and to miss ones it does.

4Fiduciary accountability cannot be outsourced. Hiring a cloud vendor or an analytics platform as a Data Processor does not transfer legal responsibility. If the processor mishandles the data, the Fiduciary is still the party the Data Protection Board looks to, which is why data-processing agreements and vendor audits matter as much as the consent screen itself.

5Withdrawal has to be genuinely symmetrical. The Act requires withdrawing consent be at least as easy as giving it. A design where "agree" is one tap and "withdraw" requires an email to a support inbox is not a minor gap — it is very likely non-compliant on its face, and the kind of asymmetric UX regulators elsewhere have already called a dark pattern.

6Scale changes the obligation. The government can designate certain Fiduciaries as Significant Data Fiduciaries, based on volume and sensitivity of data processed or risk to India's sovereignty, triggering duties like an India-based Data Protection Officer, periodic impact assessments, and independent audits. Most early-stage products aren't there yet, but a fast-growing app should assume it eventually will be.

7The rulebook was still being completed. The Act itself is in force, but operative details — exact breach-notification timelines, the technical form of "verifiable consent" for a child's data, sector retention schedules, the machinery for registering Consent Managers — depend on subordinate Rules that were still only in draft form when this page was written. Treat the Act's principles as settled and the Rules' fine print as still moving, and build for the stricter plausible reading rather than wait for certainty that had not yet arrived.

8"Reasonable security safeguards" is not a specification. The Act requires reasonable security safeguards against breaches, but does not itself prescribe encryption standards, access-control models or breach-notification formats; those come from sectoral guidance (RBI's IT frameworks for lenders, CERT-In's reporting directions) and, eventually, the Rules. DPDP makes you accountable for a breach; it does not tell you, by itself, which controls satisfy that duty.

Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and early-stage versus large

The shape of the obligation changes with the product. A consumer app like Bhrigu has a direct relationship with the Data Principal and carries the full weight of notice, consent UX, and rights-handling itself. A B2B SaaS vendor selling to enterprises is usually the Data Processor, working under its customer's instructions and a data-processing agreement; its consent burden is lighter, but its security and contractual obligations are not. A marketplace connecting one Data Principal to several independent lenders or sellers sits in the hardest spot: it must decide, purpose by purpose, whether it is itself a Fiduciary for a given piece of processing or merely the channel through which the Principal consents separately to each business — get that wrong and either the marketplace or its partners end up processing data with no valid basis at all. Scale matters on a separate axis: an early-stage company below the Significant Data Fiduciary thresholds carries fewer mandatory structures, but pays a steep retrofitting cost bolting purpose-tagging onto an undifferentiated user table after half a million users; a large, designated-significant player faces audits and impact assessments as routine, and treats consent architecture as infrastructure, not a launch-week checkbox.

Common mistakes

Table 2 — Failure patterns and how to catch them early
MistakeSymptomUnderlying errorCheap diagnostic
Policy mistaken for noticeOne checkbox links to a long privacy policyConfusing a legal document with the plain-language, itemised notice §5 requires at the point of collectionAsk a colleague outside legal to state, in one sentence, what is collected and why — if they can't, it fails
Bundled consentCan't get the core service without also agreeing to marketing or analyticsTreating "conditions of service" and "unrelated processing" as the same thing, which §6's proviso forbidsList every purpose behind the checkbox; if any is not necessary to deliver the core service, unbundle it
Legitimate-use overreachProduct team skips consent, citing "legitimate use," for something merely convenientTreating §7 as a discretionary balancing test like GDPR's, instead of a closed, literal listCheck the processing against the actual §7 text; if it isn't named, get consent instead
No working withdrawal pathUsers can consent, but "withdraw" is an email nobody answers, or deletion is soft in one table onlyTreating the consent record as a one-time compliance artefact rather than an ongoing, revocable rightWithdraw as a test user and check, 30 days later, which systems — including backups and the analytics warehouse — still hold the data

What good looks like

Three months on, Bhrigu's onboarding screen carries a short notice naming exactly three purposes — identity verification, credit assessment, loan servicing — with a "read more" link to the full policy, and two separate, clearly-labelled toggles: one locked for the processing the loan cannot happen without, one unchecked by default for being contacted about other financial products. A "manage my data" entry in account settings lets any borrower see every purpose their data serves and withdraw the optional one in two taps, the same number it took to grant it. Internally, engineering maintains a purpose registry: every database field is tagged with the specific purpose that justifies its collection, and the monthly deletion job purges the primary database, the analytics warehouse and the credit bureau's retained query log alike. Bhrigu's two lending-partner banks are treated as independent Fiduciaries for the approval decisions they make, governed by their own consent capture, not Bhrigu's — a distinction product and legal now check before adding any partner integration.

Closing

At the board meeting, Ananya recommended the unbundled, delayed-ask design, and the board approved it. Her reasoning was not primarily moral; it was a comparison of two numbers. The near-term cost was a smaller, later marketing pool — roughly 14,500 opted-in records a month instead of 38,400 never-really-opted-in ones. The benefit was removing Bhrigu's exposure to a penalty regime running into hundreds of crores of rupees for a security or consent failure, and the reputational cost of being the lender whose checkbox a court or the Data Protection Board later called a dark pattern. She also suspected, correctly as it turned out, that leads who opted in after a good repayment experience converted at a noticeably higher rate than leads who had simply failed to notice a pre-checked box. The next idea on her reading list, "Personalisation vs surveillance," picks up where this one stops: once Bhrigu has clean, purpose-specific consent, how much can it infer and recommend before the personalisation itself starts to feel like the surveillance the Act was written against?

Two questions to sit with:

1. Somewhere in your own product, is there a single checkbox standing in for two or three purposes that a user would answer differently if asked separately?

2. If a user tried to withdraw consent tomorrow, how many systems — production database, backups, analytics warehouse, third-party vendors — would actually stop using their data, and by when?

Ebong Health: Whose Consent Is It?

A case on data, consent and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

1. Opening

At nine in the evening on Tuesday, 20 October 2026, Maitreyi Vidyabhusan closed her laptop in Bengaluru and reopened it a minute later. The video call she had just left was unresolved. It was 11:30 in the morning in Toronto, where the data scientist who had joined the call was already sure of his answer, and half past eleven at night in Singapore, where a colleague had stayed up to listen.

Vidyabhusan was head of product at Ebong Health, a teleconsultation and home-diagnostics company. By Friday, 6 November, she had to put one recommendation to the board: how Ebong would treat the health data of its 42 lakh registered users once the main obligations of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 took effect in May 2027. Engineering froze new work for the Diwali season on Monday, 9 November, so a decision that missed the board would not reach a developer until 2027.

2. Company background

Ebong was founded in Kolkata in 2019 by two doctors and a software engineer, and launched in 2020 with video consultations in Bengali and English. It later added at-home sample collection and a pharmacy marketplace, and moved its headquarters to Bengaluru, keeping engineering teams in Bengaluru and Pune and a growing support desk in Singapore. In the year to 31 March 2026 it earned ₹122.0 crore: consultations ₹61.0 crore, at-home diagnostics ₹38.0 crore, pharmacy commissions ₹14.0 crore and partner offers ₹9.0 crore.

Partner offers meant insurers and wellness brands paying to reach users whose records suggested a need, for example a health-cover quote shown to a user with a recent blood-sugar result. The market is crowded: Practo, Tata 1mg, Apollo 24/7 and PharmEasy sell consultations and medicines, while Healthians and Dr Lal PathLabs compete for diagnostics. The government's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission is building a national health-record layer that Ebong intends to join.

3. The situation

Since 2020 every Ebong user had passed through one screen: a single box reading "I agree to the Terms and Privacy Policy", which had to be ticked to continue. Paragraph 11 of the policy said data might be shared with partners for offers. In March 2025 the policy was updated to add that records could train Ebong's predictive models, announced by an in-app banner; no one was asked to tick anything.

The Rules under the Act were notified in November 2025 (Figure 1). Counsel Mayukh Vidyalankar's reading was that Section 5 lets a company that holds earlier consent keep processing for the original purposes after sending a notice, but that consent must otherwise be free, specific, informed and unambiguous, and that children's data needs a verifiable parent's consent. Ebong holds 1.26 lakh child profiles, created by parents for their children, 3.0 per cent of its users. Penalties run to ₹50 crore for general failures and ₹200 crore for children's-data failures, enforced by the Data Protection Board of India.

Exhibit 1 shows who the users are. Only 14.70 lakh, 35.0 per cent, signed in during the 90 days to 30 September 2026; 18.90 lakh have been silent for over a year. Finance attributes the partner-offer revenue to the active group.

In September Ebong ran a pilot on 90,000 randomly chosen active users, 30,000 per arm, from 1 to 14 September, with results counted on 15 September (Exhibit 2). The product designer in Berlin, who built the pilot screens, argued that any future toggles should appear after a user's first completed consultation rather than at sign-up, when trust is highest and the stakes are clearest. The Pune and Bengaluru engineers estimated that either re-consent path needs about three months to build and test. The Singapore team reported the other side of the story: support tickets mentioning "privacy" had risen as the pilot's screens reached users, and the Dubai-based employer-wellness client, whose Indian staff use Ebong, had asked in writing how consent would be recorded.

4. The people

Mayukh Vidyalankar, general counsel, Kolkata, wants no processing that he cannot defend before the Board. He reads the old tick-box as thin and the 2025 model-training banner as weaker still.

Mukti Vidyasagar, head of partnerships, Edison, New Jersey, signed the insurer contracts behind the ₹9.0 crore. He argues Ebong should send the notice the Act requires and otherwise change nothing, since users have been shown the policy for six years.

Moloy Vidyarthi, data scientist, Toronto, leads the model that flags patients likely to miss follow-up tests. He fears a consenting subset will be younger and healthier than Ebong's real patients, and that the model will quietly stop working for those who most need it.

Maitreyi Vidyabhusan owns the roadmap and must name the trade-off to the board.

5. Exhibits

Exhibits 1 and 2 and Figure 1 are discussed in section 3; Exhibit 3 prices the three options set out in section 6.

6. The options

Option A: re-consent everyone. Send all 42 lakh users the arm 3 screen. Partner sharing and model training run only on fresh opt-ins; the rest remain care-only. On the pilot rates, about 5.3 lakh of the 14.70 lakh active users would be in the training set (14.70 lakh at 35.75 per cent). The campaign costs ₹1.40 crore.

Option B: notice and continue. Send every user the notice and keep sharing and training on existing data under earlier consent. Child profiles are excluded from partner offers, which removes their pro-rata 3.0 per cent of the revenue. It costs ₹0.30 crore, needs the least engineering, and leaves the 2025 model-training change resting on a banner.

Option C: end the secondary uses. Send the notice, stop identifiable partner sharing and model training on health records, and sell only on-platform sponsored content that uses no health data. It costs ₹0.30 crore, and the predictive model is shelved.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What did a user who ticked the 2020 box actually agree to, and what did a user who saw the March 2025 banner agree to? What does the Act require Ebong to do for each group?
  2. In Exhibit 2, which denominator would you use to forecast revenue, and which to judge screen design? What can and cannot be concluded from arm 3 against arm 2?
  3. Exhibit 3 assumes revenue comes from active users. What happens to each option's figure if that assumption is wrong, and what would you ask Finance to show?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 6 November, which evidence would change your mind before then, and how would you speak to Moloy and to Mukti?

8. A note for the learner

The Act makes consent a property of a purpose, not of a user. A product manager therefore frames the decision by listing each use of the data, asking which legal basis supports it, and asking whether the user could have anticipated it. Care delivery needs no toggle; offers and model training do. A well-reasoned answer separates these purposes, reads exhibits with their own denominators, and states the revenue it gives up rather than hiding it.

One defensible path is Option A, with two refinements. First, send the notice to everyone at once, since that duty does not wait on the rest of the plan. Second, ask for consent in the user's own language, as in arm 3, accepting that the pilot cannot say whether language or the benefit line did the work, and keep a small holdout to find out. The reasoning is that Ebong's partner revenue is real but rests on consent that would be hard to show, while a model trained on records of people who agreed is one Ebong can keep running. Moloy's selection concern then becomes a monitoring task: compare the consenting group's profile with the whole base every quarter. The ₹6.66 crore reduction in partner revenue is the price of that clarity and should be presented to the board as a price. Reasonable managers could prefer Option B on the legal reading or Option C on risk, provided they state what each leaves exposed.
case40v1-legal.consent.ux:
ISB · Software Product Management · Case 40

Doorva Retail Technologies: the consent flow before Deepavali

Sunday, 18 October 2026, Bengaluru. By eleven the next morning a product leader must tell the audit and risk committee what Doorva will do about a consent design that earns ₹75 crore a year and that her counsel says cannot be evidenced as consent.

1. The night before

The power cut on Lavelle Road lasted nine minutes, long enough for Lipsita Thakuria to lose her place in the deck. She was Senior Director of Product for Growth and Platform at Doorva Retail Technologies Private Limited, and she had joined in March 2022, fourteen months after the decision she was about to defend.

At eleven the next morning, Monday 19 October 2026, the audit and risk committee would ask her one question: what is Doorva going to do about consent, and when. Behind it sat the code freeze of Friday 23 October, the Deepavali Days sale from 30 October to Diwali on 8 November, a Dubai partner's audit on 15 December, a contractual floor measured on 31 January 2027, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules commencing on 18 May 2027. One working week of engineering capacity stood before the freeze.

She had a six-week experiment readout, a memo from the General Counsel, a revenue model from the Lens sales desk, and an e-mail from Toronto saying the model asked the wrong question. The memo never used the words dark pattern. It used the phrase not capable of being evidenced as consent.

2. The company, and the decision of January 2021

Doorva was founded in Bengaluru in June 2017 by Lopita Thander, as a curated beauty storefront. The app launched in March 2019 and the company was app-first within two years; in the year to 31 March 2026 it turned over ₹1,657.5 crore of gross merchandise value on 85.0 lakh orders, with net revenue of ₹600.0 crore (Exhibit 4).

The decision that constrains Monday was taken in January 2021. To sell brand partners something Nykaa and Purplle were not selling, Doorva launched Doorva Lens, selling audience segments built from first-party behaviour. A product note of 14 January 2021 set out how to make the audience large enough to sell: a prominent Accept all, a Manage link beneath it with the analytics and advertising categories pre-ticked, and a scroll past the banner treated as acceptance. The note recorded the team's estimate that a visible, equally weighted Reject would cost between 25 and 30 per cent of the addressable base. It did not say 25 to 30 per cent of what, and nobody asked.

It worked. The base went from 0.62 crore profiles in March 2021 to 2.50 crore in March 2026, and Lens from nothing to ₹75.0 crore of invoiced media revenue. Partners buying against the base wanted assurance it would not shrink, and two anchor contracts carry addressable-profile floors (Exhibit 4). The first immutable consent-record store was built in February 2026; at 31 March 2026 it held 0.46 crore records against a base of 2.50 crore, so 2.04 crore profiles rest on server logs.

3. The industry

Indian beauty retail in 2026 was crowded: Nykaa and Purplle at scale, Tira from Reliance Retail, Myntra Beauty, Amazon and Flipkart, and newer pressure as Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart added shampoo to ten-minute baskets and ONDC promised to unbundle discovery. Where repeat purchase is the business and acquisition is bought, retargeting is not a feature of the marketing stack; it is the stack, and Google's 2025 decision to leave third-party cookies in place removed the deadline for replacing it.

Regulation arrived from two directions. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 was followed by Rules notified in November 2025, whose obligations on notice, consent and record-keeping commence on 18 May 2027, with the Data Protection Board of India adjudicating. Already in force, the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns name thirteen practices, among them forced action and basket sneaking, and bind conduct today. Doorva's exposure was not only Indian. Since April 2024 it had operated the white-label storefront of Dahab Beauty Group, a Dubai retail house, under a warranty that consent management meets applicable law in each territory served, audited annually and next on 15 December 2026. Dahab was sold as a Gulf business. A traffic audit dated 24 July 2026 found that of 38.60 lakh storefront sessions in the thirty days to 23 July, 11.4 per cent — 4.40 lakh sessions — resolved to European Union IP ranges, bringing the General Data Protection Regulation and the ePrivacy cookie rules to bear on a 2021 banner.

4. The situation: what was recorded, and when

Exhibit 1 lays out the sequence. Lalmohan Toppo joined as General Counsel in January 2026, designated Data Protection Officer against the possibility that Doorva is notified a Significant Data Fiduciary. In June 2026 he asked how Doorva would prove, for one user, that consent had been given; the answer was the record-store gap above. In July 2026 a Berlin consumer group's scanner found that the Dahab storefront wrote advertising cookies before any choice was recorded.

Lipsita's response was to measure. From Monday 31 August to Sunday 11 October 2026, forty-two days, every web visitor arriving without a prior consent record was assigned to one of three banner arms: A, the 2021 control; B, a symmetric banner with equally weighted Accept all and Reject all and nothing pre-ticked; C, a purpose-first panel with every toggle off and a Save choices action. Exhibits 2 and 3 report what followed. An interim extract was pulled on 2 October and counsel's memo, dated 9 October, rests on it. The readout came on 13 October, the team argued on a call on 15 October, and on 16 October the Lens desk circulated a figure that has been in every conversation since.

Three things believed in January 2021 now sit beside later evidence. The note estimated that a visible Reject would cost 25 to 30 per cent of the base; Exhibit 2 reports the advertising purpose granted on 338,250 of 410,000 first-touch visitors in Arm A and 226,440 of 408,000 in Arm B. The note assumed annual refresh; the February 2026 build found no record evidencing one. The Dahab deal was signed on a Gulf audience; the July audit is above.

5. Exhibits

6. The people

Lopita Thander, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Position: fix this before Doorva is made to, but not in the festive quarter. Incentive: the FY27 Lens number is in her board scorecard. Not saying: a September secondary transaction values the company off Lens revenue, and the investor's diligence list includes a privacy review.

Lalmohan Toppo, General Counsel and Data Protection Officer designate, Mumbai, from January 2026. Position: the control cannot be evidenced as consent; the record store comes first. Incentive: he is the named officer if Doorva is notified a Significant Data Fiduciary. Not saying: rows 3 and 6 of Exhibit 6 were excluded on his instruction, to hold counsel's fee at ₹9.50 lakh.

Lakshay Tudu, VP Engineering, Pune, there since that centre opened in 2019. Position: Arm B is test code already and ships before the freeze. Incentive: Exhibit 6's 64 person-weeks would displace his checkout migration. Not saying: of the 11 unmapped tags, two fire on the Dahab storefront and neither has an owner.

Lavali Tanti, principal designer, Berlin, joined January 2024. Position: Arm C everywhere, because the CCPA's dark-pattern guidelines and the European Data Protection Board's cookie-banner work describe the control precisely. Incentive: her consent component is the first candidate for the design system. Not saying: in her own September 2026 sessions, 18 participants in Berlin and Bengaluru, 7 of the 18 could not find Arm C's withdrawal control inside ninety seconds.

Lohini Thengal, staff data scientist, Toronto, there since 2023. Position: Exhibit 3's order differences sit inside the pre-registered effect; the advertising-grant differences do not. Incentive: she wrote the pre-registration. Not saying: assignment was by cookie, and she puts re-randomised repeats at 6.2 per cent of Exhibit 2's 12,23,000 sessions, uncirculated.

Litesh Tamang, customer-success director for brand partners, Singapore, joined 2021. Position: nothing changes until the festive quarter closes; partners commit Diwali media in September. Incentive: Partner A's ₹18.0 crore is in his book. Not saying: Partner A's category manager has offered to drop the floor clause for a three-year term.

Lakshita Topno, head of Lens sales, Jersey City, from the opening of the US desk in September 2024. Position: no change until Lens has a contextual product independent of the advertising purpose. Incentive: an FY27 quota of ₹82.0 crore. Not saying: two US brands have asked in writing whether Lens segments rest on consent their own counsel would accept; she has answered neither.

7. Voices

“Arm C gives up 43,500 advertising-purpose profiles per lakh of first-touch visitors. We see 1.063 crore first-touch web visitors a year, so that is 46.2 lakh profiles we would not have. At ₹30 a profile it is ₹13.9 crore.”

Lakshita Topno, e-mail to leadership, 16 October 2026, 08:12 Eastern

“Your ₹30 is ₹75.0 crore divided by a base of 2.50 crore at 31 March: an average over a stock. The marginal web profile is priced by whichever contract it moves, and ₹51.5 crore of the ₹82.0 crore carries no floor at all. Also, your 1.063 crore is a 42-day cohort multiplied by 8.69.”

Lohini Thengal, same thread, 16 October 2026, 23:04 IST

“We ran the experiment on the surface that takes 22 per cent of our orders and asked it to settle a question about the app. We measured where the light was.”

Lavali Tanti, design review, Berlin, 14 October 2026
