Litesh Tamang, chat to Lipsita Thakuria, 17 October 2026, 21:40 Singapore

8. The options as Lipsita sees them

Capacity is the frame she has been working inside. The consent pod is six engineers, four in Bengaluru and two in Pune. Between Monday 19 October and the freeze on Friday 23 October there is one working week: six person-weeks. Consumer releases stop from 24 October to 12 November. From 13 November to 14 May 2027, net of holidays and leave, engineering counts 24 usable weeks, or 144 person-weeks.

Option 1. Ship Arm B on Doorva India web before the freeze. The variant exists as test code; hardening it and remapping tags is four person-weeks, ₹8.00 lakh, inside the six available. It touches surfaces carrying 22.0 per cent of FY26 orders and 27.0 per cent of the addressable base (Exhibit 5), and leaves the app sheet, the pixels, the record store and the Dahab storefront as built.

Option 2. Run the whole matrix on the Arm C pattern from 13 November. Sixty-four person-weeks and ₹128.0 lakh, landing before 18 May 2027. It covers rows 1 to 5 of Exhibit 6 and re-prompts the app base at next open, putting 182.5 lakh app profiles through a new sheet between 13 November and 31 January 2027. Row 6 is not costed.

Option 3. Hold the control through the festive quarter and start in January 2027. Sixty-four person-weeks compressed into 13 January to 14 May 2027, where 16 usable weeks give 96 person-weeks; ₹128.0 lakh across FY27 and FY28. It answers the 15 December audit with the storefront as built and takes the Partner A measurement on a base assembled under the 2021 banner.

Option 4. Split by jurisdiction: symmetric consent on EU-resolving storefront traffic and on Doorva India web, the app unchanged until the thaw. Geo-gating the banner is seven person-weeks, ₹14.0 lakh, against six available before 23 October, so either an engineer comes off checkout or it lands after 12 November. It leaves the app, the pixels and the record store as built, and reaches the July audit's 4.40 lakh EU-resolving sessions.

All four were drafted from the web experiment. Exhibit 5 reports the app at 78.0 per cent of FY26 orders and 73.0 per cent of profiles, and the app was not an arm of the test.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee sits at 11:00 IST on Monday and wants a recommendation, not a paper. The freeze is contractual with the logistics partners and will not move for a banner. Deepavali Days, 30 October to 8 November, carries roughly a fifth of the year's orders and its marketing is placed. The FY27 compliance budget has ₹140.0 lakh unspent, covering the ₹128.0 lakh matrix and nothing in row 6. The Dahab audit falls on 15 December 2026, with a 60-day cure period and then a right to terminate. The Partner A floor is measured on 31 January 2027, Partner B's on 30 April. The DPDP obligations commence on 18 May 2027, and Doorva has not been notified a Significant Data Fiduciary, so it does not know whether the heavier obligations reach it at all.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 reports five exclusive outcome columns per arm; Exhibit 6, row 1, records what the control does with a session in which no choice was recorded. From those cells, what figure would you put before the Data Protection Board of India as the control's consent rate, and how would you describe the count?
  2. Exhibit 3 prices each arm per 1,00,000 first-touch visitors over 42 days; Exhibit 4 reports the Lens base and revenue to 31 March 2026. What quantities, in neither exhibit, would you need before stating what Arm C costs over a full year?
  3. Lakshita Topno's e-mail of 16 October uses ₹30.00 and 1.063 crore; Lohini Thengal's reply that evening disputes both. Set out each one's assumption about the ₹30.00 in Exhibit 4, and what measurement would settle it.
  4. Exhibit 5 reports where FY26 orders and profiles came from; Exhibit 2 reports who was in the experiment. If Lipsita wanted for the app the evidence she now has for web, what would she have to run, over what window, and where would it sit against section 9?
  5. Counsel's memo is dated 9 October and rests on an extract of 2 October; rows 3 and 6 of Exhibit 6 are marked outside the engagement's scope. What would you require from counsel before Monday, what would you decide without it, and how would you record the choice?
  6. It is 11:00 on Monday 19 October. What does Lipsita Thakuria do about the consent flow before the 23 October freeze and after the 12 November thaw, and what does she say to the committee about the note of 14 January 2021, the Partner A floor and the Dahab audit?

Monday, 1.05 a.m.

The generator had settled into its hum and the deck was open on slide four, the one carrying Exhibit 2, where she had tried three titles and deleted all of them. Across the road two men were bolting a Deepavali hoarding to its frame.

She thought about four pages written in January 2021 by people trying to keep a company alive, and about Litesh's question, and about not knowing what number to give him. Beside the laptop lay row one of Exhibit 6 with one word in the margin in her own hand, which was whose. She had meant it for the sentence about the scroll, and was no longer sure that was where it belonged.
exp20v2-legal.consent.ux:
Consent flows and cookie UX

Is our consent flow real consent, or a dark pattern?

1. A 94 per cent acceptance rate

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Iniyavan Pattabiraman, head of product at Aruvam Care, put one number on the meeting-room screen in Chennai: 94.0. Aruvam Care sells video consultations and medicine delivery, and had 1.8 million monthly active users. The number was the share of people who tapped the green "Accept all" button on the app's first-launch privacy screen.

Ishanth Parthiban, the company's privacy counsel, did not read it as good news. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, requires consent that is free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action. Its main duties on notice and consent were expected to bite in 2027, and its penalty schedule runs to ₹250 crore. Inbasekar Ponnambalam, who led growth, replied that the roughly 96 per cent marketing consent funded the ad-measurement data behind customer-acquisition spending.

The screen itself explained the number. Accepting took one tap. Refusing everything took five, as the table shows, and the "More options" link was grey text on a white strip beneath a full-width green button.

Goal on the current screenTaps neededRoute
Accept all1Green button
Reject all optional purposes5More options, three toggles off, Save

The decision was whether to rebuild it before the company's next quarter began on 1 January, and what the rebuild should cost the business. If Pattabiraman got it wrong in one direction, a regulator would one day treat the 94 per cent as evidence against the firm. In the other, revenue would fall for nothing.

2. The idea

A consent flow is the sequence of screens through which a product asks a person for permission to use their data for stated purposes, records the answer, and obeys it. Cookie UX is the same problem in a browser, where a cookie is a small file a site stores on a device to recognise it later. A banner is the surface; the flow is everything behind it, including what the software does after the tap.

The problem it solves is old. Terms of service were long, unread and bundled, so "agreeing" carried no information. Europe's ePrivacy Directive (2002, amended 2009) required consent for non-essential cookies. The General Data Protection Regulation, applying from May 2018, defined consent as a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of wishes by a clear affirmative act. In 2010 the designer Harry Brignull coined "dark patterns" for interfaces that steer people against their own interests. Consent flows sit where those two lines meet.

Pattabiraman distilled it for the room in one sentence: a yes counts only if the no was as easy to say. The table gives the tests behind it.

TestQuestion it asksHow the current screen fares
FreeCould the person refuse without penalty or friction?Fails: 5 taps against 1
SpecificIs each purpose separately chosen?Fails: one button covers all
InformedCan they say what they agreed to?Weak: only 22% could recall what they agreed to (section 4)
UnambiguousWas it an active act, not a pre-set default?Fails in settings: toggles start on
WithdrawableIs leaving as easy as joining?Not yet checked

3. How it actually works

Practitioners tend to describe a flow as a banner. It is better described as six steps, two of which are usually left implicit. The first is notice: before any data is collected, the person is told which purposes the data serves, in language they could repeat. For Aruvam Care these were three optional purposes (analytics, personalisation, marketing measurement) beside essential ones, such as keeping a consultation connected, which need no consent.

The second step is choice, in which each purpose gets its own answer and the options carry equal visual and physical weight. The third is capture: the system stores a record of who chose what, when, on which version of the wording. The version matters, because six months later nobody can prove what a person saw without it. The fourth step is enforcement, the one most often left implicit. Software that gathers analytics must not run until the choice is made. A banner that shows a refusal while the tracker has already fired is theatre.

The fifth step is propagation: the answer must reach every downstream vendor, whether an analytics SDK (a vendor's code library embedded in the app) or an advertising partner. The sixth is withdrawal and renewal: a settings entry as easy to reach as the first screen was, and a fresh prompt when purposes change. Figure 2 shows the loop.

Run against the Aruvam screen, the loop fails at steps 2 and 4 before the design is even debated. Ponnambalam's engineers confirmed that the analytics SDK started on app launch and merely stopped uploading after a refusal, so the data was collected anyway. Fixing the banner would have left that untouched.

4. A worked example

Pattabiraman asked for a two-week test, run from 22 September to 5 October. New installs were split at random into two arms of 40,000 users each. Arm A kept the current screen. Arm B showed three equal-weight buttons, "Accept all", "Reject all" and "Choose", with the toggles starting off. The table shows what people did.

OutcomeArm A usersArm A shareArm B usersArm B share
Accept all37,60094.0%26,00065.0%
Customise1,6004.0%6,00015.0%
Reject all8002.0%8,00020.0%
Total40,000100.0%40,000100.0%

Now the money. Treat a user as marketing-consented if they accepted all, or customised with marketing on, and assume half of customisers switch marketing on. Aruvam's finance team valued each marketing-consented user at ₹40 a year in measured acquisition efficiency.

LineArm AArm B
Accept all37,60026,000
Customisers with marketing on (50%)8003,000
Marketing-consented users38,40029,000
Share of 40,00096.0%72.5%
Annual value at ₹40 each (₹ lakh)15.3611.60

Arm B kept 75.5 per cent of Arm A's value, a gap of ₹3.76 lakh per 40,000 users. The base is 1.8 million, which is 45 times 40,000, so if every user saw the screen the annual gap would be ₹169.2 lakh, or about ₹1.69 crore. That is an upper-scale illustration: the test covered only new installs, and neither returning users nor the re-prompting of existing consent was tested.

The second pass changes one input: suppose only 25 per cent of customisers switch marketing on, in both arms. Arm A has 37,600 plus 400, or 38,000 users (95.0 per cent), worth ₹15.20 lakh. Arm B has 26,000 plus 1,500, or 27,500 (68.75 per cent), worth ₹11.00 lakh, which is 72.4 per cent of A. The gap is ₹4.20 lakh per 40,000, or ₹189.0 lakh at full scale. A single behavioural assumption moved the estimate by ₹19.8 lakh.

The test had a second measure. Among users who installed between 22 and 28 September, 400 randomly chosen per arm were asked seven days after install what they had agreed to, and all 400 in each arm answered. In Arm A, 88 could say (22 per cent); in Arm B, 244 (61 per cent). The 39-point difference has a standard error of about 3.2 points, so it is not noise.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Consent is one lawful basis among several

Law lets organisations process data on other grounds too, such as performing a contract or a legal duty. A consultation cannot connect without a microphone feed, and asking permission for that is noise. Over-asking trains people to tap through, which damages the asks that do need real answers. The first question to put to any proposed prompt is therefore whether the purpose truly needs a yes, or whether another basis already covers it.

Acceptance rate measures the interface, not the person

A 94 per cent rate says the green button is easy to find. It cannot distinguish a person who agrees from one who wants the screen gone. Only a comprehension measure, like the recall survey above, separates them.

Symmetry is about effort, not appearance

Two buttons of equal size can still be unequal if one sits where the thumb rests, uses brand colour, or is labelled "Continue" while the other says "Reject and limit features".

Refusal cannot be punished

Consent is not free if the service stops when optional purposes are declined. A "cookie wall" that blocks access unless the person accepts tracking is the standard example. Essential functions may depend on essential data; nothing else may.

Granularity trades against understanding

Separate choices make consent specific, yet twelve toggles produce fatigue and arbitrary taps. Layering helps: three plain-language purposes first, detail one level down.

The test cannot tell you why the arm won, or what happens next

Arm B changed two things at once, button parity and purpose-level choice, so the data cannot say which produced the recall gain. Nor does any consent screen tell you whether the company later uses the data as promised. Counsel, not product, decides which jurisdiction's rules bind.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

The structure of the problem changes with who is being asked. In a consumer app the person is also the data subject, so the screen is the whole story and the risks are fatigue and thumb-sized interfaces. In B2B software the buyer signs a contract, but the end users inside the customer never see it; the vendor is often a processor acting on the customer's instructions, so the question becomes who must collect consent. In a marketplace there are two or more sides, each with its own notice, and data about one side (a rider, a seller) may reach the other.

SettingWho consentsCharacteristic difficulty
ConsumerThe end user, directlyFatigue; asymmetric buttons
B2BThe customer's users, via the customerRoles of controller and processor
MarketplaceEach side separatelyData crossing between sides

Size matters too. An early-stage company often uses a ready-made consent-management platform (CMP) and ships in a week, but may leave steps 4 and 5 unbuilt. A large one has dozens of vendors and several teams, so the weakness moves from the banner to propagation and to proving which wording each user saw.

7. Common mistakes

Making acceptance rate the goal

Symptom: the rate rises every quarter and nobody can say what users understood. Misunderstanding: higher is treated as better, though a ceiling near 100 per cent is what coercion produces. Cheapest diagnostic: ask 100 users a week later what they agreed to.

Trusting the banner and never checking the network

Symptom: refusals recorded, yet third-party requests visible on launch. Misunderstanding: the banner is taken to be the control. Diagnostic: open the app on a test device with a traffic proxy, refuse everything, and count outgoing requests to analytics and advertising domains before any tap.

Making withdrawal harder than agreement

Symptom: almost nobody ever revisits settings. Misunderstanding: consent is seen as a one-off gate. Diagnostic: count the taps from the home screen to withdrawal; if it exceeds the taps used to give consent, the flow is lopsided.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of the same decision looks like Figure 4: three equal buttons, plain purposes, and an essential-only default. Behind it sit a versioned consent record, trackers that stay dormant until a choice is made, and a settings entry two taps from the home screen. The team owns a recall measure alongside the revenue measure, and reports both to leadership. The practical targets are modest: refusing costs the same one tap as accepting, withdrawal is reachable in two taps, and a sampled recall rate above half the users.

9. The decision

On Tuesday 13 October, Pattabiraman recommended shipping Arm B to every new and returning user, with the analytics SDK held dormant until a choice was made. He planned against the larger of the two assumption-driven figures, ₹189.0 lakh a year rather than ₹169.2 lakh, since the true switch-on rate was never observed, and asked Ponnambalam to find that amount in better creative and first-party data. His reasoning was that a revenue number built on a 94 per cent acceptance rate was borrowed against a penalty schedule reaching ₹250 crore. A follow-up test of a simple two-button variant would show which lever drove the recall gain.

What to learn next: the dark-patterns taxonomy, which names the specific tricks a symmetry test will not catch, and the Indian and European privacy regimes themselves, which set the standard the flow must meet.

Two questions to sit with. If acceptance fell to 40 per cent and recall rose to 90, would you call the flow better, and by what measure? And where in your own product does a "yes" depend on a "no" that costs more to give?
case20v1-legal.consent.ux:
Candela Health: One Tap to Accept

A teaching case on consent flows and cookie UX

1. Opening

At 10:30 on Tuesday 20 October 2026, Kamalika Sen opened a video call from the fourth floor of Candela Health's Bengaluru office. It was 07:00 in Berlin, where the designer Krishnendu Sarania had agreed to an early start, and 13:00 in Singapore. Ms Sen, Candela's Director of Product, had until 18:00 on Friday 23 October to lock the scope of the next two releases. One item would not wait: the screen that asks a new user to consent to how Candela uses their data. Her decision was how the screen should work, and the date it would reach users depended on which design she chose.

2. Company background

Candela Health, founded in Bengaluru in 2019, sells prescription and over-the-counter medicines, home blood tests and chronic-care refills through an Android and iOS app and a website. It reported revenue of ₹318 crore for the year ended March 2026, about 96 lakh registered users and roughly 2.4 lakh new users a month. It competes with Tata 1mg, PharmEasy, Apollo 24/7 and Reliance's Netmeds, all of which chase the same repeat buyer of diabetes and thyroid medicines.

Besides margin on medicines, Candela earns about ₹9.6 crore a year, roughly 3 per cent of revenue, from letting pharma and consumer-health brands show offers to the active users who have agreed to share data with advertising partners. A smaller line, ₹2.4 crore a year, is a corporate wellness contract with Crescent Bay Hospitality Group in Dubai, whose Indian staff use Candela for health checks.

3. The situation

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires consent to be free, specific, informed and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, and as easy to withdraw as to give. The Rules notified in November 2025 phase in the main duties of data fiduciaries by mid-May 2027, and penalties for breaching the Act's duties run up to ₹50 crore, with higher ceilings for security and breach-notification failures. The Central Consumer Protection Authority separately issued guidelines in November 2023 naming 13 dark patterns, among them forced action and interface interference. Candela is not yet bound by the DPDP duties. Its lawyers expect that it will be.

Exhibit 1 shows the live flow, which Ms Sen's team inherited from 2022. One large green button accepts everything. The route to refusal is a grey link, and three of the four purposes are pre-ticked. Mr Sarania, who joined in March 2026, called it "a flow built to be tapped, not read." On 15 October, Kakoli Saharia, the customer-success lead in Singapore, forwarded Crescent Bay's annual vendor questionnaire. It asked for evidence by 30 November that "refusing optional processing takes no more effort than agreeing to it." The renewal falls on 15 December.

Mr Sarania ran a pilot from Thursday 1 to Wednesday 14 October on Android, giving 24,000 consecutive new users to each of two arms. The control arm saw the live screen. The variant showed four purposes, all off, with "Accept all" and "Reject non-essential" in equal-weight buttons. Exhibit 2 gives the results. The data were pulled on Sunday 18 October. Exhibit 3 prices three courses of action against one monthly cohort and Exhibit 4 places the dates on a calendar. The pilot is the only measured evidence Ms Sen has. The revenue figures for the two options other than the pilot's own design rest on Growth's estimates.

4. The people

Kaushiki Sikdar, general counsel, Mumbai, wants a flow she can defend to the Data Protection Board once it exists. She does not mind losing some consent if every rupee of what remains is clean. She has asked that no purpose be bundled with another.

Koushik Sutradhar, head of growth, Pune, owns the advertising and messaging lines. He argues that Candela's users already trust it with their prescriptions, that Diwali on 8 November is the busiest fortnight of the year, and that any change to onboarding should wait until after it. He has priced the lost partner revenue and wants it recovered somewhere.

Krishnendu Sarania, product designer, Berlin, built the pilot. He is wary of long legal text and of a screen so cautious that users stop reading it. He prefers asking for consent at the moment a feature needs it.

Kakoli Saharia, customer-success lead, Singapore, carries the Crescent Bay relationship. She also reads the support queue: of 41,000 tickets in September, 1,230 (3.0 per cent) complained of unwanted promotional messages. She wants the questionnaire answered truthfully and on time.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. The live consent screen, September 2026

Accepting takes one tap on a green button, 336 dp wide. Refusing takes five taps over two screens: a grey 14 sp "Manage" link, three toggles and "Save". Source: Candela product audit, 12 October 2026.

Exhibit 4. The decision calendar, 20 October to 18 December 2026. Release dates are build freezes, all Fridays.

6. The options

Option A: rewrite and keep. Replace the legal paragraph with plain-language copy and keep the single bundled screen, the green button and the Manage link. It needs 2 engineer-weeks and can ship in the 30 October release, before Diwali. It leaves the pre-ticked boxes and the five-tap refusal path as they are.

Option B: granular screen at onboarding. Ship the pilot variant: four purposes, all off, equal-weight "Accept all" and "Reject non-essential", and a consent centre in the profile for later changes. It needs 7 engineer-weeks and ships in the 13 November release, five days after Diwali. It asks for every optional consent at the first launch.

Option C: ask in context. Onboarding collects only what an order needs. Message consent is requested at the first checkout, and advertising sharing is offered after the first delivered order, each with its own explanation and an equal-weight refusal. It needs 14 engineer-weeks and ships on 18 December, after Crescent Bay's deadline. It moves the asking to a later and calmer moment.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 establish about the live screen, and what does it leave unestablished? Be specific about which columns are measured and which cells depend on an assumption.
  2. Mr Sutradhar and Ms Sikdar both cite Exhibit 3. Which figures in it can each of them rely on, and which can neither?
  3. Which of the four people's interests are in tension with each other, and which are only apparently so?
  4. What would you decide by Friday 23 October, and what would you watch in the first weeks to learn whether you were wrong?

8. A note for the learner

The lens here is a single test: could a user say no as easily as yes, and would the answer survive being read back to them? Consent that fails it is a dark pattern whatever the box says. The test is about the design of the choice, not about the rate. A well-reasoned answer keeps the legal test and the commercial figures in separate columns, notes which numbers were measured, and names the evidence that would change the choice.

One defensible path is Option B, shipped on 13 November. It gives Ms Sikdar a flow with no bundling and gives Ms Saharia a screen she can describe to Crescent Bay before 30 November. Ms Sen would tell Mr Sutradhar that the ad-sharing line stays whole for the 66.0 per cent who agree, and that Growth can earn the rest back with offers inside the app rather than outside it. She would then ask Mr Sarania to scope a version of Option C's later asks as a second phase for 2027, and to watch the opt-in rate, support complaints about messages and withdrawal rates for six weeks. If complaints did not fall, the premise of the choice would need revisiting.
exp40v2-legal.consent.ux:
Consent flows and cookie UX

Is our consent flow real consent, or a dark pattern?

1. Two screens, four days apart

On Monday 5 October 2026, Jeyanthi Rajasekaran put one number on a meeting-room wall in Bengaluru: 89.0. Rajasekaran ran product at Bilkul, a Hindi-and-regional news and short-video app with 23.4 million monthly active users and ₹137.92 crore of annual net advertising revenue. It was the share of first-launch users tapping "Accept and continue" on the privacy screen. Jashwanth Rallapalli, who ran monetisation, read it as a health metric; Jhilam Ramamoorthy, the privacy counsel, read it as an exhibit for the prosecution.

They were arguing about one screen, instrumented the week of Monday 31 August. Accepting everything took one tap and 0.9 seconds; refusing everything took four taps and 12.4 seconds, beginning with a grey text link beneath a saturated green button.

Measure, current screenAccept allReject allRatio, 1 dp
Taps to complete144.0
Median seconds0.912.413.8
First target, square pixels15,8404,3203.7
Label contrast, to 15.82.02.9
Exhibit 1. Targets are 264 × 60 and 180 × 24 pixels.

Four days later, at 14:00 in Hyderabad and 10:30 in Berlin on Friday 9 October, Jagadeeshwar Ramabadran took a call he had postponed. Ramabadran was co-founder and chief product officer of Brahmand Systems, an enterprise retail-operations platform with 212 customers, ₹196 crore of annual recurring revenue and 31 customers established in the European Union. Its largest European account, a German grocery chain worth ₹8.4 crore a year, 4.3 per cent of recurring revenue, had sent one question through its data protection officer: for one named shopper in one store, show which purposes she consented to, and prove the software obeyed.

Jalaja Rachapudi, Brahmand's privacy lead in Berlin, had already given Ramabadran the answer. Brahmand could produce the record. It could not produce the proof. Its per-purpose gate had shipped in release 4.6 on Wednesday 12 August 2026; by Wednesday 30 September, 19 of the 48 customer apps carrying its software development kit had upgraded, 39.6 per cent. One decision was about what a yes is worth; the other, whether a yes had been obtained at all.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A consent flow is the sequence by which a product asks permission to process a person's data for stated purposes, records the answer, and then behaves accordingly. Cookie UX is the same problem on the web, where a cookie is a small file stored to recognise a device. The banner is the surface; the flow is everything behind it, and the law judges the behaviour.

Terms of service were long, bundled and unread, so agreement carried no signal. Europe's ePrivacy Directive of 2002, amended in 2009, required consent before non-essential cookies were stored. The General Data Protection Regulation, applying from May 2018, defined consent in Article 4(11) as a freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous indication of wishes by a clear affirmative action, and in Article 7(3) gave a right to withdraw it as easily as it was given. In 2010 the designer Harry Brignull named the countervailing craft "dark patterns". India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, restates the standard and adds the registered consent manager.

What practitioners disagree about is whether the instrument can bear that weight. Four positions recur.

The formalist school treats consent as a legal instrument with stated elements: it will sign that equal prominence is required, not a courtesy, and will not sign that a high acceptance rate is itself evidence of invalidity, because people do agree. The behavioural school holds that the test is the measured gap — if moving a button moves the answer, the answer belongs to the designer — and will not sign that a legally shaped banner is consent. The consent-is-broken school, from critiques of privacy self-management, holds that no interface makes an informed decision out of an uninformed moment, and will not sign that better banners fix anything. The delegation school holds that forcing a decision on every surface is itself the harm, and will not sign that each purpose must be clicked on each site.

3. Mechanics: six steps, two of them invisible

Teams describe a flow as a banner; experts describe six steps, and locate most failures in the two nobody shows in review. Notice comes first: before collection, the person is told which purposes the data serves, in words they could repeat. Choice comes second, each purpose separately answerable, the options carrying equal visual and physical weight. Capture comes third, storing not the answer but its evidentiary context — wording, layout variant, locale, time.

Enforcement is fourth, the step teams skip: code serving a purpose must not execute until the purpose is permitted, and a banner recording a refusal after the analytics library has initialised is theatre. Propagation is fifth; withdrawal is sixth, and the Article 7(3) test is symmetry.

Bilkul's engineers ran an egress capture on Thursday 1 October: a device set to refuse everything, every outbound request logged. Eleven vendors sat in the manifest. Nine stopped. Two of the 11, 18.2 per cent, kept receiving the device advertising identifier — an attribution partner reading it from a shared container, and a video-player library never wired to the gate.

The quantitative treatment is not a compliance score but a selection-bias correction. Let q be the share permitting advertising measurement, rc the conversion rate observed among them, and rn the rate among the rest — which Bilkul can see, because a sign-up is recorded in billing whatever the consent state. Consent governs attribution, not the event. The population rate is q·rc + (1−q)·rn, and reporting rc alone overstates it by (1−q)(rc − rn).

In the symmetric arm q was 0.6280, rc 4.10 per cent and rn 2.60 per cent — the first from that arm's attribution data, the second from its billing log, neither shown in Exhibit 4 — so the population rate was 3.54 per cent and the overstatement 0.3720 × 1.50, or 0.56 points: reporting 4.10 overstates by 15.8 per cent. Under the old screen q was 0.9104, and if the same rc and rn held there, which was never measured, the population rate was 3.97 per cent and the overstatement 0.13 points or 3.4 per cent. On that illustrative basis the absolute overstatement multiplied 4.2 times, 0.13 to 0.56 points, as 1−q rose from 0.0896 to 0.3720. Honest consent does not make analytics accurate; it makes the correction compulsory.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four claims make the doctrine testable, and they resolve differently for the two firms. The comprehension figure below comes from 120 interviews pooled across the three arms of Bilkul's test.

Testable claimBilkulBrahmand
Symmetry changes the answerYes: 89.0% to 58.0%No consumer surface
Processing severable from productYes, three purposesNo: telemetry is the product
Answer enforced end to endFails at 2 of 11 vendorsFails for 29 of 48 apps
Person could restate the purposes34 of 120 named oneUsers unaware of the firm
Exhibit 2. The claims, applied to both.

Severability separates the two cases. Bilkul's analytics, personalisation and advertising measurement are genuinely optional: the app plays video without them. Brahmand's telemetry is not, because a store-operations system cannot schedule a shift it cannot see. Consent is the wrong instrument when the processing is inseparable from the service: permission that cannot be refused without losing the service is not freely given, and the honest route is contractual necessity, with the narrow scope that basis demands.

That is where the idea becomes actively misleading. A team reaching for a consent screen because consent sounds respectful creates three liabilities: it implies a choice it will not honour, manufactures a withdrawal right it cannot satisfy, and moves the activity out of the basis that would have supported it. Rachapudi's standing advice was that a consent dialogue in an enterprise product usually means someone skipped the basis analysis. Rallapalli's mirror case is equally real: where processing is severable and valuable, refusing to ask is a decision to fund the product otherwise.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product families break the scope of one answer. Bilkul's commerce tab shares a login with its news feed, and a 2025 consent for "improving your feed" does not cover purchase history sold to a brand. Experts version the purpose, not the product.

Two-sided products break controllership. A marketplace letting sellers place their own measurement pixels is no bystander to what those pixels do; joint controllership makes it answerable for a partner's collection, which is why many marketplaces allow only a server-side feed they gate themselves.

Regulated products break withdrawal. A lending or insurance product under Reserve Bank of India or IRDAI record-keeping duties must retain what a customer asks it to delete; the answer is a retention schedule separating regulatory core from discretionary surround.

Hardware breaks the prompt. Basera Devices' televisions have no keyboard, a ten-foot interface and four usable remote buttons, and the buyer is often not the user: a hotel group fitting 1,100 rooms consents for nobody. Firmware makes the decision durable.

AI-native features break reversibility. A trained model cannot forget one contributor on request, so training data collected under consent carries a withdrawal met only by excluding future runs. The expert move separates reversible inference consent from irreversible training consent, and declines the latter.

At the seams, ownership is the failure. The consent platform belongs to marketing, the mobile gate to engineering, the processing agreement to legal, and the egress test to nobody. Mature firms say privacy is designed in; what works is duller — a release gate that fails the build when a new vendor enters the manifest without a purpose mapping, and a quarterly egress capture with an owner.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The banner is not where consent is lost. A competent practitioner redesigns the dialogue; an expert reads the network trace. The tell-tale sign is initialisation order: a library started in the launch path is not waiting for an answer. The obvious reading — a recorded refusal means nothing was collected — confuses upload suppression with blocked collection.

The level of the acceptance rate carries almost no information. Competent practitioners audit the number; experts audit the gap between symmetric and asymmetric designs, because people do agree. The tell-tale sign is a rate stable across very different designs, which indicates preference, against one moving 31.0 points on a button change, which indicates the button.

Better consent makes your numbers worse before it makes them right. The tell-tale sign is a dashboard that improves in the week a refusal rate rises, because the measured population is more self-selected. The obvious reading is that the screen drew better users. The correction is the bias term: at Bilkul, an absolute overstatement 4.2 times its old size.

Withdrawal is the real test and is almost never instrumented. The tell-tale sign is a schema with an event for consent granted and none for withdrawn: the firm cannot state its own withdrawal rate. Article 7(3) asks whether leaving is as easy as joining, and a team that never measured the exit has no evidence.

You are not storing a decision; you are storing evidence. The tell-tale sign is a consent table with no notice-version column. The question eighteen months later is seldom what the user chose and usually what they were shown. Brahmand had that and still failed: evidence of the ask is not evidence of obedience.

The strictly-necessary bucket is narrower than most teams believe, and that is where the real fight is. The tell-tale sign is a crash reporter, a content-delivery cookie or a fraud signal in the essential tray while feeding a third party for its own ends. Reclassifying one item out costs more acceptance than redesigning the banner.

Dark patterns are mostly not designed. The tell-tale sign is version history: the reject affordance shrinking across three changes, each shipped by someone optimising a metric nobody re-examined. The obvious reading, that someone decided to deceive, is unhelpful: the remedy is a guardrail metric on the refusal path, not an ethics conversation.

Consent fatigue is a real cost that neither side may use as a defence. The tell-tale sign is prompt frequency rising while per-prompt acceptance falls: the firm spends attention to buy a weaker answer. No regulator will accept fatigue as a reason to ask less clearly, nor a growth team to ask less often.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

ContextWhere the fight is
Consumer, ad-fundedThe rate itself: it is revenue
B2B and enterpriseLawful basis, propagation, audit evidence
Platform, marketplaceJoint controllership, signal pass-through
HardwareScarce prompt, unpatchable base
AI productsTraining consent, which withdrawal cannot undo
Exhibit 3. Enforcement, step 4, fails in all five.

In consumer products the acceptance rate is a revenue line, fought in basis points. In enterprise products consent is usually not the lawful basis; the live documents are the processing agreement and the security questionnaire, and buyers enforce faster than regulators. Platforms carry other people's collection and must gate it server-side. Hardware commits for seven years at firmware freeze. AI products face an irreversibility no interface improves.

Stage changes the failure, not the doctrine. At seed stage the risk is a forgotten vendor: one analytics library added in a hurry, no manifest, no egress test. At growth stage it is the optimisation machine, which manufactures dark patterns with no author. At scale it becomes evidentiary: millions of records, dozens of notice versions, an audit asking what one person saw on one day. Where stage does not matter is enforcement: seed-stage and listed products lose consent in the same place, between the recorded answer and the running code.

8. Three worked examples

Bilkul: what symmetry costs

Rajasekaran ran a fourteen-day test from Monday 14 to Sunday 27 September 2026, randomising 180,000 first-launch users into three arms of 60,000. Arm 1 kept the current screen. Arm 2 gave "Accept all" and "Reject all" identical 160 by 48 pixel buttons, changing nothing else. Arm 3 added a plain-language description of each purpose.

Revenue per user a year, ₹58.9452.4451.58
Exhibit 4. The "of which" row is purpose-by-purpose choosers leaving advertising on: 1,224 of 3,600 is 34.0 per cent, 2,880 of 9,000 and 4,224 of 13,200 are 32.0 per cent. Revenue blends ₹61 consented and ₹38 contextual-only.

The 31.0-point fall in accepting everything is not noise: the standard error of that difference is 0.24 points, so the gap runs about 130 standard errors, and Arm 3's further 6.0-point fall about 21. Across 23.4 million active users Arm 2 costs ₹6.50 a user a year — ₹15.20 crore against ₹137.92 crore, 11.0 per cent. Arm 3 costs ₹17.22 crore, 12.5 per cent. Rajasekaran was careful about the base: only first-launch users meet the new screen, and at 1.35 million installs a month that is 16.2 million first launches in a year, so the run-rate effect by month twelve is ₹10.52 crore. The cash effect inside the year is about half that, ₹5.26 crore, because installs arrive through the year, not on day one; the full ₹15.20 crore arrives once the base has been re-prompted. The two weak links, she said, are that first-launch users monetise at the base average and that all 16.2 million persist as users.

Brahmand: the record that proved nothing

Rachapudi's pack held every consent decision and a gate reaching 19 apps, covering 22.6 million of 61.0 million end users, 37.0 per cent. The other 29 apps carried 38.4 million users, 63.0 per cent, for whom Brahmand had processed on a basis its own agreement did not describe. Deprecating release 4.5 and below would cost 14 person-months at ₹2.1 lakh each — ₹29.4 lakh of one-off engineering against the ₹8.4 crore annual renewal that account had tied to the question — the easiest number Ramabadran had seen all year, and the one his account managers had resisted for two quarters.

Basera: the failure, and what recovery cost

Between Tuesday 3 March and Tuesday 30 June 2026, Basera activated 420,000 televisions and set-top boxes with a one-click setup whose "Finish" button carried viewing-analytics consent alongside the network and language settings. It recorded 411,000 of 420,000 devices as consenting, 97.9 per cent. Jwalini Reddivari, the product director in Pune, believed it until a consumer-forum complaint and a 1,100-room hotel group's refusal arrived in one fortnight. The defect was bundling: one affirmative action cannot carry a severable purpose and a setup step, so the consent was never specific.

Basera re-prompted over the sixty days from Wednesday 15 July to Saturday 12 September 2026. Of the 411,000 devices, 376,000 came back online and 181,000 of the 376,000 re-consented, 48.1 per cent; the 35,000 that never reconnected were treated as refusing. Against the 411,000 recorded as consenting that is 44.0 per cent; against all 420,000 activated it is 43.1 per cent. At ₹46 per consenting device a year, addressable advertising fell from ₹1.89 crore to ₹0.83 crore, a loss of ₹1.06 crore, 56.0 per cent. Basera also deleted the viewing history gathered between 3 March and 14 July. Reddivari's conclusion: the ₹1.06 crore was never revenue, only an advance drawn against a consent that did not exist.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic question
Theatre: gate unwiredVendor added, no purpose mappingWhat fired before the tap?
Silent propagationConsole reports complianceWhat does egress show?
Bundled consentOne button ends setup and grants a purposeCan a user finish and refuse?
Un-evidenced recordNo notice-version columnWhat did this person see?
Unmeasured withdrawalNo withdrawal eventWhat is our withdrawal rate?
Exhibit 5. Late-detection costs are in the text.

The costs of catching these late are not symmetric, and ranking them is much of the craft. Theatre and silent propagation are cheap to fix and expensive to have had: every record collected without a basis must be deleted, and deletion destroys the history that justified collecting it. Bundling is usually the dearest, because the remedy is a re-prompt and a re-prompt reveals the true rate to everyone at once, as Basera's 97.9 per cent of activations becoming 43.1 per cent did. An un-evidenced record costs nothing until an audit, then costs a renewal. An unmeasured withdrawal rate costs nothing measurable, which is why it survives in careful organisations: nobody can price an absence.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first position holds that consent is salvageable and symmetry nearly all of it. Its evidence is strong: field studies found fewer than one banner in eight meeting minimal requirements, and that moving the refusal option off the first screen raised acceptance by roughly twenty points; the French regulator's January 2022 cookie decisions totalled €210 million. It would be wrong if, after symmetry, acceptance stayed near ninety per cent and comprehension near Bilkul's 34 of 120.

The second holds that consent cannot do the work, and the honest response is to collect less. Its evidence is the comprehension data, the fatigue data, and an industry answering every rule with a better-looking ask. It would be wrong if delegated consent — a registered consent manager, or a browser-level signal — produced both stable rates and genuine comprehension at scale. Nobody has yet.

The third is Rallapalli's, in its strongest form. Ramamoorthy put the probability of an inquiry reaching Bilkul in enforcement's first three years at 8 per cent, the expected quantum at ₹12 crore, notice-and-consent failures falling under the residual ₹50 crore head rather than the ₹250 crore security head. That is ₹0.96 crore over three years, ₹0.32 crore a year, against ₹15.20 crore foregone: 47.5 to one. On expected-penalty economics, consent quality is overpriced. It would be wrong — Ramamoorthy argued it already is — if the binding constraint were never the regulator. A consent signal an advertising platform judges invalid removes European and British demand, 6.0 per cent of Bilkul's revenue or ₹8.28 crore, with no inquiry.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this argues about button colour. Someone who has internalised it asks three questions in order: the lawful basis, because that decides whether a screen should exist; what runs before the answer, asked of a packet capture rather than a team; and what the record would prove to a stranger in eighteen months. They treat the acceptance rate as a diagnostic, not a target, instrument the withdrawal path as carefully as the happy path, and cost the bias correction into every consented metric. And they will say that a processing activity should not happen at all — the move a studied practitioner rarely makes, because it cannot be reached from inside an argument about the banner.

12. What each decided

Rajasekaran chose Arm 2 for new installs from Friday 23 October and committed to re-prompting the base over two quarters: Arm 3's extra 6.0-point fall bought information she could not yet value; Arm 2's symmetry she could defend. She also made the egress test a release gate: a symmetric screen in front of an unwired vendor is worse than an asymmetric one, adding a false representation to the same collection.

Ramabadran deprecated release 4.5 and below on six months' notice, accepted the account friction, and moved the telemetry the product depends on to contractual necessity with a narrowed retention schedule, leaving two analytics purposes on consent.

  1. Bilkul's ₹10.52 crore run-rate figure assumes first-launch users monetise at the base average of ₹58.94. If they manage two-thirds of that, does the decision change, and which of Rallapalli's arguments survives?
  2. Brahmand's gate covers 37.0 per cent of end users. At what coverage does its processing agreement become true rather than aspirational, and what does Brahmand owe the customers whose users it processed without a basis?
  3. Reddivari calls the ₹1.06 crore an advance against a consent that never existed. What would a finance director say, and what does the disagreement imply for forecasting consent-dependent income?

13. Going deeper

  1. GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes — the text the flow implements; opt-in and opt-out diverge.
  2. Dark patterns taxonomy — names the moves a consent audit looks for.
  3. Privacy by design — moves the argument upstream of the screen, to what is collected.
  4. Data, consent and the DPDP Act — the Indian regime and its consent-manager architecture.
  5. Personalisation vs surveillance — what the consented data is then used for.
  6. Security compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001 — the machinery buyers use to enforce faster than regulators.
  7. Terms of service, SLAs and contracts — where processing that is not consent-based is governed.
  8. IP, patents and trademarks for PMs — the other legal surface product decisions touch.
case20v1-legal.working.with:
Taraka: Early Pay Before Diwali

A teaching case on working with legal and compliance

1. Opening

At 6:30 pm on Tuesday 6 October 2026, Elora Lahkar, senior product manager for payments at Taraka, sat in a glass meeting room in Bengaluru with a screen full of faces. It was 3:00 pm in Berlin and 9:00 am in New Jersey and Toronto. The agenda: confirm the festive campaign for Early Pay, a feature letting a worker draw part of an earned wage before payday.

The campaign agency needed a signed booking by Friday 9 October. After that date, changing or cancelling the ₹42 lakh slate would cost 25 per cent, or ₹10.5 lakh. Launch was pencilled for Monday 26 October, thirteen days before Diwali on Sunday 8 November. Legal had not yet seen the product. The previous afternoon Ehsan Laha, Taraka's head of legal, had written one line to the product channel: "I have not reviewed this and would ask that nobody treat it as cleared." Elora had three days to decide how and when to bring him in.

2. Company background

Taraka was founded in Bengaluru in 2021 by Ekamjot Lashkar, who still serves as chief executive. It runs a payout and payroll app for gig and contract workers, the people who staff the dark stores of quick-commerce firms such as Zepto and Swiggy Instamart, the delivery fleets of Zomato and Swiggy, and contract factories. Employers upload attendance and earnings; Taraka calculates wages and pays workers into their bank accounts through UPI and NEFT. In September 2026 it paid 4,20,000 workers on behalf of 1,900 employer clients.

Revenue for FY2026 (April 2025 to March 2026) was ₹86 crore, against a net loss of ₹14 crore. Cash stood at ₹31 crore on 30 September 2026. Taraka competes with RazorpayX payroll, in-house HR systems at large staffing firms, and start-ups selling earned-wage access directly. Workers' appetite for early cash rises around Diwali, when travel, gifts and household purchases coincide.

3. The situation

Between 1 August and 27 September, Taraka's app showed an "Early Pay" tile to 2,40,000 of the 4,20,000 workers it paid in September, and 38,400 tapped "notify me" (Exhibit 1). The product specification, circulated on 29 September, proposed that eligible workers could draw up to half of their earned wages, twice a month, repaid automatically when the employer's payout cleared. Taraka would charge a flat ₹50 per draw and fund the advances from its own balance sheet.

Elora knew what the feature did commercially but not how the law would see it. A flat fee on money advanced and repaid within weeks looks, to a worker, like a service charge; to a regulator it may look like interest on a loan. If it were a loan, Taraka lending from its own book would need to sit inside the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework or work through a licensed NBFC. The feature would also use salary data supplied by employers, which brings in consent duties under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Ehsan had twice before returned a product request with a one-paragraph refusal; the product team had learnt to avoid asking.

The distributed team saw it differently. The designer in Berlin was worried that a consent screen written to close the sale would be hard to defend later. The data scientist in Toronto had built the draw-limit model and wanted a live launch to calibrate it. The customer-success lead in Singapore reported that workers on the Zepto-linked accounts were already borrowing from informal lenders in the last week of every month.

Exhibit 2 sets out the calendar that bounds the choice: the booking deadline on 9 October, Diwali on 8 November and the Dubai renewal on 30 November. Esmond Lahiry, who heads sales from New Jersey, had told Elora that a Dubai-based staffing group employing 18,000 workers in India would decide on its ₹2.1 crore annual renewal by 30 November, and that Early Pay was the feature its HR director asked about first.

4. The people

Elora Lahkar, senior product manager, payments, Bengaluru. Joined in 2022. She wants Early Pay live while Diwali spending peaks, and a product she will not have to withdraw.

Ehsan Laha, head of legal and compliance, Mumbai. Joined in 2023. He wants to be consulted before dates are promised outside the company, and asked questions he can answer with choices.

Ekamjot Lashkar, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. He wants the Diwali launch, and has said he will "back whatever legal can stand behind".

Esmond Lahiry, head of sales, New Jersey. He wants a firm date he can give the Dubai group, and fears that an open-ended review will cost him the renewal.

5. Exhibits

Exhibits 1 and 2 are discussed in Section 3 and Exhibit 3 in Section 6, where Options A, B and C are described.

6. The options

Exhibit 2 shows each option's dates. All three are priced in Exhibit 3 at the same volume: 19,200 users and ₹23.04 crore of advances a month, for the first three months live.

Option A: Launch on 26 October and review afterwards. Sign the campaign on Friday, launch as a fee-only service funded from Taraka's cash, and ask Ehsan to review the live product, which he estimates at ₹6 lakh of outside work. Taraka keeps the whole fee. The classification question stays open, and Taraka's cash carries the advances.

Option B: Hold for a formal written opinion. Sign the booking on Friday as planned, instruct outside counsel on Monday 12 October for a written opinion by Friday 4 December, then launch on Monday 4 January 2027 on whichever structure it supports. Counsel costs ₹18 lakh and the signed campaign is then cancelled at the ₹10.5 lakh penalty. The Dubai renewal falls due before launch.

Option C: Bring Ehsan in this week with a framed question. Elora would sit down with him on Thursday 8 October and ask him to rank three structures by risk: lending from Taraka's book, lending through a licensed NBFC partner, or an employer-funded advance. He would reply with options by Tuesday 13 October. Pune engineering estimates about twenty days from 13 October to build the partner integration, which moves launch to Monday 2 November, inside the agency's re-flight allowance. Priced here on the partner structure, Taraka receives 50 per cent of the fee, the partner funds the advances, and spend is ₹4 lakh of counsel time and ₹10 lakh of build.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Elora know and not know about how Early Pay would be classified, and which of those unknowns can product answer and which only legal can?
  2. Read Exhibit 3 closely. Which costs and risks does the contribution row leave out, and which assumption in Exhibit 1 would most change the comparison?
  3. Ehsan has twice returned refusals. What should Elora's one-page request on Thursday contain so that he can answer with options, and what should it deliberately not say?
  4. By Friday 9 October, which option should Elora take to Ekamjot, and what would she need to learn in the next week to change her mind?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about timing and framing. A product manager owns the outcome, but cannot see every constraint on it; legal can. The useful habit is to bring the specialist in before dates are public and to ask: here is what we want, here are the structures we can imagine, which risks does each carry and what would reduce them? That turns the specialist from a gate into a co-designer.

One defensible path is Option C. Elora sends Ehsan the specification, Exhibit 1 and three structures on Wednesday, meets him on Thursday, and signs the campaign booking only with the re-flight clause, so that the date moves with the answer. Her reasoning: the cheapest moment to learn the classification is before launch, 2 November still precedes Diwali by six days, and the lower contribution in Exhibit 3 comes without ₹11.52 crore of Taraka cash at stake or the question left open. She would tell Esmond that a decision date of 13 October allows him to give the Dubai group a launch date in the first week of November.

This path rests on assumptions that could fail: the partner may not onboard in three weeks, counsel may rate the structures differently, and the 50 per cent share is untested. A well-reasoned answer names those conditions and the date by which Elora would fall back. Other answers can be defended if explicit about which risk they accept.

Vritant Technologies: One Question on a Procurement Form

Pune, Sunday 18 October 2026. A chief product officer has until Monday morning to settle what her company will say about how its models were trained — and until Friday 30 October to sign it.

1 · Sunday night in BanerThe forty-seventh question

Gitali Mukhopadhyay had printed all forty-seven questions. They lay on her dining table in Baner, in Pune, beside a memo from her general counsel dated Monday 12 October and an interim note from a Mumbai law firm, received the night before.

Question 31 was the one. Is Client Data, or any derivative of Client Data, used to train, tune or improve any model made available by the Supplier to any other customer? Yes / No. Vipanchi Housing Finance, which asked it, accounted for ₹18.4 crore of Vritant Technologies' ₹96.0 crore of revenue in the year to 31 March 2026 — 18.4 of 96.0, or 19.2 per cent — and comes up for renewal on Tuesday 15 December. The answer falls due on Friday 30 October, signed by one of Vritant's two signatories.

At 09:30 on Monday, Gaganendra Maity wanted a position; at 11:00, Grishmita Dihingia's squad in Bengaluru locked the quarter's sprint plan. Gitali had four options on the back of the memo and no confidence in them.

2 · Company historyVritant Technologies, 2019 to 2026

Maity founded Vritant in Pune in March 2019 with two colleagues from telecom services, to sell one place from which a lender could run its customer conversations — voice, WhatsApp, in-app chat, the TRAI-governed SMS channel — transcripts stored and searchable. By October 2026 it employed 310 people: 142 in Pune, 103 in Bengaluru, 27 elsewhere in India, 14 in Singapore, nine in Dubai, six in Toronto, five in New Jersey, four in Berlin.

The decision that shapes October 2026 was taken in July 2021. Vipanchi was Vritant's first contract worth more than ₹10 crore a year, and its procurement team would not move without a clause of its own drafting. Clause 14.3 reads: Supplier shall not use Client Data, or any derivative thereof, to train, tune or improve any model, service or feature made available to any other customer of Supplier. Maity signed it. Of the eleven enterprise contracts signed between August 2021 and December 2022, nine carry the same clause, which had entered a vendor-governance template procurement teams copied from one another. Exhibit 1 shows its reach.

Source: the contract register, reconciled to the FY26 audited revenue schedule on 30 September 2026. Clause presence is a flag set by whoever filed the contract; the fourth column's wording was added by hand this month.

3 · The industryWhat Vritant sells into

Indian conversational software is crowded. Jio Haptik, Yellow.ai, Gupshup, Exotel and Ozonetel sell into the same procurement committees; Infosys and TCS sit between vendor and lender as integrators and as the parties who fill in the vendor-governance questionnaires. Open Indic speech work from Sarvam AI and AI4Bharat has made it cheap to start and expensive to be distinctive: differentiation has moved to code-mixed speech, which needs volume to learn.

Regulation shapes the product more than competition does. Vritant's clients are supervised by the Reserve Bank of India, IRDAI or SEBI, and the RBI's Master Direction on outsourcing of information-technology services requires a lender to flow its obligations down to a vendor like Vritant and keep a right to audit it. CERT-In's directions require logs kept 180 days. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the rules notified under it in November 2025 set the maximum penalty for a failure of reasonable security safeguards at ₹250 crore. Vritant's position, in every contract, is that it is a Data Processor on its clients' instructions, each client being the Data Fiduciary that must obtain consent and publish the notice. Vaarunee in Dubai falls under the UAE's federal personal-data law instead, which is why its contract carries an annexure rather than clause 14.3.

4 · The situation in detailWhat was believed in May, and the dates now on the table

Engage Copilot drafts an agent's next reply; the agent sends it, edits it or ignores it. The design document of 28 April 2026 specified one model trained on transcripts pooled across clients, because code-mixed speech could not be learned from one client's volume. Pooled training began on Tuesday 5 May 2026 on an export covering the fourteen weeks from Monday 26 January to Sunday 3 May 2026 — 98 days. The closed pilot went live on 13 July.

Three things were believed in May: that the export was de-identified, so what was pooled was not Client Data; that clause 14.3 was satisfied because inference was per client, from an endpoint in that client's name; and that consent was the clients' affair, Vritant being a processor. The interim note of 17 October reads the clause as covering a pooled checkpoint without qualification. Exhibit 2 is the redaction audit.

Exhibit 2 — Identifier classes left unredacted, in a sample of 2,000 transcripts

Scale: 0 transcripts at x = 290, 0.300 px per transcript, so the 1,412 bar ends at 290 + 1,412 × 0.300 = 713.6. The taxonomy's other 11 classes — mobile, email, Aadhaar, card, UPI handle, IFSC and five more — were redacted throughout. The eight above appear together in 1,721 of the 2,000 transcripts, or 86.1 per cent: the union of the bars, not their sum.

Source: sample drawn Monday 9 February 2026 from the conversation store, which retains 180 days, scored by two reviewers in Pune. The pipeline moved from v2 to v3 on 19 March 2026, when the speech-to-text vendor changed and the redaction rules were rewritten. It has not been redrawn.

Exhibit 3 is the evidence on which Copilot was funded. The evaluation of 11 May 2026 put the pooled model twenty points above six per-client models; the September holdout, drawn after the training window closed, put the same comparison at 12.9 points.

The questionnaire arrived on Friday 2 October 2026, and Gautamee Baruah's team in Singapore routed it to product rather than to legal, as it had the previous four. Gitali took the architecture to Gunadhar Mahalanabis on Tuesday 6 October — five months and a day after pooled training began, and the first time he had seen it. He asked for the May checkpoint's lineage, the redaction audit and the consent notices, and received the audit of 9 February and a lineage extract compiled on 9 October. His memo of 12 October rests on those two and on the clause.

On Wednesday 14 October, Dihingia established what the extract had not: training lineage goes to a build log retained thirty days, so no attestable record survives of which clients' transcripts entered the May checkpoint. The 2025 per-client checkpoints, she added, had never been deleted. External counsel was instructed on 15 October; the full opinion is promised for Thursday 5 November, six days after the questionnaire is due. Exhibit 4 lays the dates against each other.

Exhibit 4 — Timeline; the lower strip expands October and November 2026

Scale: upper strip, 1 January 2026 at x = 70, 1.5385 px a day, so 9 February sits at 70 + 39 × 1.5385 = 130.0; lower strip, 1 October 2026 at x = 70, 11.0 px a day, so 30 October sits at 70 + 29 × 11.0 = 389.0; the shaded bands are the September holdout, October 2026 and the Diwali shutdown.

5 · The peopleEight positions

Gitali Mukhopadhyay, 41, chief product officer, Pune, since 2022. Treats the form and the architecture as one decision; Copilot is her whole FY27 roadmap. Has not said that the 28 April design document, which names pooled training, carries her approval and never reached legal.

Gaganendra Maity, 52, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Wants the form answered on time and architecture on its own clock; he is six weeks into Series C talks in which Copilot is the story. Has not repeated what he told the board in August 2021, that clause 14.3 was boilerplate.

Gunadhar Mahalanabis, 47, general counsel, Pune, since 18 August 2025. Will certify neither answer until the May checkpoint's composition is established; he is one of the two signatories. Has not mentioned an associate's note of 24 March 2026 flagging the v3 redaction rewrite, which he filed for the next quarterly review.

Grishmita Dihingia, 38, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru. Puts a clean rebuild at 126 person-weeks; her squad of nine is also the only team that can ship the FY27 roadmap. Has not volunteered that the thirty-day log retention was her cost decision in 2024, nor that the 2025 checkpoints sit in cold storage.

Gurmehar Neog, 35, head of data science, Toronto. Calls pooling the product rather than an implementation detail; his headcount case rests on Copilot. Has not said that Panel A's test set was de-duplicated by transcript identifier, not utterance text.

Gautamee Baruah, 44, head of customer success, Singapore. Wants clients told before procurement finds out; her variable pay is 70 per cent weighted to gross renewal. Has not reported describing Copilot's pooled training, approvingly, to Dhauladhar's head of operations on 9 September 2026.

Gargee Mushahary, 33, head of design, Berlin. Holds the consent notice to be the client's instrument, not Vritant's; she owns the notice component clients embed. Has not raised that three of the notices in Exhibit 5 render through it with the purpose list the client supplied, unreviewed.

Gobinda Marak, 49, chief digital officer, Vaarunee Financial Group, Dubai. Holds that Arabic-and-English draft quality is what Vaarunee bought; his 2027 cost-per-contact target assumes Copilot. Has not told Vritant that Vaarunee's board asked him in September to find a second vendor by the third quarter of 2027.

Gunjit Mallabarman, who runs North American sales from New Jersey, has two United States lenders in late-stage evaluation, both calling pooled training across customers a disqualifier.

6 · VoicesIn the team's own words

“A checkpoint fitted on those transcripts is a derivative on any ordinary reading. 14.3 restricts use; it is not a data-protection test. I was asked in October to approve a design, not in May to advise on one.”

Gunadhar Mahalanabis, memo to the executive team, Monday 12 October 2026

“This is a Mumbai contract problem. Vaarunee has no clause 14.3 and our annexure permits aggregate analytics. Tell me in writing this month.”

Gobinda Marak, call with Vritant, Thursday 15 October, 17:30 GST / 19:00 IST

“Nobody is asking you to lie. The form asks about Client Data. We took the identifiers out. What we do not have is fourteen weeks of engineering to spend first.”

Gaganendra Maity, one-to-one with Gitali Mukhopadhyay, Saturday 17 October

7 · The optionsAs Gitali currently frames them

Gitali wrote the four options on Saturday night. Exhibit 6 prices all four over the twelve months from 1 November 2026 at one volume: Vritant's FY26 throughput of 2.14 crore conversations across 47 clients.

8 · The deadline and the hard constraintsWhat cannot move

The questionnaire is due Friday 30 October 2026, signed by Maity or Mahalanabis; Vipanchi's policy treats a late or qualified return as a finding, and the renewal is minuted on Tuesday 15 December.
