exp20v2-legal.working.with:
Working with Legal and Compliance

How a product manager brings counsel in early and comes away with options instead of a no.

1. Forty-nine days

On Monday 7 September 2026, Vetrivel Ekambaram, group product manager for lending at Loknidhi, a Hyderabad non-bank lender regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), had forty-nine days until the planned launch of Top-up Now. The feature showed an existing customer a banner saying her credit line had been raised, with one tap to draw the extra money. Loknidhi had 41 lakh monthly active users, and 6.4 lakh of them qualified. At a 9 per cent take-up and an average draw of ₹8,000, the feature would disburse ₹46.08 crore in its first thirty days, with launch ahead of Diwali on 8 November.

He also had a memory. In 2025 his team had shown a finished Auto-Pay Nudge to the legal department on day 41 of a 49-day plan. Seventeen engineer-days of rework and a five-week slip followed. The lawyers had not been obstructive; they had been handed a decision already made, and a lawyer asked to bless finished work has only one safe answer.

Vasumathi Eswaramoorthy, deputy general counsel, promised three working days on any request. Vikraman Erukulla ran compliance. Vetrivel's choice was small and consequential: polish the build first, or take an unfinished idea to two people who might say no by Thursday.

Figure 1 sets the two schedules side by side. In 2025 the first contact came after the build was nearly complete, so every legal comment landed as a defect. In 2026 the first contact came on day 3, so the same kind of comment landed as a requirement while the design could still bend.

2. The idea

Working with legal and compliance means treating them as a source of options rather than a gate at the end. Two terms first. Legal, or counsel, interprets what a law, regulation or contract requires and advises on the risk of departing from it. Compliance designs and monitors the controls that keep the company inside those requirements, and reports to regulators. They overlap, but they are not the same job.

The problem the practice solves is a mismatch of information. The product manager knows the user, the revenue and what the screen actually does. Counsel knows the rules and what regulators have punished. Exposure, the money and disruption a company would lose if a rule were broken, is only visible when the two are combined. Contact made late forces a yes or no on finished work; contact made early produces versions.

The intellectual lineage is the privacy-by-design movement of Ann Cavoukian, then Ontario's privacy commissioner, who argued from the 1990s, and in seven formal principles around 2009, that protection is cheaper built in than bolted on. Modern rules, including India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP), reward that habit by scaling duties to risk. Vetrivel's sentence for the meeting: "I am not asking whether we may; I am asking which versions of this are safe enough, what each costs, and who must sign the one we choose."

3. How it actually works

Step 1 is the brief: the objective, the user, the data used, the money that moves, the screens as they will look, what the manager is unsure about, and the date by which a decision is needed. On 10 September, day 3, Vetrivel sent Vasumathi exactly that, with the banner mock-up. Screens matter because a feature's legal character lives in what the user sees, not in its name.

Step 2, triage, is usually implicit. Someone has to decide which questions belong to counsel, which to compliance, and which to the privacy and security teams. Here two issues surfaced. As Vasumathi read the RBI's digital lending rules, a credit limit may not be increased without the borrower's explicit consent on record. And the scoring used account data the customer had shared at onboarding for a different purpose, which the DPDP Act treats as a problem because consent must be specific to a purpose.

Step 3 asks for options, not a verdict: what must be true for this to be acceptable, and what are the cheapest ways to make it true? Step 4 is the one practitioners skip. Counsel supplies a rough likelihood and size of harm for each option; the manager supplies build days and the revenue effect. On 16 September, day 9, she returned two versions on the fourth working day, because pricing them took longer than her promised three. On 18 September, day 11, the chief business officer chose one, and Vikraman logged the decision and its date for later monitoring.

Steps 5 and 6 are what make the loop a loop. A decision with no signature is a hope, and a feature that later gains a new data source or a larger limit is, legally, a new feature. Vikraman's team therefore attached a re-review trigger to the log: any change to eligibility, pricing or data use sends the brief back to step 1.

4. A worked example

The two versions were these. Version A shipped as designed. Version B added a screen asking for the customer's explicit consent to the higher limit, showed the key fact statement (a one-page summary of the loan's price and terms that the RBI requires before acceptance), and asked for fresh consent to use her data for this purpose. B added a week to the schedule and, by the team's estimate from a similar prior consent screen, cut take-up from 9 to 7.5 per cent. Vasumathi's judgement, which she labelled rough, was a 25 per cent chance that A would draw a regulatory finding in the first thirty days and 4 per cent for B, with a cost of ₹600 lakh if it did (refunds, remediation and a forced pause). All figures below cover thirty days from each version's own launch and are in ₹ lakh.

LineVersion AVersion B
Eligible users6,40,0006,40,000
Take-up9.0%7.5%
Customers drawing (eligible x take-up)57,60048,000
Disbursed at ₹8,000 each4,608.003,840.00
Contribution at 3% of disbursed138.24115.20
Chance of finding (counsel's estimate)25%4%
Expected loss (chance x 600)150.0024.00
Net (contribution less expected loss)-11.7691.20

Version A earns more contribution, 138.24 against 115.20, yet nets less once expected loss is counted: 138.24 less 150.00 is -11.76, while 115.20 less 24.00 is 91.20. The point is not the precision. It is that the question "can we?" had become "which version, at what price?"

Now change one input. Suppose the consent screen hurts more than estimated and B's take-up is 6.0 per cent. Customers drawing fall to 38,400, disbursal to 3,072.00, contribution to 92.16, and net to 68.16. B still wins. The more useful calculation is the break-even: A matches B's original 91.20 only if its expected loss is 138.24 less 91.20, or 47.04, which is a 7.84 per cent chance (47.04 / 600). Against the weaker B at 68.16, the threshold is 11.68 per cent (138.24 less 68.16 is 70.08, divided by 600). If counsel's 25 per cent is even roughly right, A loses by a wide margin.

One caution on basis. Contribution is counted for thirty days although a drawn loan keeps earning, while the ₹600 lakh is a one-time hit assumed to land in the same window. That understates A more than B, because A disburses more, but the order would only flip if contribution accrued for about 5.5 times the thirty-day figure (23.04 k > 126 gives k > 5.47). The window is a convention, and a careful reader should know it.

5. Seven nuances

Legal and compliance are different functions

Counsel answers "what does the law require and how risky is this reading?" Compliance answers "are we in fact doing what we said, and can we prove it?" A feature can pass the first and fail the second, when the control exists on paper and not in the code.

A "no" often answers a vague question

"Is this okay?" invites the cautious reply. "Here are two designs, the data each uses and the date I need to decide; which risks does each carry?" invites a comparison. The discipline is in how the question is built, not in persuasion.

Risk appetite belongs to the business

Counsel advises; an accountable executive decides how much exposure to carry. Managers who treat counsel's caution as a veto, or counsel's tolerance as their own cover, have both misread whose decision it is.

Probabilities are judgements

The 25 and 4 per cent are informed guesses. Ask for ranges, ask what would move them, and use the break-even to see whether the choice depends on the number at all.

Lawful is not the same as fair, and rules come in layers

Statute, regulator direction, contract and the company's own policy each bind differently. A design can be legal and still be one a customer would feel tricked by; the law is a floor, not a design principle.

Written advice has a privilege and a trail

Privilege protects confidential legal advice from disclosure in disputes, and forwarding it widely can weaken that protection. Ask counsel how they want questions and answers recorded before copying a channel.

Advice has a date and an edge

The DPDP rules are phasing in, and regulators issue clarifications. An opinion is valid for a stated version of the law and of the feature. Counsel also cannot tell you whether customers will accept the design, or whether the feature is worth building.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

SettingWhere exposure sitsWhat changes in practice
ConsumerRegulators and individual customers; disclosures, consent, fairnessScreens are the legal object, so counsel needs mock-ups early
B2BContract terms, service levels, liability capsCounsel is often negotiating; the manager brings the promise, counsel the clause
MarketplaceTwo sides plus the platform's own dutiesWho is the seller of record, and who holds the data, are the first questions
Early-stageFounder-level, one outside lawyerFewer reviews, so ask for a ranked list of the three risks that matter
Large companySpecialist teams and committeesQueues and intake forms; the brief and the decision date do the work

At Loknidhi's scale, a three-day turnaround target exists because there is an intake process. A ten-person start-up with a retained lawyer works the other way round: no queue, but hours are paid for and the manager must know which question is worth them.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Bringing legal in after the buildReview requests cluster in the last two weeks; launch dates slipLegal is an approval stageSubtract the date legal first saw the feature from the launch date
Asking a yes-or-no questionOne-word replies; later surpriseA single answer is what counsel producesCount the options in the last request
Treating sign-off as the decision"Legal approved it" in a post-incident reviewCounsel owns the riskName the executive who chose and recorded the risk

8. What good looks like

Good is the schedule in Figure 1's lower lane. A one-page brief goes out within the first week. Counsel replies with options and ranges, not a verdict. The manager brings build days and revenue, the accountable executive chooses, and the compliance head records the choice and sets a re-review trigger. Nobody is surprised in week seven, and the customer reaches a screen that asks her permission. The manager states the decision date at the outset, frames each question as a risk and its options, and gets the answer back in writing with a named owner.

9. Closing

The chief business officer chose Version B on 18 September, on Vetrivel's recommendation, and the launch moved to Monday 2 November, one week later than planned. The reasoning was not that A was illegal. It was that A's own revenue advantage disappeared at any counsel estimate of the chance of a finding above 7.84 per cent, and nobody in the room believed the chance was that low. Three questions remained: whether the consent screen could be made clearer without cutting take-up further, whether the pre-approved offers should be trialled on a smaller group first, and who would own the re-review.

Next, study how product management works in regulated domains, where counsel and compliance sit inside the roadmap process instead of beside it; the habit above is its first step.

Two questions to sit with. (1) Which decision on your current roadmap has been reviewed only after it was built, and what would it have cost to ask on day 3? (2) If counsel's probability were off by a factor of three, would your choice change, and how would you find out before deciding?
exp40v2-legal.working.with:
Working with Legal and Compliance

Why counsel answers the question you ask, and how to ask one that returns a priced menu instead of a refusal.

1. Two decisions on different clocks

On Monday 17 August 2026, in a converted mill off Pune's Mumbai–Bengaluru highway, Yamalini Gnanaraj had sixteen days to choose about eleven words. Mithuna Devices sold a ₹4,999 wrist band tracking sleep and pulse; 3.4 lakh units had shipped since October 2024, the run-rate was 9,200 a month, and 42,000 of the 1.9 lakh monthly actives paid ₹149 a month for Mithuna Plus. Her feature, Rhythm Watch, flagged irregular pulse patterns. The engineering was finished; the sentence on the carton was not, because the moment it named a condition rather than a sensation the band became a medical device under India's Medical Devices Rules, 2017, needing a licence from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. Carton artwork locked on Wednesday 2 September. Software froze on Monday 12 October. The band reached shelves on Monday 23 November. The legal question had to be settled forty days before the feature it described could be tested. Four routes were open: the wellness wording; the wellness wording backed by a validation study; a licensed medical-device claim, nine to fourteen months out; and a cleared third-party algorithm, whose term sheet had to be signed by Friday 28 August.

Three weeks later and 900 kilometres south-east, on Tuesday 8 September, Yugandhar Gudipati faced a quieter version. Murasu Health Cloud adjudicated health-insurance claims for sixteen insurers and third-party administrators out of Chennai, on ₹48 crore of recurring revenue — a mean of ₹3.00 crore per customer — and processed 9.6 lakh claims a year, 6.2 lakh of them carrying a free-text discharge summary, about 65 per cent. An assistant that read the summary and proposed an adjudication with a citation cut handling time from 11.4 minutes to 7.1. Murasu was not the data fiduciary for any of it; its customers were, and its authority to touch the data came from sixteen master services agreements it had signed itself. In March 2026 a similar feature was paused for seven weeks when a customer's security reviewer found it had trained on that customer's claims. He did not want a second pause, and he did not want to ask his deputy general counsel, Yennila Gurubaran, whether the company could train on customer data, because he already knew that answer.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

The practice has a precise shape. Working with legal early means putting a decision in front of counsel while more than one design can still be built within the schedule, framed not as a request for approval but as options with the risk each carries and who bears it. The output sought is not a yes. It is a price list.

The problem it solves is a cost curve, not a cultural one. Barry Boehm's 1981 observation that a defect grows roughly an order of magnitude more expensive with each phase it survives applies here with one cruel addition: a late legal constraint usually cannot be engineered away at all, because it binds what the product may say or keep, not how it is built. Ann Cavoukian's privacy-by-design principles, formulated at the Ontario Information and Privacy Commissioner's office from the mid-1990s, made the architectural case; GDPR Article 25 turned it into law in 2018, and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with Rules notified in 2025, built the expectation into a fiduciary-and-processor structure.

Four schools disagree substantively, not temperamentally. The gatekeeping school treats sign-off as a release stage; it signs risk appetite is set by the board, not by a product manager and not a product team may accept residual legal risk on its own record. The embedded product-counsel school, grown up inside platform companies through the 2010s, signs the second and refuses the first: counsel who sees options prices them, counsel who sees finished work can only bless or block. The privacy-by-design school refuses both framings, since Cavoukian's principles reject zero-sum trade-offs; it signs the cheapest control removes the data and not residual risk can be traded against functionality. The three-lines school, from the Institute of Internal Auditors' 2013 paper, signs the first line owns the control — product, not compliance — and not legal owns the decision.

3. Mechanics: how a priced menu is actually built

Experts do not begin with a meeting; they begin with their own paper. Yugandhar's first act on 8 September was to pull the improvement-rights clause from all sixteen agreements, because “may we train on customer data?” has no single answer at Murasu. It has four, written down.

The inventory converts one unanswerable question into four answerable ones, and fixes the denominators: ten contracts permit some form of training, six do not. Yugandhar's memo described four builds with the precondition each needed, and asked Yennila for three things per option — the probability of an adverse event, the loss if it happened, the cost to mitigate. She returned them on Friday 11 September, inside her three-working-day commitment.

The formal treatment is simple, and its simplicity is the point. For each option, expected first-year cost E = p × L + M + D × c: p the probability of the adverse event, L the loss given it, M mitigation, D days from the priced menu of Friday 11 September to the option's first rupee of revenue, c the cost of a day. Murasu set L at ₹400 lakh in every row — one mean-ACV customer terminating for cause at ₹300 lakh plus ₹100 lakh of re-adjudication, notification and model rebuild — and c from the plan: ₹5 lakh per customer-year, ten of the sixteen expected to licence it, so ₹50 lakh a year or ₹0.137 lakh a day.

Two second-order effects follow, both usually left implicit. First, the cheapest option is not the strongest product. Retrieval-only saves 2.6 minutes a claim rather than 4.3 — about 60 per cent of the benefit — so the commercial forecast fell from ten licences to six. Charge the four lost licences against Option A and its burden is ₹23.75 lakh plus ₹20.00 lakh forgone, or ₹43.75 lakh, against Option C's ₹51.02 lakh: A still wins, but by ₹7.27 lakh, and ties if retrieval-only converts between four and five of the sixteen. Second, incentives. A lawyer who writes “no” bears nothing if the no was wrong; one who writes “Option C, residual risk 0.04” has put a falsifiable number on a record that outlives the launch. Resistance to options-framing is not obstruction but a rational response to accountability, and a practitioner who treats it as obstruction loses the lawyer.

4. When the idea holds, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as tests. Murasu passes all three; Mithuna does not.

First: two materially different designs must still be buildable inside the schedule. “Early” is a property of the option set, not the calendar. Murasu passes easily on 8 September, with all four options live. Mithuna passes only until 2 September, and only on the carton: once the artwork locks the two surviving routes differ only in-app, and those close on 12 October, so one feature has two deadlines for two legal questions — a distinction the hardware schedule creates and the roadmap conceals.

Second: counsel must be able to price the options, which requires written instruments or observable precedent. Murasu passes: sixteen contracts, readable, with clauses that exist or do not. Mithuna largely fails. There is little published Indian practice on where a wellness notification becomes a diagnostic claim, so Yadagiri Gorrepati, Mithuna's head of regulatory affairs, could bound the magnitude confidently and the probability only loosely. Where counsel cannot price, the right ask is not “give me options” but “tell me what would have to be true for each of these to be defensible” — a request for the test, not the verdict.

Third: the downside must be compensable in money. Here the approach turns actively misleading, because expected-cost arithmetic recommends gambles right on average and fatal once. Murasu's worst case is money, bounded by a terminating customer. Mithuna's is not: a stop-sale on its only SKU runs at ₹4.60 crore of gross revenue a month, and Yadagiri Gorrepati's working assumption was three months for a re-registration cycle, and the Medical Devices Rules attach consequences to persons as well as companies. The correct rule there is a constraint: rule out whatever worst case the balance sheet cannot absorb, then optimise inside what is left.

5. Hard edges and organisational seams

In a multi-product company the consent store is shared, so one team's lawful basis is another's ceiling: a string drafted for billing will not carry a recommendation engine, and the second team learns this six weeks from launch. On a two-sided marketplace the sides are not symmetric in law — often fiduciary to the consumer, merely a processor for the merchant — so one “user data” policy is wrong on one side. In regulated domains the regulator is a second customer with its own service level: CERT-In's 2022 directions give six hours to report an incident, a requirement about logging and on-call. In hardware plus software lead times invert the order of decisions, and firmware in a user's hand cannot be rolled back. In AI-native products the training-data question is a contract question before a privacy one — Exhibit 1, not the statute, decided Murasu's menu — and model behaviour is a distribution, so “the assistant will never” is unkeepable where “a human approves every adjudication” is keepable.

The seams are where the practice fails. Intake queues batch weekly, so a Tuesday question and a Thursday one are the same question a week apart; and a thumbs-up in a group chat reads as approval to the team and as nothing to the lawyer who sent it. What mature companies do, as against what their process maps claim, is not more review: pre-cleared patterns, self-certification for anything matching one, sampling audit rather than universal gating, and a register where every accepted item has a named owner and a dated review. The map shows a legal-review gate; the register is the real control.

6. Nine distinctions that separate command from competence

Early means before the option set closes. The tell is a team that books counsel in week one and brings a finished specification in week six: early twice, asked once. The obvious reading — that early is a date — misses that a calendar can be generous while the design is fixed.

A “no” usually answers the broadest version of your question. The tell is that it arrives faster than the stated service level: a fast refusal means the lawyer recognised a category, not that she assessed your case. Narrow, do not escalate.

Counsel's scope is the firm's exposure, not your feature's. The tell is an objection naming a different product, or a customer you do not serve. The obvious reading is that she misunderstood; usually she saw something you cannot.

Options-framing transfers accountability onto counsel, so resistance is rational. The tell is a request for the question in writing. Experts volunteer it and name the risk owner.

Read your own contracts before you ask. The tell is that the first request is a clause inventory, not a meeting. A lawyer asked to summarise sixteen agreements takes two weeks; one pricing four options against an inventory, three days.

Residual risk is only accepted if it has an owner and a number. The tell is a memo naming a person and an amount. “Legal is comfortable” is the absence of a decision, and it evaporates under audit.

Privilege is an architecture, not a label. The tell is two documents — a factual record of what the product does, and a separate advice document — not one memo stamped confidential. The stamp on a mixed document protects neither half.

A regulator's silence is an unpriced option, not permission. The tell is someone saying nobody has been fined for this yet. Enforcement arrives in waves, and the first selects on visibility.

The cheapest control removes the data or the claim. The tell is a winning option with fewer fields or quieter words, not more consent screens. A disclosure is a sprint; deleting a field is an argument with a stakeholder.

7. What actually changes by product type and stage

In consumer products the binding constraint is what the interface says, because the user has no negotiating counterparty and the claim is the contract; the legal question is a copy question and belongs with design. In B2B and enterprise it is the paper, as Murasu shows: the statute sets a floor, the agreement sets the envelope, and a PM who cannot read a limitation-of-liability clause cannot size their own downside. In platforms and marketplaces the live question is allocation — who indemnifies whom, and whether the cap covers the exposure the platform creates. In hardware lead times dominate, so questions sequence backwards from the longest physical commitment. In AI products the novelty is narrower than the discourse suggests: provenance, honesty of the claim, and human-in-the-loop design are old questions at new volumes.

Stage changes less than is said. Early-stage teams have no counsel and should buy four hours of advice on the decisions expensive to reverse — data architecture, claims, the first enterprise contract template — not a general review. At scale the problem inverts: plenty of counsel, no triage, so the discipline becomes pattern libraries and sampling. The practice is identical at both ends; only the scarce resource changes.

8. Three worked examples

Murasu, the inventory. The gain came from reading sixteen clauses before asking one question. Asked broadly, the answer would have been governed by the three prohibiting contracts, which hold ₹840 lakh of the ₹4,800 lakh book; the four-way split showed Option A needed nothing from any of the sixteen, retrieval at inference being service delivery rather than development. It shipped 23 October rather than 15 December.

Mithuna, the carton. The print run was 1.1 lakh cartons at ₹7.40, about twelve months of cover at the current run-rate. Cartons were due at the warehouse on 18 November, so changing the wording after the 2 September lock means scrapping ₹8.14 lakh of board and a three-week reprint the 23 November shelf date cannot absorb. Resolving the same sentence at the 17 August design review costs one meeting. That ratio, not a principle, is why hardware teams run legal ahead of engineering.

Marutham Freight, the failure. The Coimbatore load-matching marketplace brought counsel in early and still lost, because it asked whether the product was lawful rather than who bore the loss when it went wrong. Counsel confirmed lawfulness. In the quarter to December 2025, 1,240 of 14,800 consignments moved with an e-way-bill mismatch — 8.4 per cent — and gross penalty exposure across shippers, at a mean ₹41,000 of tax at risk, was ₹5.08 crore before adjudication or set-off: an upper bound, larger than anything the contract contemplated. Marutham's liability cap was twelve months' fees, ₹3.74 lakh mean across the 38 affected shippers, or ₹1.42 crore — 28 per cent of that gross upper bound, the remainder sitting outside any cap and, by default, on the shippers. Yennarasu Govindasamy's recovery ran eleven weeks, from the 14 January 2026 discovery to 1 April: a pre-submission check cut mismatches to 128 of 14,200 in the June quarter, 0.9 per cent, and a retro-fit indemnity was signed by 31 of the 38. The lawful-or-not question was answered correctly and had never been the question.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Asking for approval instead of options. Warning sign: the request contains the words “sign off”. Diagnostic: can counsel answer in one word? If yes, it is not a question. Late cost: a week of calendar per round-trip, and a refusal with nothing to appeal.

Treating the statute as the whole constraint. Warning sign: nobody has opened a contract. Diagnostic: which of our own agreements forbids this? Late cost: the seven weeks Murasu lost in March 2026, when a customer's reviewer found it first.

Confusing lawfulness with allocation. Warning sign: counsel says “yes, that's legal” and the team is satisfied. Diagnostic: if this goes wrong, which party pays, under which clause? Late cost: up to ₹3.66 crore of Marutham's upper-bound exposure sat outside any cap, carried by the 38 shippers.

Accepting risk without an owner. Warning sign: the decision lives in a chat thread. Diagnostic: whose budget absorbs this, at what number? Late cost: unprovable at diligence, so an acquirer prices it at the maximum.

Sequencing legal behind engineering. Warning sign: the first legal milestone falls after a physical or contractual lock. Diagnostic: what is the longest irreversible commitment here? Late cost: Mithuna's ₹8.14 lakh of board and a missed shelf date.

Optimising expectation on a non-compensable tail. Warning sign: a spreadsheet multiplying a small probability by a company-ending number. Diagnostic: could we pay this next month? Late cost: correct on average, gone once.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether to write residual risk down. Yekanath Guntupalli, an external technology-law partner in Bengaluru, holds that an undocumented acceptance is not a decision and that registers are what make product teams responsible. Yennila Gurubaran holds that a register is a discovery target converting a judgement call into evidence of knowledge. His position rests on governance evidence that unowned risks recur, hers on litigation experience that the record is read by an adversary, not an auditor. He is wrong if adversarial exposure dominates regulatory exposure; she is wrong if the firm's main risk is repetition.

Expectation against constraint. One camp holds that every risk has a price and refusing to compute it is cowardice; the other that tail risks are categorically different and expectation arithmetic assumes infinite capital. The first is wrong if ruin probabilities are material at the scales firms operate; the second if firms overestimate tails, which some insurance pricing suggests.

Embedded counsel against an independent second line. Embedding buys speed and context; critics argue it produces capture, counsel who co-authored a design being unable to refuse it. The evidence is thin both ways.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this arrives with an inventory rather than a request, the probability and the loss already estimated so counsel corrects numbers instead of inventing them. They name the risk owner unprompted. They can state without checking which of the next quarter's decisions are irreversible and what the longest lock in the plan is. They read a refusal as evidence the question was too broad, and re-ask within a day rather than escalating within an hour. And they can tell a risk the company should price from one it should not take — the judgement the arithmetic cannot make.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Yamalini Gnanaraj shipped the wellness wording, froze a conservative in-app message on 12 October, and commissioned a ten-week retrospective validation study on 8 September, due 17 November — too late for the freeze, early enough for a stronger claim after launch. Her reasoning was the constraint test: at 0.45 the diagnostic wording carried ₹6.21 crore of expected loss against a ₹1.74 crore gain, and the ₹13.80 crore worst case equalled 7.3 months of current burn. Yugandhar Gudipati took Option A, began the six amendments in parallel as a 15 December path to Option C, and recorded Yennila Gurubaran's 0.03 with his own name against it.

Q1. Exhibit 2 holds the loss at ₹400 lakh for all four options. Which row's loss figure is most likely wrong, in which direction, and does correcting it change the ranking?

Q2. Mithuna's 0.06 and 0.45 are elicited, not measured. What evidence available before 2 September would have moved them, and what would obtaining it have cost?

Q3. If a written register raises adversarial exposure, under what conditions is the register itself the larger risk — and who in a company is positioned to make that call?

13. Going deeper

  • Terms of service, SLAs and contracts — the instruments that set your envelope; without them, no Exhibit 1.
  • Product management in regulated domains — the regulator as second customer, the licence as asset.
  • Privacy by design — the architectural school, removing questions rather than pricing them.
  • Data, consent and the DPDP Act — the fiduciary-and-processor split that decided Murasu's duties.
  • GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes — the same mechanics at higher penalties, with extraterritorial reach.
  • Personalisation vs surveillance — purpose limitation turning growth features into legal questions.
  • Consent flows and cookie UX — where a lawful basis is built or quietly broken.
  • Security compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001 — attestations that let a buyer accept your answers unaudited.

Pratibimb Technologies and the Certificate in the Deck

What SOC 2 and ISO 27001 prove, what they cost, and who is actually asking

1. The night before

At twenty to eleven on Sunday 15 November 2026, Bidyut Indasi sat at his dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with two documents and a calendar open: a certificate issued to his company in November 2024, and a procurement policy published on 22 October by the Dubai hospital group that paid Pratibimb Technologies ₹2.9 crore a year.

The calendar was the problem. At nine next morning the leadership team expected one path and a number; on Thursday 26 November the audit committee expected it in writing; on Monday 30 November a Mumbai audit firm would release a slot it was holding. And on Wednesday 25 November, ten days away, the second annual surveillance audit on the 2024 certificate fell due, unbooked.

At 10:40 pm a message arrived from Bireshwar Itahari in Edison, New Jersey, where it was Sunday lunchtime. "Palmara's man told me a Type I plus a plan has worked for them before. Don't over-engineer this." Bidyut did not reply. He had spent the weekend with the policy, the certificate and his own one-page overview.

2. Pratibimb Technologies, 2017 to 2026

Bhavani Itakhulia and two colleagues founded Pratibimb Technologies in Bengaluru in June 2017. Pratibimb Bridge pulls results off laboratory analysers, maps them into hospital record systems and hands extracts to insurers' claims desks and to employers running staff health plans. At 30 September 2026 it reported annual recurring revenue of ₹71 crore — a stated figure, not rebuilt from any exhibit here — across 112 paying customers, with 196 employees, 61 in engineering. Figure 1 places them.

One decision from two years ago shapes everything on his screen. In September 2024 a Mumbai general insurer worth ₹46 lakh a year told Pratibimb that re-empanelment required "ISO 27001 certification or equivalent" by 30 November 2024. An accredited body quoted ₹24 lakh and seven months; Prohori Quality Registrars quoted ₹3.2 lakh and eleven weeks. Pratibimb took the second. The certificate issued on 26 November 2024 against ISO/IEC 27001:2013, valid three years to 25 November 2027, with annual surveillance. Its scope reads:

"Information security management system for the design, development and support of the Pratibimb Bridge integration platform at the Pune development centre, Hinjawadi, Pune."

It was accepted. So, in June 2025, was a Pune non-banking lender's wellness empanelment worth ₹27 lakh a year: ₹73 lakh between them.

3. The industry

The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission gave health records a national addressing layer, and networks of the kind represented by Apollo Hospitals, Max Healthcare, Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis Healthcare and Thyrocare now expect vendors to speak it. Insurers answer to IRDAI on outsourcing and everyone to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; CERT-In's 2022 directions require a reportable incident to be notified within six hours. Pratibimb's buyers are audited bodies themselves, laboratories under NABL and hospitals under NABH, and they ask whether a certifier is accredited by a body such as NABCB. Its nearest competitor, Palash Health Cloud of Hyderabad, has published a SOC 2 Type II report since early 2025. Abroad a second rule applies: UAE Federal Law No. 2 of 2019 requires health data generated in the Emirates to be stored there.

4. The situation in detail: January 2025 to 13 November 2026

From January 2025 a one-page security overview, still in circulation, went out with proposals carrying the line "ISO 27001 certified" and not the scope statement, taken then for boilerplate nobody read. In April 2025 the employer-benefits module shipped, built outside Pune. In February 2026 a Singapore insurer's vendor-risk team read the scope statement and parked a ₹54 lakh opportunity, recorded then as an outlier.

Prohori ran the first surveillance audit in November 2025 as a sixty-minute video call; its letter of 18 November 2025 says the system was "reviewed against the Annex A controls of ISO/IEC 27001:2022". The certificate names the 2013 standard, and the International Accreditation Forum's transition period for certificates against that standard ended on 31 October 2025. The second surveillance audit falls due by 25 November 2026; Prohori's ₹1.85 lakh invoice is unpaid.

On Wednesday 12 August 2026 at 12:10 pm a customer's engineer reported that a bucket of lab-result exports was readable by any authenticated tenant session, and had been since 24 July. Across the twenty days, 2,318 export files belonging to 11 of the 94 India tenants were reachable. Pratibimb filed with CERT-In at 7:40 pm on Thursday 13 August. A ₹4.60 lakh forensic review dated 28 August 2026 says it examined "all available access logs" and found no retrieval from outside the tenants' own sessions. Exhibit 6 lists each environment's log settings.

Basabi's gap assessment of Friday 9 October 2026 found 41 open items (Exhibit 3). On 22 October Palmara Health Group issued vendor security policy v4, requiring for every renewal from 1 April 2027 "a SOC 2 Type II report covering an observation period of at least three months, or an ISO 27001 certificate from a body accredited by a signatory to the IAF multilateral arrangement, covering the production environment in which our data is processed". The contract renews on 1 June 2027. Proposals followed from Pratyaksh Assurance Services LLP on 4 November and Pariman Certification Services on 6 November (Exhibits 2, 4); Bratati Ilakhia's debrief reading on 11 November (Exhibit 5B); Byomkesh Ilambazari's capacity note on the 12th (Exhibit 3B). On the 13th the audit committee chair asked for one page.

exp20v2-legal.security.compliance:
Security compliance: SOC 2 and ISO 27001

What the two standards prove, what they cost, and who asks for them

1. A spreadsheet called "Stuck"

On Monday 9 February 2026, Sowmini Chilukuri, head of product at Jalakam Payroll, opened a spreadsheet her sales lead had titled "Stuck". Jalakam is a Chennai company of 118 employees that sells payroll and statutory-filing software to mid-sized Indian firms. The sheet listed five enterprise deals, each with an annual contract value (ACV, the revenue a contract is worth per year), and each held at the same stage: security review.

The largest, worth ₹180 lakh a year, belonged to a private lender with sixty branches. Its information-security officer, Sahana Cheruvu, had written that Jalakam must produce either a SOC 2 Type II report or an ISO 27001 certificate before contract signature, with a deadline of 31 July. Jalakam had neither. It had capable engineers, single sign-on, encrypted backups and a folder of answered questionnaires, none of which a stranger could verify.

The bar in Figure 1 shows how the ₹432 lakh (₹4.32 crore) divides: ₹96 lakh wanted SOC 2 specifically, ₹72 lakh wanted ISO 27001 specifically, ₹228 lakh would take either, and only a ₹36 lakh deal asked for neither. Sowmini had to decide which standard to pursue, in what order, and whether to fund both. A wrong choice meant a year of programme spend on a document nobody had asked for, or a missed deadline on the largest deal in the pipeline.

2. The idea

SOC 2 and ISO 27001 are two independent ways for an outsider to vouch for how a company protects information. A control, in both, is a specific safeguard that someone can inspect: for example, a rule that no engineer may push code to production without a second person's approval. Both standards ask the company to choose its controls, run them, keep evidence, and let a third party test the claim.

They were invented to end a duplication problem. Without them, each enterprise buyer would audit each vendor, and a vendor with sixty customers would host sixty visits and answer sixty overlapping questionnaires. One shared examination, readable by all buyers, replaces most of that.

SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) comes from the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, the AICPA. It dates from 2011, when it succeeded an older accounting auditing statement, SAS 70, first issued in 1992. A licensed accounting firm writes an opinion against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria: security, which is always included, plus optional availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. ISO 27001 descends from a British standard of the mid-1990s, BS 7799, and became an international standard in 2005. It was revised in 2013 and again in 2022. An accredited certification body, in India accredited under the National Accreditation Board for Certification Bodies (NABCB), certifies that the company runs an information security management system (ISMS): a documented cycle of risk assessment, controls and review.

Sowmini could say this sentence in any meeting: "It is a third party's signed statement about how we run security, over a defined scope and period, so that buyers read one document instead of running sixty audits."

3. How it actually works

Both programmes run the same underlying sequence, and the steps are easier to see in Jalakam's own case. First comes scope: which product, systems, offices and people sit inside the boundary being examined. Jalakam chose its production payroll platform, its Chennai office and its two cloud accounts, and excluded an internal marketing site.

Second is risk assessment and control selection. ISO 27001 requires a written risk assessment and a Statement of Applicability, a list of which of the 93 controls in its 2022 Annex A apply and why any are left out. SOC 2 has no such list; management designs controls and the auditor checks that they cover the chosen criteria. Third, the controls must actually be put in place: policies written, access reviews scheduled, laptops encrypted, vendors assessed.

The fourth step is the one practitioners leave implicit: evidence. A control that operates but leaves no trace does not exist for an auditor. Suganya Chellamuthu, Jalakam's head of engineering, bought a compliance automation platform to pull approvals, access lists and logs automatically, because screenshots gathered by hand in the last week are where audits go wrong.

Fifth, the controls run for a period, and the auditor samples from that period. In a SOC 2 Type II audit that observation window is typically three to twelve months; ISO 27001 requires an internal audit and a management review before the external audit. Sixth is the external audit, then the report or certificate, then upkeep: ISO certificates last three years with annual surveillance audits; SOC 2 reports are renewed annually. Figure 3 lays the plan on a calendar.

4. A worked example

Sowmini priced three options for year one. Each had four parts: the automation platform (₹7 lakh), outside help to prepare, audit fees, and staff time, valued as the engineering work it displaced. Running both standards shares the platform and most evidence, so staff time rises only from ₹6 lakh to ₹9 lakh. All figures are Jalakam's estimates, in ₹ lakh.

Unlocked is not won. Sowmini assumed a 50 per cent chance of winning each unlocked deal and a 70 per cent gross margin. Second pass: change one input. If the win chance is 25 per cent, expected ACV halves, to 75, 81 and 99 lakh, and gross profit falls to 52.5, 56.7 and 69.3.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

SOC 2ISO 27001
OutputAuditor's report and opinionCertificate, three years
ExaminerLicensed accounting firmAccredited certification body
ControlsCompany-designed, mapped to criteriaChosen through risk assessment

Attestation is not certification

A SOC 2 report has no pass mark. It contains an opinion, which may be qualified, and a list of exceptions. ISO 27001 yields a binary certificate. Reading the two the same way misleads.

Type I against Type II

Type I says controls were suitably designed on one date. Type II says they operated across a window. A Type I proves a plan, not a habit, and careful buyers say so.

Scope decides everything

Both documents describe only the stated boundary. A certificate for the head office says nothing about the platform where payroll data lives, and a SOC 2 report that covers only the security criteria says nothing about availability. Always ask what is inside.

Same label, different bar

Because companies choose their own controls, two SOC 2 reports can differ greatly in rigour. The ISMS gives ISO 27001 more uniform scaffolding, but a company can still scope itself narrowly.

Reports age

A SOC 2 report covers a past period; buyers usually want one ending within twelve months, and sometimes a bridge letter covering the gap. ISO surveillance audits sample only part of the system each year.

Compliance is not security

Neither standard promises that a breach will not happen. They show a competent process, which is weaker evidence than a penetration test, an attempt by hired specialists to break into the product itself.

Questions before relying on a document

Who issued it? What period or date? What was excluded? Were there exceptions? Which suppliers, such as the cloud host, were carved out? An unaccredited certifier's certificate means little.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In consumer products, individual buyers rarely ask; pressure comes from regulation, such as India's CERT-In directions of 2022 (six-hour incident reporting) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and from app-store review. B2B software is where both standards bite hardest, because procurement teams gate purchase on them, as Sahana Cheruvu did. In marketplaces, two sides complicate matters: large sellers or payment partners ask for evidence, while payments add a separate standard, PCI DSS.

Size changes the question. An early-stage firm like Jalakam often starts with a Type I or a single standard, using an automation platform, and treats it as a sales unlock. A large company runs several standards, a dedicated risk team and continuous monitoring, and treats them as licences to operate.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Evidence sprintExceptions cluster in the audit windowControls only need to work at audit timeSample one control monthly
Wrong scopeBuyer's questionnaire names a system missing from the reportScope is an audit detail, not a sales factMap buyer data flow to boundary
Prestige choiceCertificate in hand, next RFP asks for the otherOne standard is "the" standardTally the last twenty questionnaires

Each of these is cheap to catch early and expensive once the audit fee is paid. In the second and third, a decision that looked administrative turned out to be commercial, and the cheapest diagnostic is a look at the buyer's own questionnaires before any money moves.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Jalakam begins by counting what buyers asked for, not what sounds impressive. It fixes a scope that matches what its customers' data touches, builds one control set that serves both standards, collects evidence automatically from day one, and tells each buyer exactly which period and boundary the document covers. The report is treated as a living process, with a named owner and a monthly review, rather than a trophy.

9. The decision, and what comes next

Sowmini chose both, in sequence. Her reasoning was the 22 per cent break-even. She asked the sales lead how many of the last ten comparable enterprise deals had closed once security review was cleared; the answer was four, or 40 per cent. That is the same population as the unlocked deals in the model, below her 50 per cent assumption, and above 22 and the 25 per cent stress case, though a sample of ten cannot rule out a rate near 22. On that evidence the extra 11 lakh, which also covers the ₹72 lakh ISO-only deal, was cheap insurance. The SOC 2 window opened on 2 March, with the ISO risk work under way since February, and Suganya Chellamuthu owned both calendars.

To go further, study security questionnaires and requests for proposals, then contract terms such as service-level agreements, because a report becomes binding only when written into a contract.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Jalakam's estimate of 50 per cent were really a guess, what evidence from past deals would you gather to replace it? Second, which exclusion from scope would make you distrust an otherwise clean report?
case20v1-legal.security.compliance:
Nidhan Cloud and the Auditor's Calendar

A decision case on SOC 2, ISO 27001 and what an attestation is worth

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Arnab Haque, vice-president of product at Nidhan Cloud, opened a calendar invitation he had been avoiding. It was titled "Security attestation: decide," and it was set for Friday 23 October at 6:30 pm in Bengaluru, which is 9:00 am for Anindita Hajong in New Jersey and 9:00 pm for the customer team in Singapore. By the end of that call the leadership group expected him to name one programme and release a budget. An audit firm had told him that it could hold a slot only if an engagement letter was signed by 30 October.

The reason for the haste sat in Anindita's inbox: a Dubai retail and hospitality group wanted to sign a ₹1.4 crore annual contract in the first week of February 2027, and its procurement panel would not sign without a security attestation.

2. Company background

Nidhan Cloud, founded in Bengaluru in 2019, automates accounts payable for Indian businesses. It reads supplier invoices, matches them to purchase orders, checks GST and e-invoice details, deducts TDS and releases vendor payments through partner banks over NEFT and UPI. On 30 September 2026 it had annual recurring revenue of ₹58 crore, 1,350 customers and 210 employees, with engineering in Bengaluru and Pune, a designer in Berlin and customer success in Singapore.

Its early customers were mid-sized manufacturers and distributors that wanted something lighter than an ERP module. Buyers now compare it with RazorpayX, Zoho's finance products and Tally Prime's payment add-ons. Since 2025 the company had pushed upmarket, towards non-banking lenders, group companies and Gulf subsidiaries of Indian conglomerates, and those buyers send a security questionnaire before they send a purchase order.

3. The situation

Until this year Nidhan answered such questionnaires by hand, attaching a penetration-test summary from an outside firm. Arnab spent the previous week learning what the two famous labels actually mean. A SOC 2 report is not a certificate. A licensed audit firm examines a company against the American Institute of CPAs' Trust Services Criteria (security is mandatory, while availability and confidentiality are optional extras) and issues an opinion. A Type I report says the controls were suitably designed on one named date. A Type II report says they also operated effectively across an observation window, usually three to twelve months. ISO 27001 is different in kind. An accredited certification body audits the company's information security management system, meaning its risk register, policies and internal audits, against a scope the company itself defines. The certificate lasts three years, with a surveillance audit each year.

Exhibit 1 shows why the question had become urgent. In the twelve months to 30 September 2026, 84 opportunities reached security review. A buyer named SOC 2 or ISO 27001 in 37 of them, and 14 of those 37 were lost or stalled with the buyer citing the security review, carrying ₹3.22 crore of annual contract value. Indian enterprises leaned towards ISO 27001, while Gulf and Singapore buyers mostly asked for SOC 2. Aparajita Hatikakoty, in Singapore, reported that Gulf buyers asked for SOC 2 by name. The Dubai panel's written policy accepted a SOC 2 Type I report at signature if a Type II report followed within nine months.

The cost of each route is in Exhibit 2, and the calendar is in Exhibit 3. A large non-banking lender in Mumbai, worth ₹95 lakh a year, had separately told Anindita that its vendor re-empanelment closed on 30 June 2027 and that its policy named ISO 27001. Regulated lenders and brokers, answering to RBI and SEBI expectations on outsourced technology, pass such demands down to vendors, and the DPDP Act gave procurement teams a further reason to ask.

4. The people

Anindita Hajong, head of sales in New Jersey, owns the Dubai relationship. She wants a document in the customer's hands before February and regards the choice between labels as secondary to having either one dated.

Abhik Hatimuria, chief technology officer in Pune, would carry the remediation: enforced device management, access reviews, logging and change control. Having watched the platform team slip a roadmap commitment twice this year, he wants the narrowest scope an auditor will accept.

Aparajita Hatikakoty leads customer success from Singapore. She hears security objections after contracts are signed, when customers ask for evidence at renewal, and she wants a programme that keeps producing evidence every year rather than once. Three of her Singapore accounts have already asked what Nidhan will show at their next renewals.

5. Exhibits
