6. The options

Option A: SOC 2 first. Sign with the audit firm by 30 October, spend about six weeks on remediation from 2 November, obtain a Type I as at 11 December and run a Type II window from 14 December to 14 June 2027, with the report expected in mid-July. It costs ₹107 lakh over 24 months (Exhibit 2). A Type I report would exist before the Dubai signing week; no ISO 27001 certificate would exist in the programme's first year.

Option B: ISO 27001 first. Build the management system from 2 November, pass Stage 1 on 15 February and Stage 2 on 12 April, and receive a certificate around 21 May 2027, valid for three years. It costs ₹91 lakh over 24 months. The certificate would arrive after the Dubai signing week and before the Mumbai lender's June deadline.

Option C: stay with questionnaires. Hire one response analyst, publish a trust portal, renew the penetration test and revisit certification in 2027. It costs ₹42 lakh over 24 months and commits no engineering time to remediation. Every buyer who needs a report or certificate would still be answered with a questionnaire.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. In your own words, what does a SOC 2 Type I report prove, what does a Type II add, and what does an ISO 27001 certificate prove that neither SOC 2 report does?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, count the 37 certificate requests that each label would have satisfied. What does the count say about demand, and what does it leave out?
  3. Place the Dubai and Mumbai dates against Exhibit 3. Which option meets which deadline, and what does each deadline's policy let Nidhan substitute?
  4. Which option would you commit to on Friday, what would you defer, and what evidence in the next six months would make you change course?

8. A note for the learner

Treat a certification as a purchased answer to a question buyers keep asking, and price it against the deals that depend on it. Exhibit 1 sets that stake at ₹3.22 crore of lost annual value in twelve months, against a cost of ₹42 to ₹107 lakh over twenty-four. A sound answer states what each label proves, matches each deadline to a dated deliverable, and treats the cheapest option as a real alternative rather than a straw one.

One defensible path is Option A, with a trigger for ISO 27001. The Dubai policy accepts a Type I report and a Type II within nine months of signature: a signing on 5 February 2027 allows until early November, and the mid-July report sits comfortably inside that. Option B cannot produce a document before the signing week, while Option C does not produce one at all. The Mumbai lender is then the open risk, since its June date falls before the Type II report and its policy names a different standard. Nidhan can ask whether the lender will accept a Type I report plus a dated ISO 27001 plan, and can start the ISO programme in mid-2027 on the same evidence platform if the lender says no. The path accepts some duplicated audit effort in return for meeting the nearest deadline with real paper. A different cohort, weighting the India enterprise segment more heavily, could reasonably start with ISO 27001 and defend that choice.
exp40v2-legal.security.compliance:
Security compliance: SOC 2 and ISO 27001

Two certifications dominate enterprise software procurement, and almost everything a product manager is told about them is a sentence short. What each instrument asserts, what it costs in rupees and engineering weeks, and where the standard answer stops being true.

1Two decisions, five weeks apart

On the morning of 6 October 2026, the procurement portal of a Nashville-based provider network returned a single line to Thamaraiselvi Dharmavaram: vendor not eligible — SOC 2 Type II required at execution. Dharmavaram is vice president of product at Kurinji Health Cloud, a Chennai company that sells claims-integrity and clinical-data-exchange software to hospital groups. It had 164 employees on 1 September 2026 and, at 30 September, recurring revenue of ₹54 crore — ₹5,400 lakh. The blocked contract was worth ₹6.4 crore a year — ₹640 lakh — and was due to start on 31 March 2027.

Dharmavaram's problem was a calendar, not a budget. A Type II report attests that controls operated across a stated window, and the shortest window this buyer would accept was six months. The earliest Kurinji could honestly begin was 1 January 2027, closing on 30 June and reported on about 15 August — four and a half months after the signature she was trying to win. No money bought that time back.

Five weeks later, on 10 November 2026, Tejaswini Duvvuri took a different version of the same problem to her board in Hyderabad. Kinnera Systems has 46 people and ₹7.2 crore — ₹720 lakh — of recurring revenue; it reads scanned policy documents and call recordings for banks and insurers. A European insurer's request for proposal, due 15 January 2027, required a current ISO/IEC 27001 certificate before go-live on 1 July 2027, against a contract worth ₹1.9 crore — ₹190 lakh — a year. Kinnera's model quality rests on an evaluation environment where engineers replay real customer documents against candidate prompts. Exclude that environment from the certified scope and the certificate lands on 1 April with three months of slack; include it and the remediation pushes it to 1 June, leaving one month before the gate. The programme costs ₹42.9 lakh either way. Duvvuri's choice is not about money. It is about what a certificate is for.

Both scenes run forward from the decisions: everything after 10 November 2026 is planned, not observed.

2What the two instruments actually assert

Both regimes answer a question that predates software: a buyer wants assurance about controls inside an organisation it cannot inspect, and multiplying its own audits across every customer is absurd — a vendor with 200 enterprise accounts would host 200 audits of the same servers. The answer is a third party who inspects once and publishes a result many buyers may rely on. The accounting profession built that machinery for financial statements and extended it to service organisations; the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants issued what became SOC 2 in 2011, resting on five Trust Services criteria — Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality and Privacy — of which only Security is compulsory.

ISO/IEC 27001 descends from British Standard 7799 of the mid-1990s, became an ISO standard in 2005 and was revised in 2013 and 2022, with every 2013 certificate expiring by 31 October 2025. Its lineage is the quality management system, not the audit opinion. It does not ask whether named controls worked over a period; it asks whether the organisation runs a management system that identifies risks, treats them, measures the treatment and corrects itself — clauses 4 to 10. Annex A's 93 controls are a reference list, filtered by a Statement of Applicability saying which apply and why.

Exhibit 1. The attributes that determine how a buyer may use each instrument.
SOC 2 Type IIISO/IEC 27001:2022
InstrumentAttestation reportCertificate of conformity
Signed byLicensed CPA firmBody accredited to ISO/IEC 17021-1
Object examinedControls meeting chosen Trust Services criteriaManagement system, clauses 4–10, plus Annex A per the Statement of Applicability
Time basisA window; Kurinji's: 1 Jan–30 Jun 2027A point in a three-year cycle, surveilled annually
Buyer receivesOpinion, description, tests and exceptionsCertificate naming a scope; report private
CirculationRestricted, under non-disclosureCertificate public, report confidential
Visible failureQualified opinion, or exceptionsMajor nonconformity: no certificate

Three schools disagree about what follows. The signalling school holds that these are market infrastructure: their function is to cut the buyer's verification cost, so their value is measured in sales cycle removed and questionnaires avoided. It will sign that a report's marginal worth equals the deals it opens; it will not sign that a certified vendor is safer than an uncertified one. The management-system school reverses the emphasis: the certificate is a by-product, and the value is risk assessment, internal audit and management review surviving two surveillance visits and a recertification. It will sign that an audited management system changes how decisions get made; it will not sign that evidence gathered for an auditor is security work. The control-effectiveness school, largely engineers, holds that both frameworks measure the existence of controls rather than their strength. It will sign that coverage is not strength; it will not sign that audits are worthless, conceding that the hygiene they force — access reviews, logging, offboarding — eliminates the cheapest attacks.

3Mechanics: what the programme actually costs

Expert practice separates three cost pools that amateurs merge: fees, which are quoted; engineering remediation, which is not; and the annual recurrence, which is what matters past year one. Kurinji priced engineering at ₹1.1 lakh a person-week, fully loaded, and audit effort at ₹0.8 lakh an auditor-day. Effort is not negotiable the way fees are: a mandatory document of the International Accreditation Forum keys auditor-days to the effective number of personnel and the complexity of the scope, which is why Kurinji's certification body quoted 13 auditor-days for Stage 1 and Stage 2 together — ₹10.4 lakh — and 4.5 days for each surveillance visit.

Exhibit 2. Kurinji, year-one cost of three paths, ₹ lakh. Remediation is 22, 28 and 32 person-weeks at ₹1.1 lakh.
Cost line, year 1SOC 2 aloneISO 27001 aloneBoth together
Gap assessment and policy build6.07.59.0
Remediation engineering24.230.835.2
Tooling and licences9.49.411.6
Auditor or certification-body fees13.510.423.9
Penetration test, CERT-In empanelled5.55.55.5
Programme management7.87.811.7
Total66.471.496.9

The joint path costs ₹40.9 lakh less than the ₹137.8 lakh of the two paths run separately, a saving of 29.7 per cent. Decomposed against that two-programme baseline, it is mostly remediation (19.8) and tooling (7.2), because an access-review process or an encrypted log pipeline satisfies both regimes at once; 5.5 comes from running one penetration test rather than two, and the rest from gap assessment (4.5) and programme management (3.9 — a saving against two programmes, even though the joint line is three-quarters of a full-time equivalent against a single programme's half). None of it is fees: the two bodies are different organisations under different rules, and ₹23.9 lakh is simply ₹13.5 lakh — a ₹4.5 lakh Type I plus a ₹9.0 lakh Type II — added to ₹10.4 lakh.

Year two is the figure nobody quotes. Running both instruments steadily costs ₹9.0 lakh for the annual Type II re-audit, ₹3.6 lakh for a 4.5-day surveillance visit, ₹11.6 lakh of tooling, ₹5.5 lakh for the penetration test and ₹6.2 lakh of programme time — two-fifths of a full-time equivalent at the ₹15.6 lakh a year the year-one line implies: ₹35.9 lakh a year, indefinitely. The operational saving on the other side is easily overstated. In the financial year to March 2026 Kurinji answered 41 security questionnaires averaging 228 questions each, at 11.5 hours of engineering and security time apiece: 471.5 hours, or ₹12.97 lakh at a loaded ₹2,750 an hour. A Type II cuts that average by nearly two-thirds, to 4.2 hours, saving 299.3 hours — ₹8.23 lakh, under a tenth of the year-one programme. The case must be made on market access or not at all.

4When the reasoning holds, and when it misleads

The conditions can be stated as claims a product manager can test before spending anything. First: a named buyer with a policy gate and a dated contract is in hand. Both pass, unequally. Kurinji's ₹96.9 lakh sits against ₹640 lakh of first-year revenue from one account, and is 1.79 per cent of its recurring revenue; Kinnera's ₹42.9 lakh is 5.96 per cent of its own, about 3.3 times the relative burden, against a contract worth ₹190 lakh a year. Second: the gate is a policy, not a preference. Here Kurinji nearly fooled itself. Seven deals in its FY2027 pipeline, worth ₹1,860 lakh together, named a report as a gate; three of them — ₹880 lakh — sat with buyers whose policy permits a documented exception approved by their security officer. Only four, worth ₹980 lakh, were genuinely blocked. Third: the risk the framework examines is the risk the buyer fears. Kinnera fails this one. Its insurer's real anxiety is whether customer documents train a model and where they travel; neither the Trust Services criteria nor clauses 4 to 10 ask that directly, and a certificate answering a different question invites a false sense of completion on both sides. The reasoning is actively misleading in three situations: a consumer product no enterprise buys, a company before product-market fit, and any team that lets the report stand in for a threat model it never wrote.

5Hard edges: seams, scopes and stacks

The difficulties cluster at organisational seams rather than in the standards. A multi-product company must decide whether one report covers everything — cheaper, but it drags the least mature product into the audit — or whether each product carries its own, doubling fees and letting a buyer discover the module it just bought is outside scope. Platforms face a sharper version: the buyer's risk sits with third parties whom no certificate covers, so mature operators publish a seller-onboarding standard beside their report and admit it is weaker. In regulated sectors the instruments are necessary and insufficient at once: India's CERT-In directions of April 2022 impose six-hour incident reporting and 180-day log retention regardless of any certificate, the Reserve Bank's IT governance directions expect board-level ownership and vendor audit rights, and bank onboarding usually demands a penetration test by a CERT-In empanelled auditor as well. Hardware companies fail at the factory: signing keys, device provisioning and test benches sit in physical places easy to leave outside a scope statement and impossible to leave outside a customer's threat model. AI-native products fail at the sub-processor, where a model provider's report is carved out of yours. ISO/IEC 42001, published for artificial-intelligence management systems in December 2023, exists for this; few buyers ask for it yet. What mature companies do, as against what they say, is keep two scopes — the certified boundary, and a private register of systems touching customer data — and close the gap over two cycles.

6Eight distinctions that separate the expert

Scope is the whole instrument.
A certificate certifies a named boundary; exclusions are lawful and invisible from outside. The tell-tale is a scope statement shorter than the product list, or one naming the legal entity rather than services and sites. "They are certified" is wrong because the sentence has no object.
An unqualified opinion may be full of exceptions.
The opinion letter and the test results are different documents inside one report, and experts read the results, where each control shows what was sampled and what failed. The tell-tale is a buyer asking for "a clean SOC 2": the phrase is not in the standard, and whoever uses it stops at page one.
You buy the window, not the report date.
A report issued 15 August 2027 covering January to June says nothing about August. The gap is bridged by a letter that is management's assertion, not audit work; the tell-tale is a bridge letter signed by the vendor and filed as though the auditor wrote it. A Type I tests design at a point in time; its only honest use is scheduling.
The certified object is the management system, not Annex A.
Annex A is a reference set filtered by the Statement of Applicability; conformity is to clauses 4 to 10. The tell-tale is an organisation that can produce 93 control descriptions but not a risk-treatment plan with owners and dates, or a minuted management review.
Complementary user entity controls transfer work to the buyer.
Every report lists controls the customer must operate for the opinion to mean anything: single sign-on, its own keys, its administrators. The tell-tale is a customer filing your report in its compliance pack without having implemented one. Keep a register and raise it during implementation: after a customer's own mis-configuration that list is the only defence.
Carve-outs break the chain of assurance.
A sub-service organisation can be carved out or included; carved out is normal and means its controls were not examined. The tell-tale is a three-deep stack — application, cloud, model provider — where nobody holds the third party's current report or knows its window.
Choosing the auditor is a positioning decision.
The firm's stance on sampling and exception thresholds sets the engineering load, and buyers' security teams quietly grade the signature. The tell-tale is a report from a firm nobody in the buyer's sector recognises, which triggers the full questionnaire anyway: the instrument's purpose fails silently while the certificate hangs on the wall.
The binding deadline belongs to the buyer's calendar.
Vendor-risk reviews cluster in a customer's own audit months, and a report landing three weeks after that window costs a year of waiting. The tell-tale is a renewal questionnaire arriving in the same month every year. Experts set the window backwards from their largest accounts' review months, which makes it a product decision.

7How it differs by product type and company stage

Consumer products are the honest exception: almost nobody asks, and the binding constraints are app-store rules, the payment processor's own PCI DSS obligations and privacy law — India's DPDP Act, the GDPR, state statutes in the United States. Business software sold to small firms needs a trust page and, eventually, a Type II. Enterprise buyers stack instruments: report, questionnaire, penetration-test summary, sub-processor list and a contractual right to audit, in that order of increasing pain. Platforms carry third parties they cannot certify, hardware companies carry sites, AI products carry data-use questions no certificate answers. What does not differ, and is worth saying plainly, is the control content: access management, change control, logging and vendor review look nearly identical throughout. The variation is in the buyer's verification ritual, not the security work. Before product-market fit, buy nothing and answer questionnaires by hand. With a named deal, a Type I or a scoped ISO certificate is the cheapest instrument that unblocks it. Past roughly 50 people and the first enterprise logo, a Type II window becomes the constraint on the sales calendar and someone must own it. At scale, regional variants arrive — Germany's C5, the automotive TISAX assessment, FedRAMP for United States federal buyers — each a separate business case with its own pipeline.

8Three programmes, with numbers

Kurinji's case resolves into arithmetic. Across the last 36 enterprise opportunities it closed 11, a win rate of 30.6 per cent. Applied to the full gated pipeline of ₹1,860 lakh, the unrounded 11/36 implies ₹568 lakh of expected annual contract value, or roughly six times the year-one cost — the number a founder quotes. Applied to the ₹980 lakh genuinely blocked — the four deals that include the Nashville contract, and the rate is assumed to carry across to deals a report unblocks — it implies ₹299 lakh, or 3.1 times. The honest number is half the flattering one and still decisive: a programme that survives only on the flattering denominator is not safe.

Kinnera's case resolves into scope. Its ₹42.9 lakh comprises ₹5.2 lakh of advisory, ₹15.4 lakh of engineering at fourteen person-weeks, ₹6.8 lakh of tooling, ₹8.0 lakh of certification-body fees at ten auditor-days, ₹3.6 lakh for the penetration test and ₹3.9 lakh of programme time. The figure is identical whether or not the evaluation environment sits inside the boundary; what changes is the remediation sequence, and therefore the date.

The third programme failed. Kavalam Instruments, a Coimbatore maker of cold-chain telemetry gateways with 78 people, certified to ISO 27001 in September 2024 with a scope covering "the cloud platform and the Bengaluru development centre"; the firmware laboratory and manufacturing test floor were outside it. In February 2026 a vaccine distributor's own review found one provisioning key common to 11,400 gateways shipped during 2025 — a finding the certificate could not have caught, because the systems holding the key were never examined. A ₹4.8 crore three-year framework was paused. Recovery took seven months and ₹72.0 lakh: ₹9.6 lakh for an extended-scope special audit, ₹30.8 lakh of firmware and provisioning re-engineering at 28 person-weeks, ₹12.4 lakh of key-management hardware, ₹7.2 lakh for the customer's re-audit and retest, and ₹12.0 lakh of programme and legal time.

Exhibit 3. The cash column is programme cost in the first two rows and remediation in the third: not like-for-like, not totalled.
CompanyWhat was boughtCash, ₹ lakhPlanned result
Kurinji Health CloudType I, then Type II over 1 Jan–30 Jun 2027, plus ISO 2700196.9₹640 lakh contract to execute 31 Mar 2027
Kinnera SystemsISO 27001, evaluation environment inside scope42.9Certificate due 1 Jun 2027; 1 Jul go-live holds
Kavalam InstrumentsISO 27001 scoped to cloud and one development centre72.0₹4.8 crore framework paused seven months

9Failure modes and their early warnings

Five failures recur. A scope drawn for the certificate rather than the risk announces itself when the scope statement is shorter than the product list; the diagnostic question is "which customer data flows through a system outside this boundary?", and Kavalam's post-incident review, which priced the same defect at each stage it could have surfaced, shows the late cost. A window that misses the buyer's review month announces itself when the report date was set by the auditor's convenience; ask which month each top-ten account runs vendor review, and the cost of missing is a renewal year. Evidence theatre announces itself when the control inventory matches Annex A exactly; ask what the last internal audit found that the tool could not see, and the cost of a late catch is exceptions in a report already circulating. An unchased carve-out announces itself when no sub-processor report is on file; ask who holds the model provider's current report and its window. Compliance owned outside the product organisation announces itself when the management-system owner cannot name next quarter's roadmap; ask which roadmap item is late because of a control commitment, and discover at Stage 2 what could have been designed in.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is about causation. The signalling position, at its strongest, is that no published evidence shows certified firms suffering materially fewer serious incidents once size and sector are held constant, and that firms holding current reports have been breached through problems the criteria never examine. It would be wrong if someone produced incident data, controlled for exposure, in which certified firms fared better. The management-system position concedes the absence of that study and argues the mechanism is slow and indirect: a company that must restate its risks and face an auditor annually makes different decisions, and the effect shows up in trivial incidents rather than headline ones. It would be wrong if programmes three certification cycles deep were indistinguishable from box-ticking on any operational measure.

The second disagreement is about sequencing, and this page's own figures cut against the received view. The retrofit argument says build the management system early, because bolting controls onto a large estate costs more per head. Yet Kurinji has budgeted 32 person-weeks across 164 people — 0.195 weeks a head — while Kinnera budgeted 14 across 46, or 0.304. Two observations settle nothing, and the comparison is not like-for-like: Kinnera's fourteen weeks buy a narrower scope, by first-time hands. But a practitioner who quotes the retrofit argument as settled should be asked for numbers.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks whether the company is certified. Someone who has internalised it asks for the scope statement and the test results first, and reads the exceptions before the opinion. They can name the three questions in a 228-item questionnaire that actually gate the deal. They refuse scope games on arithmetic rather than principle, having priced what a customer's own audit costs when it finds the gap. And they never say the report means the product is secure, because they know which sentence in it says otherwise.

12The decisions, and questions for discussion

1. Kinnera could have certified two months earlier by excluding the evaluation environment. On what evidence would that exclusion have been defensible, and who should have authority to approve it?

2. Kurinji's blocked pipeline shrank from ₹1,860 lakh to ₹980 lakh once buyers' exception policies were read. Which other figures in a compliance case are open to the same correction, and how would you test them?

3. If the signalling school is right that these instruments do not reduce incident rates, what should a product manager stop doing — and what should replace it?

Dharmavaram chose to run both programmes together for ₹96.9 lakh, to take a Type I as of 1 January 2027 so that an auditor's signature sits in front of procurement on 31 March, and to write the window and the 15 August report date into the contract as a commitment carrying a service credit. The analyst accepted that because the policy's purpose — an opinion on operating effectiveness — is scheduled rather than waived. Duvvuri chose to put the evaluation environment inside the scope, accept 1 June 2027 for the certificate, and add a data-use addendum answering the insurer's real question, which her certificate does not. Both chose the instrument that fits the calendar they were handed, and both were explicit about what it does not prove.

13Going deeper

Security basics for PMs
The threat model a certificate presumes; unreadable without it.
RFPs and security questionnaires
Where the report is spent, and what it retires.
Terms of service, SLAs and contracts
Window commitments, audit rights, credits.
Enterprise security requirements
The buyer demands stacked around the report.
Privacy by design
Turns the privacy criterion into a product decision.
Data, consent and the DPDP Act
India's statutory floor; no certificate meets it.
GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes
Why ISO 27701 and regional codes join later.

case20v1-legal.ip:
A Name Before Diwali

Jhinuk Technologies and the BillSathi launch

1. Opening

At 6.30 pm on Wednesday 21 October 2026, Sudipta Chattopadhyay, vice-president of product at Jhinuk Technologies, sat in a glass meeting room in Sector V, Salt Lake, Kolkata, with a trademark search report and a launch plan. The plan called for a bill-scanning feature, BillSathi, to go live to every paying merchant on Tuesday 27 October, twelve days before Diwali on 8 November. The report, delivered on 14 October, listed a registered mark that looked uncomfortably like the feature's name. By noon on Friday 23 October she had to tell the printer and the release engineers in Bengaluru and Pune which name to use.

2. Company background

Jhinuk Technologies was founded in Kolkata in 2019 by Subhasish Changkakoti and two classmates. Its app, Jhinuk Khata, handles billing, stock and GST invoices for small retailers and wholesalers, on a subscription averaging ₹3,000 per merchant a year. At 30 September 2026 it had 62,000 paying merchants, annual recurring revenue of ₹18.6 crore (62,000 × ₹3,000) and about 210 staff. It competes for the shopkeeper with Vyapar, Khatabook and Zoho Books, and for the accountant with Tally and Busy. Merchants pay by UPI, and growth has come mostly through distributors in the textile, hardware and sweet markets of West Bengal, Odisha and Assam. The house mark JHINUK has been registered in classes 9 and 42 since 2021; the app's code and screens are protected by copyright without registration. The scanner was built by engineers in Bengaluru and Pune on a text-recognition model trained in Toronto by Sagnik Chatterjee, a data scientist who also ran the beta analysis. Customer success in Singapore, led by Sunil Chutia, supports merchants in Bengali, Hindi and Assamese across three time zones, and reported that beta merchants had started calling the feature simply "the Sathi".

3. The situation

The scanner reads a photograph of a supplier's paper bill and turns it into a purchase entry. Merchants buy heavily before Diwali, so the launch was timed to it. A beta had run since 7 September with 14,000 invited merchants under the working name BillSathi, proposed by the Berlin designer in a naming sprint on 24 July. Of the 14,000, 2,100 (15.0 per cent) pre-booked an annual add-on at ₹1,200. Applying 15.0 per cent to the 48,000 merchants outside the beta (62,000 less 14,000) forecasts 7,200 purchases in the first 90 days, or ₹86.4 lakh, of which product analytics expects 4,800 in the first seven weeks.

Nobody had searched the name before the beta. Jhinuk ordered a search on 5 October. Exhibit 1 summarises the report. The entry that matters is BILLSAATHI, a word mark registered in class 9 (downloadable software) to Jalukbari Software LLP of Guwahati on 14 March 2022. It differs from BillSathi by one letter and is pronounced the same. Jalukbari's app was last updated on 11 February 2025 and shows about 1,400 installs. Sharmila Chetia, Jhinuk's outside counsel, told Sudipta on Monday that a petition to remove a registered mark for non-use could not be filed before mid-June 2027, and that an app with recent updates would be hard to call abandoned. She added that the beta, though invited-only, had been public use of the name since 7 September, and that each further week under it lengthened the record Jalukbari could cite. No letter from Jalukbari had arrived, and she had not yet been asked for a formal opinion. Exhibit 3 places the dates on one line.

4. The people

Subhasish Changkakoti, chief executive, Kolkata. He wants a decision that does not distract the company from a Series B process opening in January 2027, when investors will ask who owns what.

Sourav Chaliha, head of sales, Jersey City, New Jersey. Joining at 9.00 am his time, he has promised a Dubai trading house, which buys from several thousand Indian merchants, that the feature arrives before Diwali. He wants 27 October held.

Sneha Chakladar, brand designer, Berlin (3.00 pm there, 3.5 hours behind India until clocks change on 25 October). She chose the name and drew the logo, and does not want to see the work discarded, and has said the logo took five weeks of testing in Berlin and Kolkata.

Sharmila Chetia, partner at a Kolkata intellectual property firm. She wants to be asked before a name is printed, not after, and can deliver a written opinion in two working days, but cannot say what Jalukbari would do. She is also candid that a registration is strong evidence, not a guarantee, of how a court would see the two names.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 prices the three options below on one forecast: the same 7,200 first-90-day purchases at ₹1,200, whatever the option.

6. The options

Option A: launch as BillSathi on 27 October. All collateral is ready, the beta's brand recognition carries forward, and the forecast 7,200 purchases proceed on schedule. Jhinuk would file its own application in classes 9 and 42, for ₹1.2 lakh. It would be using a name one letter from a prior registration for identical software, and leaves the dispute for Jalukbari to raise or not.

Option B: rename now and relaunch on 15 December. Jhinuk would choose a new name, clear it from scratch and launch with nothing to dispute. The cost is a seven-week slip across Diwali, a written-off identity and ₹45.3 lakh of certain cost. It leaves Jhinuk without a feature to show the Dubai trading house until December.

Option C: launch on 27 October as Jhinuk Scan, and approach Jalukbari. The feature goes out under Jhinuk's registered house mark plus a plain descriptive word. Counsel would give a written opinion by 23 October and open a coexistence or assignment discussion over BILLSAATHI. The cost is ₹12.5 lakh, the beta name is shelved, and the outcome of the approach is unknown.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which of the four marks can Jhinuk claim rights in, which can it not, and what does Jalukbari's 2022 registration and 2025 update history tell you about the strength of its position?
  2. Using Exhibits 2 and 3, which costs in each option are certain and which are contingent? What does the forecast base assume, and how would you test it?
  3. What must Sudipta get from counsel by noon on Friday 23 October, and what can she decide herself?
  4. Which option do you choose, what evidence would change your mind, and what do you say to Sourav and Sneha?

8. A note for the learner

Intellectual property decisions rest on three questions: what can we protect, what can we not use, and when do we call counsel. Here the answers are separable. Jhinuk can protect JHINUK, which is distinctive and registered; its code through copyright; and, with a filing, a combined mark such as JHINUK SCAN. It cannot own the word "scan", which merely describes the function, and a method of scanning bills is a poor candidate for a patent because Indian law excludes computer programmes as such. It cannot safely use a name that is nearly identical to a mark registered earlier for the same goods; the beta, which began in September 2026, gives no priority over a registration from March 2022. The mistake worth carrying away is sequence: counsel was called after the name, the logo and the beta, when it was cheapest before.

One defensible path is Option C. It keeps the launch inside the Diwali window, so the 7,200-purchase forecast is not touched, and it keeps the brand anchored on the one mark Jhinuk already owns. The ₹12.5 lakh is certain and small beside the ₹55.0 lakh scenario and the ₹28.8 lakh of delay-forgone bookings. It also leaves the BillSathi question open for a negotiated answer rather than a litigated one. The path depends on three checks before Friday: a one-page clearance of JHINUK SCAN, a written opinion from Sharmila, and a look at whether beta merchants responded to the name or to the feature. If any of these fails, the choice should be reopened.
exp40v2-legal.ip:
IP, patents and trademarks for PMs

What you can protect, what you cannot use, and when to call counsel — two companies, one body of law, opposite answers.

1Two decisions, a week apart

On Friday 9 October 2026 Nithilan Yegappan was in a Hosur tooling shop with a part he was not allowed to photograph: the second-generation enclosure of the wrist-worn sleep band sold by Gauraiya Devices, the Coimbatore firm where he ran product, a clamshell whose clasp doubled as the charging contact. Gauraiya shipped 2,80,000 units in the year to 31 March 2026 at an average realisation of ₹1,650 — ₹46.20 crore of revenue at a 34 per cent gross margin. The enclosure was due on Croma and Reliance Digital shelves on 14 November 2026, the buyers' preview was on Tuesday 20 October, and a registered design in India must not have been publicly disclosed before the application is filed. Nithilan had six working days.

Seven days later, on Friday 16 October, Nethra Yetukuri had the opposite problem in Bengaluru: her company already owned something, and it had cost more than planned. Granthavali Technologies sold contract-intelligence software — ₹58.30 crore of annual recurring revenue across 212 paying accounts on 30 September 2026, a mean of ₹27.50 lakh an account. It had filed a provisional specification in August 2024 on how its model split a master services agreement into obligations; the international application published on 12 February 2026; and on 4 September 2026 the examiner objected that the invention was a computer programme as such. Entering the national phase in the United States and Europe by the thirty-month deadline of 8 February 2027 — 115 days away — would cost ₹18.70 lakh nobody had budgeted.

Both are intellectual-property decisions; neither is a legal question. The law is identical for both, the right answers are opposite, and why they are opposite is this topic.

2The idea: five unrelated monopolies that share a name

“Intellectual property” is a collective noun for instruments with almost nothing in common: each has its own subject matter, term, registration requirement and — decisively — its own theory of who is protected. The expensive error is to reason about one using another's logic.

Exhibit 1. The five instruments in Indian law; the last column is the one practitioners skip.
InstrumentProtectsIndian termRegistrationCannot do
Patent (1970 Act)a new, non-obvious, applicable invention20 years from filingyes, examinedcover a programme per se (s.3(k))
Copyright (1957 Act)expression; code is a literary workauthor's life plus 60 yearsno; filing is evidence onlystop independent reimplementation
Trade mark (1999 Act)a sign of origin, for goods specified10 years, renewable indefinitelyregistration or usereserve a word rivals need
Registered design (2000 Act)shape and ornament, judged by eye10 years plus 5 on renewalyes; prior disclosure is fatalcover how it works
Trade secretconfidential commercial informationas long as secrecy holdsnone; no Indian statutesurvive lawful reverse engineering

The history explains the incoherence. The Venetian statute of 1474 and the English Statute of Monopolies of 1624, which banned royal monopolies but carved out fourteen years for the true and first inventor, framed the patent as a bargain: exclusion for disclosure. Copyright arrived separately with the Statute of Anne in 1710. Trade marks came later still, out of the tort of passing off, and their beneficiary was never the producer but the buyer, who can repeat a purchase without re-investigating the seller — which is why a descriptive word cannot be monopolised.

India's own history is the instructive part. The Ayyangar Committee report of 1959 argued that the 1911 Act's product patents on medicines exported rent without building domestic capability, and the Patents Act 1970 abolished them in pharmaceuticals, food and chemicals; the generics industry was the consequence. TRIPS reversed it — product patents returned in 2005, but with section 3(d), barring a new form of a known substance absent enhanced efficacy, applied by the Supreme Court in 2013 to the beta-crystalline form of a known leukaemia compound. Indian patent law is no neutral transplant: the bargain is worth striking only when the disclosure is new.

Four schools disagree about what follows, and about propositions, not moods. The incentive-and-bargain school (Nordhaus, Kitch) signs “without exclusion, disclosed invention is under-supplied, because you cannot sell information without revealing it” but not “claims should be narrow by default.” The cumulative-innovation school (Merges and Nelson; Heller and Eisenberg; Bessen and Meurer on notice failure) signs “in software a claim's boundary is unknowable before litigation, so patents tax entry” but refuses the abolitionist line that all patents are rent-seeking. The appropriability school (Teece; the Yale and Carnegie-Mellon surveys, where firms outside chemicals rank lead time and secrecy above patents) signs “for most software the patent is a financing artefact, not a moat” but cares about secrecy and brand. The search-cost school (Landes and Posner) signs “the only trade-mark injury is confusion as to origin” but not that goodwill has value independent of use.

3Mechanics: the clock, the claim and the money

Expert practice has three mechanical cores. The first is the clock: everything is measured from the priority date, the date of first filing anywhere, and nothing done after it repairs what was done before.

Three consequences follow that teams miss. The twelve-month window from a provisional specification is the cheapest deferral the system sells: an agent's drafting time buys a year to decide. Publication at month 18 is unconditional and irreversible — the specification is public whether or not a patent ever grants, so a withdrawn application is a disclosure made for nothing. And examination is not automatic: the request must be filed within 31 months of priority, the 2024 Rules having cut the old 48-month window, and the first report can arrive years behind it while pre-grant opposition stays open to anyone.

The second core is the claim. A patent's scope is its independent claims and nothing else, and infringement requires every element of a claim to be present, so a longer claim is a narrower claim. The element an engineer is proudest of is usually the one that makes the claim unenforceable.

The third core is money, and it submits to arithmetic. Niveda Yeleswarapu, the Chennai patent agent both companies used, priced Gauraiya's options over five years.

Exhibit 2. Gauraiya's five-year protection budget for one product, quoted on 7 October 2026.
InstrumentYear 0–1 outlay (₹ lakh)Years 2–5 outlay (₹ lakh)Five-year outlay (₹ lakh)
Utility patent family, India and United States via PCT9.6014.4024.00
Registered design, India, one article0.450.000.45
Word mark, three classes, India1.050.301.35
Trade-secret programme (access control, deeds, exit process)1.804.806.60
Total12.9019.5032.40

₹24.00 lakh of the ₹32.40 lakh — 74.1 per cent — sits in one instrument. Is it worth it? Conditional on a granted claim that actually reads on a rival's product, Niveda put three outcomes on the table: a licence or settlement at ₹1.80 crore with probability 0.15; an acquisition diligence premium worth ₹40 lakh with probability 0.45; nothing at all with probability 0.40. In lakh that is 0.15 × 180 + 0.45 × 40 + 0.40 × 0 = 27 + 18 = ₹45 lakh conditional on an enforceable grant. Against the ₹24.00 lakh cost, the break-even probability is 24.00 ÷ 45 = 53.3 per cent: Gauraiya must believe it better than even money that it ends up with a claim a rival cannot design around. Niveda's own estimate, given Figure 2, was 0.33 — an expected value of ₹14.85 lakh, ₹9.15 lakh short of cost. The calculation omits option value and the signalling value of a grant in a Series B data room: both real, and both where a PM who wants the patent will hide. Neither it nor Exhibit 3 is discounted; discounting would shrink the later figure in each and push both conclusions further the way they already point.

When to call counsel follows from the clock, not the budget. Three triggers: before anything is shown outside a confidentiality obligation; before a name goes on a box; and before any third party touches the artefact.

4When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: the protectable thing is what customers choose on. Gauraiya passes — buyers at ₹1,650 choose on the feel of the clasp, which a registered design covers. Granthavali fails: enterprises choose on recall and precision against their own paper, which no instrument reaches. Second: imitation is cheap and lawful. Gauraiya passes emphatically; a moulded shell is copied in weeks. Granthavali mostly fails — a rival must rebuild the corpus and the evaluation harness, no part of the published specification. Third: exclusion outlasts the product. Fifteen years of design term against a two-year hardware cycle is generous; twenty years against an architecture with an eighteen-month half-life is worthless. Fourth: you can detect infringement. Gauraiya can; Nethra cannot see inside a rival's pipeline.

The frame actively misleads in two situations. One is reasoning from instrument to strategy, which ends in a patent on a feature you will delete next year. The other is the appropriability trap: where lead time and switching costs already do the work, buying exclusion is buying what you have, and the purchase reliably produces only a published disclosure. Granthavali was in the second situation and spent ₹13.00 lakh before anyone said so.

5Hard edges and organisational seams

Multi-product firms discover that marks do not travel. Granthavali's word mark sat in class 42 (software as a service) but not class 9 (downloadable software); when it shipped a desktop add-in, a third party already held the identical word in class 9. Two-sided businesses inherit someone else's problem: a marketplace carries a statutory safe harbour as an intermediary, but the Delhi High Court held in 2018 that an operator which curates, warehouses and promotes a listing stops being a passive conduit — which is why Gauraiya's takedown worked. Regulated categories add machinery: section 3(d), the regulatory-use exemption in section 107A, and compulsory licensing under section 84, first granted in 2012.

Hardware plus software fails at the contract-manufacturer seam. Gauraiya's Hosur agreement assigned “jointly developed improvements” to both parties, which sounds fair and is not: in several jurisdictions each co-owner may license the whole without the other's consent, so the clause lets your supplier arm your competitor. AI-native products fail differently. There is no text-and-data-mining exception in the Copyright Act; section 52's fair dealing is a closed list of purposes, not an open standard, so the American fair-use argument for training does not transfer. Model weights are neither obviously a literary work nor patentable as such, leaving secrecy and contract as the only instruments that bind.

The deepest seam is organisational. The engineer who knows what is novel has no incentive to file; the budget sits in legal, which cannot see the roadmap; between them is the product manager, measured on neither. Mature companies put one standing question into the design review — what in this release is both new and visible? — and give the answer a named owner. What they say they do is run an IP committee, which meets twelve weeks after the trade show.

6Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The priority date is the only date, because every other deadline runs from it. India applies absolute novelty: any disclosure outside an obligation of confidence destroys it, and section 31 shelters only a Gazette-notified exhibition, not a buyers' preview. The tell is a data-room slide dated before the filing; the test is legal availability, not actual audience.

A patent is a right to exclude, never a right to practise. Owning a claim on a feature says nothing about whether shipping it infringes somebody else's. The tell is a PM saying “we have a patent, so we're clear” — a confession that no freedom-to-operate work has been done.

A longer claim is a weaker claim. Figure 2 is the general case: the element that makes the product distinctive is what lets rivals escape. The tell is an engineer saying, with pride, that claim 1 describes the product exactly — and a claim that describes your product exactly describes nobody else's.

Classes are not categories. A registration covers the goods specified and nothing adjacent. The tell is a brand team announcing the company “owns the name” after one filing. Wrong twice over: passing off reaches goodwill built by use, while the register reaches only where you filed.

Copyright stops copying, not competition. It protects expression, so a rival who reimplements the same function from scratch owes nothing, and section 52(1)(ab) permits the acts necessary to obtain information essential for interoperability with an independently created programme. The tell is counsel asserting rights over a list of field names.

In India, trade secrets rest on confidentiality, not restraint. There is no trade-secret statute, and section 27 of the Contract Act voids agreements in restraint of trade, so the post-employment non-compete is largely unenforceable. Protection is need-to-know architecture, confidentiality deeds and a disciplined exit. The tell is a twelve-month non-compete beside a monorepo every engineer can read.

Copyleft triggers on distribution, and firmware is distribution. A reciprocal licence's obligations are conditions on a copyright grant, enforced by stopping your shipment, and a binary on a device leaves the building in a way a hosted service did not — the reason the Affero variant exists. The tell is a bill of materials listing strong copyleft beside counsel saying “we don't distribute.”

Defensive publication is an instrument, not a surrender. A disclosure put into the public domain destroys everybody's novelty, including your own, for a fraction of a filing's cost — right when you want freedom to operate rather than exclusion. The tell is a portfolio where everything was filed and nothing asserted.

7How this differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the load-bearing instruments are the mark and the registered design, because purchase is fast, visual and repeated. In B2B and enterprise software the mark matters for procurement and little else does, because switching cost is the moat and the buyer never sees the implementation. On platforms and marketplaces the interesting rights belong to third parties, and the product question is the enforcement workflow: how fast a verified complaint produces a delisting. In hardware the registered design is the cheapest real exclusion available, and the contract-manufacturer agreement decides ownership. In AI products the centre of gravity moves off the register entirely, to input rights and secrecy.

Stage changes the answer less than people expect: the instruments do not change, only the budget and the sequence. A seed-stage company should spend on assignment hygiene and one mark, because an ownership gap is the IP problem most likely to kill a financing. At Series B the patent's signalling value peaks and its enforcement value bottoms, which is when most bad filings happen. What does not differ by stage: the priority date, the month-18 publication, and the fact that nobody recovers a disclosure.

8Three worked examples

The cheap instrument that worked. A look-alike of Gauraiya's first-generation enclosure appeared on a marketplace at ₹899 on 3 March 2026. Because Gauraiya held a registered design the listing came down on 10 April — 38 days, during which the copy sold 11,400 units, 300 a day. Gross profit per unit is ₹1,650 × 0.34 = ₹561, so at an assumed one-in-four substitution rate — an assumption, not a measurement — those 38 days had already cost 2,850 units and ₹15.99 lakh. What the design avoided is the counterfactual: ninety more days at 300 a day is 27,000 units, so 6,750 substituted sales and ₹37.87 lakh, against ₹0.45 lakh of cost — 84 times the outlay. No patent was involved, and none would have been faster.

The mark that could not be registered. Gauraiya's sub-brand Restscore drew an objection on 22 June 2026 for lack of distinctiveness. Fighting it with evidence of acquired distinctiveness cost ₹3.40 lakh, which Niveda gave a 0.35 chance of succeeding; if it failed, a rename eighteen months later over an inventory she projected at 3,22,000 cartons at ₹18 each.

Exhibit 3. The Restscore decision, in ₹ lakh. Expected cost in the first row is 3.40 + 0.65 × 57.96.
OptionOutlay nowChance it settles the matterCost if it does notExpected cost
Press the objection with evidence of acquired distinctiveness3.400.3557.9641.07
Rename before the 14 November launch25.201.000.0025.20

Renaming now costs ₹25.20 lakh — 1,40,000 cartons at ₹18 — and is ₹15.87 lakh cheaper in expectation. Gauraiya would have to put failure no higher than (25.20 − 3.40) ÷ 57.96 = 0.376, a 62.4 per cent chance of success, before fighting won. Nobody would sign 62 per cent.

The bargain that failed. Granthavali's failure was not grant risk but sequencing. The provisional was filed in August 2024 on an obligation-segmentation method that was, in substance, a training objective and a decoding strategy. The complete specification, filed on 1 August 2025, described both fully, because a specification must enable the invention, and it published on 12 February 2026. By the time the examiner raised section 3(k) on 4 September 2026, ₹13.00 lakh had been spent and the method sat with every competitor running a patent alert; one rival shipped a comparable segmenter in May 2026. Nethra cannot prove it read the publication, and that is the point: she bought a disclosure and received nothing. Recovery had three parts: she reframed the remaining ₹18.70 lakh as a fresh decision rather than a sunk-cost completion; she moved the next generation's advantage to the evaluation corpus, a trade secret that will never be filed; and she used the publication as what it had accidentally become, a defensive publication blocking anyone else from claiming the method against her.

9Four failure modes and their early warning signs

Disclosure before filing. Early sign: a conference slot or buyer preview that precedes any filing date. Diagnostic: what is our priority date, and what did we show before it? Caught late, an acquirer's counsel finds it, and it costs the family plus the warranty.

The descriptive mark. Early sign: the name tests best precisely because it describes the product. Diagnostic: would a competitor need this word to describe its own goods? Caught late, it costs a rename at grown inventory — Gauraiya's ₹57.96 lakh against the ₹25.20 lakh a rename before launch would cost.

The unassigned contributor. Early sign: a prototype, logo or model built by a freelancer on a statement of work with no assignment clause. Diagnostic: name every person who committed to this repository and the instrument that assigns their output. Caught late, it becomes an indemnity carve-out and a holdback.

Copyleft in a shipped binary. Early sign: no bill of materials, or one nobody reviews before a firmware release. Diagnostic: which components leave the building, and under what licence? Caught late, the remedy sought is an injunction on shipment, in launch week.

10Where competent people genuinely disagree

Do software patents reward invention or tax entry? The notice-failure case rests on real evidence: litigation costs in software exceed the profits attributable to the patents, and claim boundaries are not knowable before a court construes them. The opposing case rests on evidence as real — founder surveys find filing driven by deterrence and financing, and portfolios measurably improve venture terms. The two sides measure different payoffs. It resolves against notice-failure if financing effects persist where software claims were abolished, and against the financing view if investors price published applications like granted ones.

Should an AI-native company file at all? Steelmanned, yes: section 3(k) is a test, not a prohibition, the 2017 computer-related-inventions guidelines leave a path for a claim with a technical effect, and in diligence a granted Indian patent is an asset secrecy cannot substitute for. Steelmanned, no: the enabling disclosure publishes at month 18 into a field that iterates in six, so the bargain hands rivals a recipe for a claim that may never grant. Granthavali is one data point on the second side; it would take a cohort of published machine-learning families, and a measure of whether rivals accelerated, to move anyone.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks counsel “what are the risks?” and receives a list. Someone who has internalised it asks “between these two options, which costs less and why?” and receives a decision. That person files fewer applications and files them earlier; keeps a dated invention log; puts the month-18 publication on the roadmap as a launch event with an owner; and can say which one of the five instruments is load-bearing here and why the other four are not. A reliable tell is a PM who can describe what the company decided not to protect, without flinching.

12Decisions, and three questions

Nithilan filed a design application on Monday 12 October 2026, eight days before the buyers' preview, and renamed the sub-brand rather than fight the objection. He kept one narrow utility filing — on the sensor-fusion step, with the accelerometer recited as hardware — and dropped element (e) from claim 1 over his engineers' objections. His reasoning: at ₹561 of gross profit a unit, the instrument that delists a copy in 38 days beats the one that yields a claim in four years.

Nethra let the thirty-month deadline of 8 February 2027 pass unused, spending part of the ₹18.70 lakh instead on two further trade-mark classes and on the data-rights terms in her customer contracts. Her reasoning: the disclosure was made, the examiner had priced the Indian claim, and the advantage had moved to a corpus no register can hold.

1. Exhibit 2 buys four instruments with ₹32.40 lakh. Reallocate that budget for a software-only product at the same revenue, and defend the row you cut to zero.

2. Granthavali's specification became public on 12 February 2026 and cannot be withdrawn. Treating the ₹18.70 lakh as a fresh decision, what would the company have to observe over the next two years to conclude that the publication was worth its price?

3. Suppose section 27 of the Contract Act were amended so that post-employment non-competes became enforceable in India. Which of the two portfolios changes more, and in which direction?

13Going deeper

Open-source licences
Decides whether Gauraiya can ship firmware at all.
Data rights for training and fine-tuning
Where Nethra's advantage now lives.
Privacy by design
Element (e) was a privacy choice before a claim problem.
Data, consent and the DPDP Act
Consent limits what a corpus may lawfully contain.
GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes
An India-trained model meets other regimes' rules.
Personalisation vs surveillance
The sleep data that makes the band valuable is the liability.
Consent flows and cookie UX
