Indian School of Business · Software Product Management

Koshika Labs: the mark, the method and the corpus

Bengaluru, Sunday 18 October 2026

1. The night before

The office off Bannerghatta Road had gone to night setting at eight, and by half past ten Tanushree Dowerah was working in the dark with two laptops and an eleven-page printout headed Privileged and confidential — preliminary view, dated Friday 9 October 2026 and written by Tiyasha Debnath of Kartavya Law Partners after a fortnight in which three letters arrived from three counterparties who did not know of each other.

On the first laptop was the decision. Kanzi Modern Trade LLC, Koshika's largest customer, wanted its expansion order countersigned: ₹14.40 crore for 3,600 camera rigs across its Dubai, Muscat and Dammam operations, over eighteen months from 1 November 2026. Attached was Schedule 7, warranting that Koshika owned or was licensed to use every piece of intellectual property in the product and that the product infringed nobody. Tirtha Dasgupta expected it signed by Monday lunchtime Dubai time.

On the second laptop was a tab she had opened and closed four times that day: a recording from November 2023 in which her own chief technology officer explained, to two hundred people in Mumbai, how Koshika estimated shelf share from one photograph.

2. Company history

Koshika Labs Private Limited was incorporated in Bengaluru in July 2019 by Tirtha Dasgupta, a category analytics manager at a packaged-foods distributor, and Tapan Dhar, who had built vision systems for a Pune machine-tools firm. Their planogram-compliance app did not sell. What sold was the thing they built to speed up their own demos: a method that took one photograph of a shelf, from wherever a person stood, and returned each brand's share of visible facings.

The method needed labelled shelf photographs and in 2020 Koshika had none. On 12 November 2020 the founders signed a six-month pilot memorandum with Kuntala Retail Private Limited, a Hyderabad hypermarket chain trading as Kuntala Bazaar, giving Koshika's agents access to 31 Kuntala stores. Clause 9.3 of its four pages said all data generated during the pilot vested in Kuntala. Dasgupta signed without counsel because the pilot was unpaid and the alternative was no data at all. Nobody had read the clause since.

The product was named KHOJI in January 2021 and the mark filed in Class 9 the next month. The Mark-2 rig, which replaced the moulded front bezel with a printed label, began shipping on 1 April 2025.

3. The industry

Retail execution measurement in India is crowded and oddly structured. The buyers are packaged-goods companies and their distributors, who want to know whether the shelf space they paid for exists; the sellers are feet-on-street audit firms, crowdsourcing outfits and a few computer-vision companies. Demand has been pulled by modern trade, quick commerce and the ONDC network: Reliance Retail, DMart, Zepto and Blinkit have between them changed what a brand manager in Mumbai expects to know by Tuesday about Saturday.

Regulation bears on the product in two places. Shelf photographs contain shoppers, which brings the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 into frame; and an invention the Indian Patent Office characterises as a computer programme per se draws an objection under section 3(k) of the Patents Act, 1970, which drafting tends to meet by narrowing a claim towards apparatus. Exposure beyond India is material: of ₹27.40 crore of revenue in the six months to 30 September 2026, ₹6.80 crore came from the Gulf and ₹3.20 crore from the United States — ₹10.00 crore, or 36.5 per cent, from two jurisdictions where Koshika holds no registered trade mark (one UAE application pending, nothing filed in the United States) and no granted patent (Exhibit 2).

4. The situation in detail: what was on the file at each date

On Thursday 16 November 2023 Tapan Dhar spoke for twenty-two minutes at a retail-technology conference in Goregaon, Mumbai. His slides described the single-frame method, including the oblique-projection correction step, and the session was recorded. The belief inside Koshika then, in a two-line email from Dasgupta, was that the talk was good for hiring and the method too specific to copy.

On Thursday 18 April 2024 Koshika filed a provisional application at the Patent Office in Chennai; that is the priority date from which the PCT, United States and European clocks in Exhibit 1 run. The complete specification followed on 9 April 2025 and a PCT application on 15 April 2025. On 3 July 2026 the First Examination Report arrived with two objections: lack of novelty over a granted United States patent held by Kadence Retail Vision Pte Ltd of Singapore, and section 3(k).

In June 2023 Dowerah renamed the software layer from KHOJI Studio to Koshika Console, so that the hardware carried the brand; since that month the registered Class 9 mark has not been used on a software product. The Registry's report of 28 July 2026 cited KHOJEE in Class 35, entered on 4 March 2019 for Koyal Retail Services Private Limited, Delhi.

Then, in the nine days to 6 October, three letters. Kadence's counsel wrote on 28 September 2026, received on the 30th, alleging that Koshika practises the claims of Kadence's granted United States patent — the '418 patent, as both sides now call it — and citing the November 2023 recording as evidence. Koyal's counsel wrote on 5 October, calling KHOJI deceptively similar to KHOJEE and stating that Koyal will oppose. Kuntala's company secretary wrote on 6 October, enclosing clause 9.3 and asking within thirty days what became of the pilot data. Kritisa Capital's ₹180 crore term sheet of 30 September requires clean title to all registered and material unregistered intellectual property, and runs forty-five days.

5. The people

Tirtha Dasgupta, co-founder and chief executive. Countersign Monday and work the IP file in parallel; the Series B is priced off annualised recurring revenue, which the Kanzi order moves. Not saying: he approved the November 2023 talk over a written objection from Dhar, and the deck Kadence attaches is the one he asked for.

Tanushree Dowerah, senior director of product, the protagonist. Will not warrant what she cannot verify by Monday; she owns the Kanzi roadmap and the United States launch. Not saying: she approved the 2022 stock-imagery licence without reading clause 4.2, and has not told anyone that the rename in Exhibit 1's Class 9 row was hers.

Tapan Dhar, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune. Design around the '418 claims, and the accuracy cost of doing so is inside the noise; he is sole named inventor on the pending application. Not saying: the replacement has run on 140 of the 760 United States rigs since 3 August 2026, unmentioned to Kadence and the board, and over August and September its mean absolute error on 6,200 audited facings was 4.8 percentage points against the production method's 3.1.

Tamal Duarah, vice-president of sales, New Jersey. Take the licence: ₹96.85 lakh a year against United States revenue of ₹6.40 crore annualised (₹3.20 crore in H1 FY2027, doubled) is 15.1 per cent, and forty per cent of his package rides on an FY2027 quota of ₹8.20 crore. Not saying: two of his three largest prospects asked for the warranty Kanzi wants, and on 24 September 2026 he said yes.

Tanaya Dam, director of customer success, Singapore. Nothing that risks Kanzi; she manages the Gulf, United States and rest-of-world accounts, which in H1 FY2027 were ₹6.80, ₹3.20 and ₹0.90 crore — ₹10.90 crore, of which the Gulf is 62.4 per cent. Not saying: Kanzi's procurement head told her on 12 October 2026 of a competing bid at ₹11.80 crore against Koshika's ₹14.40 crore.

Tapasya Dastidar, principal data scientist, Toronto. The corpus is the exposure that cannot be bought off, and no error gap of that size is noise; a retrain without the pilot labels is a programme she would lead. Not saying: she ran the ablation on 28 September 2026 — the 1,86,400 Kuntala images removed, held-out mean absolute error 5.6 points against the production model's 3.2 on the same 4,400 audited facings — and has shown it to nobody.

Tiyasha Debnath, partner, Kartavya Law Partners, on a monthly cap of ₹4.50 lakh. Warrant only what is on a register; a contested proceeding moves to a larger firm and out of her cap. Not saying: her paragraph on the November 2023 talk rests on one attendee's recollection that the session was closed-door, and she has not seen the recording.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Schedule 7 is boilerplate. Every vendor signs it and in seven years nobody has called one in.” — “Not when three people write to us in nine days about three pieces of one product. I can tell Kanzi we own the firmware. I cannot tell them we own the labels.”

Tirtha Dasgupta and Tanushree Dowerah, leadership call, Friday 16 October 2026, 18:40 IST.

“The '418 claims recite a calibration target in frame. We have not needed one since 2024. If the examiner thinks that reads on us, he has read their claim 1 and our abstract and stopped.”

Tapan Dhar, #ip-war-room, 17 October 2026, 09:12 IST.

“Then why is the branch on 140 rigs.”

Tapasya Dastidar, same thread, 23:47 on the 16th in Toronto, which is 09:17 IST on the 17th.

“Whether we infringe is a question about claim scope. Whether we can warrant that we do not is a question about what we have in writing, and what we have is a memorandum whose author has not seen the primary evidence.”

Tiyasha Debnath, email to Dowerah and Dasgupta, 17 October 2026, 14:05 IST.

“The rig number depends entirely on whether the fleet is one fleet or two. Kartavya thinks it is one. I have held a Mark-1 bezel.”

Titir Devnath, design review, 16 October 2026, 11:30 in Berlin, 15:00 IST.

8. The options as Dowerah sees them

A. Countersign Schedule 7 as drafted. Kanzi's ₹14.40 crore order proceeds and the Series B keeps the revenue line the term sheet was built on. The warranty is uncapped and covers every piece of intellectual property embodied in the product. The three letters stay where they are.

B. Countersign with a carve-out and a cap. A revised Schedule 7 on Monday, limiting the warranty to the registered rights in Exhibit 1, disclosing the Kadence correspondence and capping liability at twelve months' fees. It needs Kanzi's lawyers to re-paper inside a delivery window that opens on 1 November.

C. Take the Kadence licence and sign. Exhibit 6 prices year one at ₹96.85 lakh over 760 rigs, with US$240,000 of past sales demanded separately, against a Kadence response date of 30 November. The licence covers the United States assertion.

D. Pause the countersignature for a fortnight. Kanzi is told Schedule 7 is under review; Dowerah commissions an analysis of the recording and a freedom-to-operate opinion, and takes one paper to the board on 29 October. The fortnight ends on 2 November, with Kanzi's window already open and Kuntala's 5 November date, Kritisa's 14 November expiry and the 18 November European date still ahead.

Each of the four is a decision about Monday's signature, each owned by Dowerah alone, and none touches the two items in Exhibit 1 nobody has asked her about: whether to enter the European regional phase, and whether the Class 9 registration is worth keeping. Dhar has said more than once that the patent Koshika defends and the patent it prosecutes are one claim.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Kanzi expects Schedule 7 countersigned by Monday 19 October 2026, 13:00 Dubai time, which is 14:30 IST. Kuntala's reply date is 5 November 2026, Kritisa Capital's exclusivity expires on 14 November, Kadence's deadline is 30 November, and the remaining dates in Exhibit 1 run on into December and January. Tuhin Deb, the partner leading the round, wants an IP annexure before the board meets on Thursday 29 October.

Money and people are tighter than the dates. Cash and liquid investments stood at ₹22.60 crore on 30 September 2026, and net burn averaged ₹1.85 crore a month over H1 FY2027, being ₹11.10 crore over the six months; on that run-rate the 30 September balance funds 12.2 months, to early October 2027. Kartavya's retainer does not cover United States work. Dhar has nineteen engineers, eleven committed to the Kanzi delivery from 1 November, and the Deepavali fortnight falls in early November.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 3, set out the earliest date on which each of the four parties that wrote to Koshika since 28 September 2026 can compel it to act. Which is nearest, and is it the date the company is organised around?
  2. Exhibit 4 reports the Kuntala pilot as 25.9 per cent of images. What other denominators does the exhibit support, and which should price clause 9.3?
  3. Exhibit 5's totals differ by a factor of 2.26, and its footnote gives the unit rates behind three of the five lines. Which of those rates are questions of fact and which of judgement, and which could be settled by Monday?
  4. Dhar treats the gap between 4.8 and 3.1 percentage points as noise; Dastidar does not. What measurement, not on this page, would settle it, and what does producing it disclose?
  5. Rank the four options by what each protects and exposes. Then pick the undisclosed fact in section 5 which, surfacing on Tuesday, would move your ranking furthest.
  6. What should Dowerah do on Monday morning, and what should she say to the board on 29 October about a model the company may not own, a mark it may not keep, and an application that cites the patent being asserted against it?

The rest of Sunday night

At twenty past eleven Dowerah opened the recording for a fifth time and watched all twenty-two minutes. At minute fourteen Dhar put up a diagram of the oblique correction and said, to laughter, that the clever part was that you did not need anything in the frame to calibrate against. She wrote the sentence down with its timestamp.

Then she made two lists on one sheet. On the left, what she could put in writing by half past two on Monday afternoon: what was on a register, two dates, one retainer. On the right, what Schedule 7 would have her warrant. She drafted a message to Dasgupta, read it, and did not send it.
exp20v2-legal.ip:
IP, patents and trademarks for PMs

1. A name, an algorithm and a deadline

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Madhulika Velagapudi, head of product at Elavani, a Chennai meal-planning app with 1.8 lakh monthly active users, received a two-line email from outside counsel Mukund Vellaichamy: "The preliminary register look-up on Saapadu Select is back. Call me before you approve the print order." The print order for hoardings, packaging inserts and app-store assets was due to lock on Friday 25 September. The premium tier, priced at ₹199 a month, was set to launch on Tuesday 3 November.

The look-up, a quick scan of the public Trade Marks Registry, found a registration for SAAPADU SELECT in Class 43 (restaurant and catering services) held by Eruvaka Saapadu Kitchens, a Coimbatore caterer, and a pending application by the same firm in Class 9 (downloadable software), filed in 2025. Elavani had not filed anything. Meanwhile the chief executive, Mythri Valliappan, wanted a second question settled before launch: whether the pantry-matching routine behind the tier, which suggests dinners from whatever a household already owns, could be patented to keep rivals off it.

Money was at stake in plain terms. If the name had to change after launch, Elavani would write off ₹52 lakh of marketing, ₹18 lakh of design and packaging assets and ₹8 lakh of legal cost, a total of ₹78 lakh. Changing it before print would cost about ₹6 lakh. Velagapudi had seventeen days to learn enough law to choose between those two numbers, and to decide what, if anything, to ask the patent attorney.

2. The idea

Intellectual property (IP) is a set of legal rights over things that are not physical: names, expressions, inventions and secrets. It exists because such things are cheap to copy and expensive to create. A rival can imitate a recipe-ranking screen in an afternoon; building it took Elavani eleven months. Law answers by granting the creator a limited, enforceable exclusivity, on the theory that without it nobody would invest. The exclusivity is deliberately temporary or conditional: a patent expires, a trademark lapses if unused, and copyright never covers a bare idea, so that the public keeps the freedom to build on what others have made.

The rights were developed piecemeal. Venice issued an early patent statute in 1474; England's Statute of Monopolies followed in 1624; the Paris Convention of 1883 made national rights portable across borders; and the TRIPS Agreement of 1995 set minimum standards for every World Trade Organization member, India included. India's current statutes are the Patents Act 1970, the Copyright Act 1957, the Designs Act 2000 and the Trade Marks Act 1999.

The sentence Velagapudi could repeat in a meeting: IP is not one right but four groups of them, each guarding a different thing on a different clock, so the first job is to say which thing we are protecting or about to infringe.

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 is the map Velagapudi drew on a whiteboard. Read it left to right as four questions. Does the thing identify who sells it? That is a trademark question. Is it a technical method that is new and not obvious? Patent. Is it text, code, imagery or music someone wrote? Copyright. Is it valuable because competitors do not know it? Secrecy, enforced by contract.

The steps practitioners leave implicit are four. First, identify the owner: a contractor who wrote code owns it unless a signed assignment says otherwise, whereas an employee's work generally belongs to the employer. Second, identify the clock: a trademark opposition window, a patent's twelve-month period to convert a provisional filing into a complete one, or a launch date. Third, separate what we can protect from what we may use. Vellaichamy's look-up addressed only the second, which is why it arrived before any filing. Fourth, evidence: a dated record of when the name was first used, when code was written and by whom, which later decides who prevailed.

4. A worked example

Velagapudi framed the name decision as two options. Option A is to launch without clearance. Option B is to commission what the look-up was not, a professional search and written opinion, file in three classes, and rename before print if the search shows a problem. She wrote down her inputs. Option A carries a 20 per cent chance of a conflict claim within eighteen months, judged by Vellaichamy from the look-up hit, and a loss of ₹78 lakh if it happens. Option B costs ₹35,000 for the search, ₹85,000 for the opinion, and ₹27,000 to file in Classes 9, 35 and 42 at ₹9,000 a class (the fee for a company; smaller applicants pay less). That is ₹1,47,000, or ₹1.47 lakh. The assumed chance that the full work confirms a conflict is 25 per cent, which forces a pre-launch rename at ₹6 lakh; a residual 4 per cent chance of a later claim remains, at the same ₹78 lakh, applied conservatively to all cases.

LineWorking₹ lakh
A. Expected loss, no clearance0.20 × 7815.60
B1. Search, opinion, filing0.35 + 0.85 + 0.271.47
B2. Expected pre-launch rename0.25 × 61.50
B3. Expected residual claim0.04 × 783.12
B. Total expected cost, clearance1.47 + 1.50 + 3.126.09
Saving from B15.60 − 6.099.51

Clearance saves ₹9.51 lakh in expectation, so the answer is to buy it. Now change one input. Suppose the name were an invented coinage with no register hits, so the chance of a claim under Option A fell from 20 per cent to 5 per cent, holding B's inputs unchanged. A becomes 0.05 × 78 = ₹3.90 lakh, below B's ₹6.09 lakh, and clearance no longer pays on expected value alone. Break-even sits at 6.09 ÷ 78 = 7.8 per cent: above it, search; below it, launch. The answer flipped because one probability moved, which is why the probability, not the arithmetic, deserves the argument. The 25 per cent and 4 per cent figures are judgements, not measurements; a PM should write them down, show them to counsel and let counsel change them, because a disagreement about a number is far easier to resolve than a disagreement about a feeling. A second input worth testing is the loss: with a soft launch that risked only ₹20 lakh, Option A would cost 0.20 × 20 = ₹4.00 lakh and Option B 1.47 + 1.50 + 0.04 × 20 = ₹3.77 lakh, nearly a tie.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Registration is not the only protection

An unregistered name used long enough to carry goodwill can be defended by an action for passing off, a common-law claim that a rival is misrepresenting its goods as yours. Registration makes enforcement far easier but does not erase another firm's earlier use.

Priority beats preference

Eruvaka's earlier filing date, not Elavani's user numbers, decides who wins the register. Search the pending applications as well as the granted marks.

Similarity, not identity, is the test

Registries and courts ask whether an average consumer, with imperfect recollection, would be confused about origin. Saapadu Select and Saapadu Choice can clash; so can a different spelling or sound-alike.

Classes narrow, but only somewhat

A mark is registered for stated goods and services, grouped in forty-five Nice classes. Related classes still collide: a meal app and a caterer serve the same diner, so Class 9 and Class 43 are neighbours, not strangers.

Algorithms are not inventions in India

Section 3(k) of the Patents Act excludes "a mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms". A pantry-matching routine claimed as pure logic is likely refused; one tied to a demonstrable technical effect may survive. The question for a patent attorney is therefore narrow and specific.

Copyright guards expression, never the idea

A rival may build a different app that also turns a pantry into dinners. It may not copy Elavani's code or recipe text. The line between idea and expression is where most disputes live.

Using is not owning

Fonts, stock photos and software libraries arrive under licences that may forbid commercial or app-store use. A licence grants permission on terms; read those terms before shipping.

The symbols mean different things

The ™ sign may be used by anyone claiming a mark. The ® sign may be shown only once the mark is registered; using it earlier is a misstatement a rival can exploit, so check the register before approving artwork.

What no search can tell you

A clean search shows that nothing was found, not that nothing exists; unpublished patent applications stay hidden for eighteen months and unregistered users never appear. Before relying on a result, ask who compiled it, which registers it covered, and on what date.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

In consumer products the name is the asset, because the brand is what a household remembers; trademarks dominate and searches should precede every launch. In B2B software, buyers audit contracts more than logos, so the live questions are who owns customer-specific code, what the licence terms are, and whether the product infringes a third party's patent; indemnity clauses carry the weight.

A marketplace adds a third party's content. Sellers upload photographs and brand names that may infringe others' rights, so the platform's takedown process and terms of use matter as much as its own marks.

Early-stage companies cannot afford to protect everything; they should clear and file the name, secure assignments from every contributor and keep the rest secret. Large companies run patent portfolios and routine searches, but also attract more claims, because they are worth suing.

7. Common mistakes

Treating registration as clearance

Symptom: a launch deck says "we have filed, so we are safe." Misunderstanding: filing grants a place in the queue, not a right against earlier owners. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether anyone searched for earlier marks before the filing date, and ask for the report.

Assuming the contractor's work is ours

Symptom: an agency that built an early app version refuses a request years later. Misunderstanding: payment does not transfer copyright. Diagnostic: find the signed assignment; if there is none, get one this week.

Patenting what is better kept secret

Symptom: a team plans to file on its ranking weights. Misunderstanding: a patent publishes the method, so competitors read the recipe. Diagnostic: ask whether anyone could detect copying from outside; if not, secrecy usually serves better.

Calling counsel after the commitment

Symptom: legal sees the name for the first time on a printed proof. Misunderstanding: advice is a cost, not a gate. Diagnostic: check the calendar for the last date a change is cheap.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of this decision begins in July, not September. The name enters a shortlist of three, each cleared against granted and pending marks in Classes 9, 35, 42 and 43 before any design work is paid for. Contributor assignments are collected at onboarding. The patent question goes to counsel as one page: what is novel, what technical effect it produces, and what it would cost to disclose. The PM can say, for every asset, which of the four rights covers it and when the next deadline falls. Counsel is briefed in writing, with the launch date, the markets, the budget at risk and the alternatives already considered, so the reply addresses the choice rather than the law in general.

9. Closing

Velagapudi called Vellaichamy on 10 September. He told her that Eruvaka's Class 9 application, if allowed, would give it priority over anything Elavani filed. Applying her own numbers, she chose Option B; when the opinion confirmed the conflict, she renamed the tier "Saapadu Plus" after a fresh check, file in three classes before print, and confirm assignments from the the agencies that built the early versions. For the pantry routine she asked for a one-page opinion on Section 3(k) and filed nothing, so the weights stayed secret. Her reasoning was that a ₹6.09 lakh expected cost, of which ₹1.47 lakh was certain, beat a ₹15.60 lakh expected loss (a 20 per cent chance of losing ₹78 lakh).

To go further, study open-source licences, which govern the code Elavani borrows, and data rights for training and fine-tuning, which govern what a model may learn from. Both are questions about what you may use, the half of IP this page only began.

Two questions to sit with. First: which asset in a product you know best would be hardest to defend if a rival copied it tomorrow, and which of the four rights would you even reach for? Second: at what probability of conflict would you stop paying for a search, and who in your organisation would have to agree?

Indian School of Business · Case 40

Malancha Labs: What the Pass Remembers

Bengaluru, Sunday 18 October 2026

1. The night before

At twenty to ten on Sunday night, Yashomita Gayen sat on the floor of her flat in Bengaluru's Cooke Town with two printouts that described the same company and did not agree. One was an external readiness assessment of Malancha Labs, dated 14 August, scoring the privacy programme fifty out of a hundred. The other was her own compliance tracker, pulled Friday 2 October, reporting 143 of 184 controls complete. She had signed off on both.

On Monday she had to tell Yashvardhan Gohain, who had founded Malancha Labs seven years earlier and still read every spec himself, whether Release 9 would ship group-wide on Tuesday 1 December. R9 would break the Pass apart: unbundle one pre-ticked consent box into four purposes, put a 24-month limit on prescription images that had never had one, cut till basket history from 84 months to 18, tokenise phone numbers 13 months after a member's last visit. Nine chains and four diagnostic groups ran on the Pass; 202.2 lakh members were enrolled, all but the pilot's enrolees on a single box.

The pilot had closed eighteen days earlier. At 21:40 IST she had a call with Yuvina Guharoy in Toronto, ten past noon there, and Yashoraj Guin in Berlin, ten past six. Her notes ran to one line: what is the Pass actually for.

2. Malancha Labs, 2019–2026

Gohain and two classmates started Malancha Labs in June 2019 on a small, dull problem: Indian pharmacy chains could not tell a repeat customer from a new one. The Pass was a white-label loyalty and refill-reminder layer that sat on a chain's till software, took a phone number, and messaged when a chronic medicine was due. By 2026 it was a ₹264 crore business with the chain's brand on the front of it.

One week in July 2021 shapes everything available today. To win Mandara Chemists, then 1,100 stores and now 1,912, Malancha did two things. It built one undifferentiated event lake, where every till line, reminder, prescription image and lab result landed in the same store with no retention policy attached, because policies cost sprints and the round was closing. And on Friday 9 July 2021 it signed a master services agreement whose clause 11.4 gives Mandara a full export of its members' event history on demand. Together they mean Malancha can neither delete what it does not want without renegotiating what it promised, nor find what it holds without reading the whole lake.

3. The industry

Indian pharmacy retail in 2026 is a fight between four kinds of company for the same customer. Apollo Pharmacy and MedPlus run large owned chains; Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Reliance's Netmeds sell online and build their own member graphs; Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis Healthcare and Thyrocare sit on diagnostics; quick-commerce platforms have begun putting pharmacy counters inside dark stores. Malancha's chains are those without an in-house data team, which is why losing the Pass would lose them their customer memory.

Three regulatory facts bear on the product. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, assented 11 August 2023, requires itemised notice, consent tied to a purpose and erasure once that purpose is served; its Rules were notified in November 2025 with phased obligations, and Malancha's legal note of 2 September 2026 reads the substantive duties as binding from 13 May 2027. The CERT-In direction of 28 April 2022 requires security logs retained 180 days within India. And Mandara has twice asked for the ABHA identifier, which would attach a national health identity to Exhibit 1's basket history.

Malancha's global exposure runs through one client. Mishwar Health Group of Dubai runs 184 clinics and pharmacies across the UAE under the DIFC regime, with a Frankfurt subsidiary whose members fall under the GDPR. Its contract requires member records to stay inside the UAE.

4. The situation in detail: what was believed, when, and what was measured later

Belief, July 2021 to March 2026. That consent was settled. Every member had enrolled by ticking one till box covering reminders, chain-wide loyalty, prescription storage and the brand-analytics panel sold as Malancha Insights. An audit from Monday 2 to Sunday 15 February 2026 recorded 34,434 enrolments from 36,400 customers offered the Pass, 94.6 per cent, and the figure went into the Series C pre-read as evidence consent was free. Gayen approved its design and knew it counted only customers who were offered the Pass; her R9 charter names a promotion contingent on shipping.

Measurement, April to September 2026. The R9 pilot ran 183 days in 118 Mandara stores in Pune and Nagpur, against 124 matched control stores in Nashik and Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar on the old box. Exhibit 2 holds both arms.

Belief, April 2026. That the base could be re-consented in-app. A prompt went to 24.6 lakh app-active members between Monday 10 and Sunday 23 August 2026; 4.92 lakh responded, 20.0 per cent of those prompted, and 1.722 lakh of them granted brand analytics, 35.0 per cent of responders and 7.0 per cent of those prompted. Finance's budget, approved 28 September, assumes 20.5 lakh re-consents across the 202.2 lakh base.

Belief, August 2026. That the programme was most of the way there. Mrinmoyee Assurance Partners of Gurugram scored seven of nine control domains against an extract as at 31 July and reported Friday 14 August (Exhibit 5), leaving two unassessed. The tracker of Friday 2 October (Exhibit 6) counts line items, and counts those two as done.

Event, 5 October 2026. Mandara's chief information officer opened an early re-tender for the contract that renews 9 July 2027, bids due Friday 15 January 2027. His letter gives no reason.

5. The people

Yashvardhan Gohain, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants R9 shipped before the Mandara bid, to lead with it. Incentive: a ₹520 crore Series C whose pre-money rests on Insights growing. Not saying: an investor's counsel has asked for the retention policy in writing.

Yaminikanta Ghoshdastidar, chief legal officer and data protection officer, Mumbai; joined April 2024. Argues the schedule is the obligation and the screens the easy half. Incentive: the DPO is a named office. Not saying: clause 11.4 may be unenforceable against a deletion duty, and she has not told the board.

Yunus Gharami, vice-president, platform engineering, Pune; joined January 2020. Built the 2021 lake; says remote config pushes R9 to 900 outlets a day. Incentive: a re-architecture R9 funds. Not saying: that path has only run on the 118 pilot stores.

Yuvina Guharoy, principal data scientist, Toronto; joined August 2023. Holds Insights can be rebuilt on store-week aggregates. Incentive: a paper and a conference slot. Not saying: the conference abstract naming Malancha is already submitted.

Yeshwanth Garai, senior vice-president, enterprise sales, Newark, New Jersey; joined June 2023. Carries the Insights number and the Mishwar renewal. Incentive: commission weighted to Insights bookings. Not saying: he has told both brands the panel will not shrink.

Yogamaya Golder, director, customer success, Singapore; joined November 2021. Says the field cannot absorb a consent change and a till upgrade in one quarter, and puts crew throughput at 28 outlets a day in peak season against Gharami's 40. Incentive: a renewal bonus across nine chains. Not saying: Mandara's CIO told her in September that the re-tender is about price.

Yashoraj Guin, design lead, privacy experience, Berlin; joined February 2025. Designed the four-toggle screen. Incentive: the screen becoming the industry's pattern. Not saying: brand analytics went last because an earlier order tested worse, and the pilot never ran it.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"We will be the first platform in Indian pharmacy retail to ask for four things instead of one, and we will say so on the Mandara bid. I will not be the chief executive who was asked about retention and said roadmap."

Yashvardhan Gohain, board pre-read, 12 October 2026

"The screens are not the obligation. A purpose that ends does not leave the data behind it lawful. We hold 78.8 lakh members' prescription images and no deletion job for any of them."

"On dental care, eleven weeks, one chain, the store-week aggregate model recovered 4.2 points of incremental basket penetration against 4.9 for the member-level model. It is the only category I have run. I would neither generalise nor ignore it."

"Everyone is arguing about the toggles. Nobody has asked what the reminder needs. A molecule, a date, a quantity. It has never needed a photograph of a doctor's handwriting, and the till has the first three."

Yashoraj Guin, design thread, 14:05 Berlin, 16 October 2026 (17:35 IST)

"Remote config will carry the toggle screen. It will not carry 2,180 outlets below till version 4.2, and the chains freeze till software from 25 October to 20 November for Diwali. Eleven days between the freeze and 1 December, and Yogamaya and I do not agree on what a crew does."

Yunus Gharami, call with Gayen, 18 October 2026, 20:15 IST

8. The options as Yashomita Gayen sees them

Gayen had written four options on one page on Friday. Finance prices all four against one base, the 202.2 lakh members of 30 September 2026, and the FY2025-26 Insights yield of ₹40.0 per panel member-year, being ₹71.2 crore over an average panel of 178.0 lakh. Of R9's 99 person-weeks, 60 were spent to 30 September and 39 remain.

A. Ship R9 group-wide on 1 December 2026. Four toggles at every till, the Exhibit 4 schedule, tokenisation at 13 months. Costs 39 person-weeks and a ₹6.4 crore campaign: a ₹21 per-member till incentive on the 20.5 lakh re-consents Finance assumes, plus ₹2.1 crore of SMS, IVR and in-app messaging across the full base, a little over a rupee a member.

B. Ship the screens now, defer retention and minimisation to FY2027-28. Sixteen of the 39 person-weeks; no campaign, since only new enrolments see the screens. The legacy base keeps its bundled consent and stays in the panel.

C. Split the Pass into a clinical core and an opt-in offers layer. A minimal service record for reminders, plus a separate store for loyalty and analytics a member joins deliberately. Estimated at 71 person-weeks on 14 October, plus ₹1.9 crore to re-paper thirteen client agreements.

D. Commit publicly, implement over eighteen months. Announce the 24-month limit at the Mandara bid on 15 January 2027 and apply the schedule by 31 May 2028. Nothing to pay before 1 December; the 39 person-weeks spread over six quarters.

None of the four is written against Guin's claim about three fields, Guharoy's dental-care result, or Golder's September conversation.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets Wednesday 28 October. Mandara's bids are due Friday 15 January 2027; Mandara is 96.4 lakh of the 202.2 lakh members and 1,912 of the 5,047 outlets. Series C diligence opens 7 January 2027 on a ₹520 crore round. Cash stood at ₹214 crore on 30 September 2026, a stated balance-sheet figure.

Six engineers are free from Monday 19 October, with six working weeks to 30 November. The till-software freeze from 25 October to 20 November bars deployment, not development, leaving eleven days from 21 November to 1 December for field work on 2,180 outlets below till version 4.2, six crews at 40 outlets a day by Gharami's figure and 28 by Golder's. Clause 11.4 survives any release Malancha ships alone. The CERT-In floor is 180 days. Mishwar's records cannot leave the UAE. And the lake has one schema, so a retention rule binds every class sharing a table with it.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Taking each of the six data classes in Exhibit 4 in turn, does the case give you enough to judge whether the retention period follows from the stated purpose? Where it does not, name the missing fact.
  2. Exhibit 2 reports 94.6 per cent from the February 2026 audit and purpose-level figures from the pilot. State each one's denominator and measurement date, construct the like-for-like comparison, and say what it does and does not establish about the cost of unbundling consent.
  3. The August prompt reached 24.6 lakh members, 4.92 lakh responded and 1.722 lakh of those granted brand analytics; Finance assumes 20.5 lakh re-consents across 202.2 lakh members. Which base should a December forecast use, what do the non-responders mean for each option, and how would you test the assumption before 1 December?
  4. Exhibits 5 and 6 report different pictures of the same programme. Reconcile them, accounting for the two scoring bases, the twenty-six self-attested items, the twelve points of unassessed weight and the gap between the dates. Which would you put to the board on 28 October, and what would you say about the other?
  5. Clause 11.4, the CERT-In 180-day floor and Mishwar's residency requirement each resist a different row of Exhibit 4. For each, say what Malancha would have to change, contract or architecture or product, and whose agreement that needs. Then say which options each constraint permits.
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October 2026. What does Gayen do, and in what order, between now and the Mandara bid of 15 January 2027? Draft what she says to the board about the trade she is making, including the number she is least able to defend.

Sunday, 11:52 p.m.

The call had ended forty minutes earlier. Guharoy had gone back to her holdout. Guin had sent a screenshot of the four toggles and no text. Gayen had not replied.

She put the two printouts side by side again. Somewhere between them were photographs of 78.8 lakh members' prescriptions, taken at tills in Hyderabad and Nagpur and Kochi by staff who had said sir, just put your thumb here, and a clause signed one Friday in July 2021 by a man no longer at Malancha. In eight hours she had to say a date out loud.

She opened the thread with Gohain, typed can we talk at 8, and looked at it.
exp40v2-legal.privacy.principles:
Privacy by Design

Collecting less, keeping less and explaining more — as a property of the schema, not a paragraph in the notice.

1. Two product managers, one question

On Monday 2 March 2026, Rajalakshmi Buddharaju, head of product at Ilavenil Cover, asked her general counsel a question. Ilavenil, a Chennai company, files health-insurance claims for 11,40,000 registered users; its intake form collects 34 data elements. For how many could he name the purpose? Raghuram Bezawada came back on Friday 13 March with 26. The other eight had no purpose owner: three held sensitive health detail, five were conveniences — employer name, referral code, marital status, device model, preferred language. Ilavenil's largest insurer partner wanted an impact assessment by Friday 29 May, 88 days out, and Rupavathi Bandlamudi, who ran growth, credited the five conveniences to a propensity model and would not surrender them.

Nine hundred kilometres north-west, Rangaswami Botcha faced the same question in hardware, where it does not wait. Iravatham Telematics, in Pune, fits 4,200 trucks across 38 fleet customers with a box combining GPS, an accelerometer and a driver-facing camera. Its next unit, the IRV-3, froze its bill of materials on Friday 17 April 2026 — day 46 — and ships from a Hosur contract manufacturer from Monday 6 July; whatever privacy properties it has will be soldered in. His platform engineer, Rathnavel Bollineni, wanted fatigue detection on the device, with only an event flag leaving the vehicle. Revanth Bellamkonda, fleet head at Irumbu Carriers and the customer behind 940 of the 4,200 vehicles, wanted raw footage kept 365 days to defend insurance disputes. The driver being recorded was party to neither conversation, and was not paying.

Both are deciding the same thing, and it is narrower than the phrase suggests. Privacy by design is a set of claims about which copies of which fields exist, for how long, and under whose stated purpose — and the honest version of any such claim is set by the longest-lived copy, not the policy.

2. The idea, and the traditions that disagree about it

Privacy by design is the discipline of fixing a product's privacy properties in its schema, defaults and data flows at specification time rather than in its notice text after launch. Three levers do the work. Data minimisation: collect only what a stated purpose needs. Purpose limitation: use it only for that purpose. Storage limitation: delete it when the purpose ends. It was invented against asymmetric accumulation: whoever adds a field enjoys the convenience this quarter, while the exposure and the regulatory answer fall on whoever is in the chair three years later.

The intellectual history runs through traditions still arguing. The Fair Information Practices of the early 1970s, codified in the 1980 OECD guidelines, made privacy procedural: notice, choice, access, correction. Ann Cavoukian, then Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, published seven foundational principles of Privacy by Design around 2009; Article 25 of the GDPR made a version binding from May 2018, and ISO 31700-1:2023 made it auditable. Helen Nissenbaum's contextual integrity, from 2004, moved the question from volume to the appropriateness of a flow. Cynthia Dwork's differential privacy, from 2006, insisted that a privacy claim without a mathematical bound is a promise, not a property. India's DPDP Act, 2023 sits in the first tradition, with structural duties added under Section 10.

These are not stylistic preferences. Each school disagrees about propositions a practitioner must take a position on, stated below as each would defend them.

SchoolThe proposition it would signThe proposition it would not sign
Fair Information PracticesA disclosed, consented secondary use is legitimate.Some collection is impermissible even with free consent.
Structural (Cavoukian, “code is law”)The default nobody changes is the real policy.A well-drafted notice cures a data-hungry default.
Contextual integrity (Nissenbaum)A reading fine for a clinician is wrong for an underwriter, at identical volume.Less data is always more private.
Formal guarantee (Dwork, on-device)A claim with no quantified bound is marketing.Governance substitutes for a guarantee.
Consequentialist / marketUsers trade data for value at rates a holdout can measure.Stated preferences measure willingness to pay.

Buddharaju's eight fields are indefensible under all five while no purpose is named for them — which is why Bandlamudi's reply is to name one for her five, and why the hard cases begin at field nine.

3. Mechanics: the register, the copy census, and three pieces of arithmetic

Expert practice is mostly bookkeeping done before code exists. The first artefact is a purpose register: one row per field carrying its purpose, the lawful basis, a named owner who is a person rather than a team, and a retention clock written as an event plus a duration rather than a date. Two steps are left implicit and are where the discipline lives: the deletion job ships in the same pull request as the collection code, and the register is generated from the schema by a build step that fails on an untagged column.

The second artefact is the copy census, the one most teams skip. Fields do not live in one place.

Three pieces of arithmetic convert the register into decisions. The first is a steady-state identity borrowed from queueing: stored volume equals arrival rate times retention. Iravatham's 4,200 vehicles each produce six harsh-braking clips a day, so a 180-day window holds 25,200 × 180 = 45,36,000 clips and a 30-day window holds 7,56,000. Nothing about the product changes; the exposed population falls six-fold.

The second is an expected-loss sketch. Ilavenil's cyber-insurance broker priced its annual probability of a reportable breach at 0.04, and remediation, notification and churn at ₹185 per record with sensitive health detail present and ₹140 without. Over 11,40,000 records that is 0.04 × 11,40,000 × 185 = ₹84.36 lakh a year, falling to 0.04 × 11,40,000 × 140 = ₹63.84 lakh if the three sensitive fields go: a ₹20.52 lakh difference. The second-order point matters more. Minimisation moved the cost per record, not the probability, which access control and patching set. Sold internally as breach prevention, it has been mis-sold.

The third is re-identification arithmetic, where intuition fails hardest. Ilavenil's actuarial extract strips names and phone numbers and keeps PIN code (1,420 distinct values), birth year (48) and gender (2). It covers all 11,40,000 registered users, every one of whom has filed at least once, because registration happens at the first claim. Under a Poisson occupancy approximation — the crudest of the uniqueness models the re-identification literature works with, and cruder than the copula method of Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye in Nature Communications in 2019 — a record is unique in its cell with probability e−λ, λ being the population divided by the cell count. One date field destroys a dataset that was comfortable.

Quasi-identifiers in the extractDistinct cellsλ = 11,40,000 ÷ cellsP(unique) = e−λExpected unique records
PIN code, birth year, gender1,36,3208.3630.02%266
… plus year of first claim (3)4,08,9602.7886.16%70,191
… plus month of first claim (36)49,07,5200.232379.27%9,03,691
… plus exact date of first claim (1,096)14,94,06,7200.0076399.24%11,31,335

Cells = 1,420 × 48 × 2 = 1,36,320, times the date granularity in each row; 1,096 is the extract's three-year claim window, which is also its retention period. Expected unique records = 11,40,000 × P(unique). This is a model: it assumes records fall independently and with equal probability across cells — which the real skew in PIN codes, birth years and claim dates violates — and that an adversary holds every quasi-identifier named.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are better stated as testable claims than as agreeable principles. Claim one: the field's value is realised inside the retention window you would otherwise choose. True for Bandlamudi's propensity features, which move a renewal within twelve months. False for Iravatham's collision footage, whose value arrives in a dispute two to three years out — which makes Bellamkonda's 365-day request a real purpose rather than greed, and also the wrong number for it: the clock he asked for is shorter than the dispute he named.

Claim two: the data subject is also the buyer. True at Ilavenil, where the person whose health detail is collected is the person installing the app, so minimisation can be sold as benefit. False at Iravatham, where the driver is the subject and the fleet owner the buyer, so minimisation has no purchaser and only regulation and the risk committee carry it.

Claim three: no other obligation compels retention. Fails at Ilavenil: Section 8(7) of the DPDP Act requires erasure when the purpose is served but carves out retention required by other law, and insurance record-keeping holds settled-claim documents for years, so a ninety-day deletion promise cannot lawfully be kept. Passes at Iravatham, where nothing compels keeping footage and Bellamkonda's 365 days is a commercial preference, not an obligation — which is why it is negotiable and the claim documents are not.

Claim four: the collection decision is cheaply reversible. True in software, where a field dies in a sprint. False in hardware: once the IRV-3 ships on 6 July with a sensor and no on-device inference, every unit collects what that board collects for five years.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where minimisation degrades a safety function — fatigue detection needs the camera — “collect less” argues for a worse product; the honest move is to relocate the computation, not remove the input. Where an inappropriate flow is the problem, volume is the wrong dial: one risk score sent to an underwriter breaches context more gravely than a hundred fields sent to a clinician. And where “we don't store it” conceals “four processors do”, the language is a shield.

5. Hard edge cases, and what the seams actually look like

In a multi-product company the unit of purpose is the company, not the app. A shared identity graph makes a field collected for claims available to a lending team two floors away, so purpose limitation rests on a boundary nobody owns.

In two-sided products the subject and the payer come apart, as at Iravatham.

In regulated products there is a collection floor: a bank cannot minimise its way out of identity verification. The expert move is to minimise the copies — verify through an offline Aadhaar XML or a DigiLocker document, then store the result and reference, never the artefact.

In hardware-plus-software the board is the policy. A microphone on the bill of materials is a microphone for five years, and the consent interface is often one LED. Botcha's real choice on day 46 is whether the SoC can run inference, not what the retention setting says.

AI-native products break two assumptions. Training is a purpose that consumes everything, and deleting a row does not remove its influence from a set of weights: model-level deletion is unsolved, so mature teams curate corpora at ingestion.

At the seams, what mature companies do differs from what they say. They say they run a quarterly data-inventory review. What holds is a registry check in continuous integration that fails the build on an untagged column, a reconciliation of warehouse tables against the register, and a dated exceptions list.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: minimisation is a property of the schema, not of the form. The tell is a signup form with six fields and an analytics payload with forty. A short form reads as a lean product; it is not, because the SDK rather than the form decides what is collected.

Two: retention is set by the longest-lived copy. The tell is a ninety-day policy beside a warehouse table with a 400-day partition. The policy reads as governing. It does not: a policy is a sentence, a partition is a configuration, and a regulator sees the configuration.

Three: purpose limitation binds an organisation you will not be running. The tell is a purpose statement containing “including”, which converts a limit into an enumeration. A broad purpose looks like optionality; it destroys the register, because a purpose permitting everything refuses nothing.

Four: consent is the weakest basis for a core function. The tell is a main screen that breaks when three per cent of users decline a permission. Consent is the most respectful basis and the most revocable; a function resting on it acquires a dark pattern within two quarters.

Five: “anonymised” is a claim about a join, not a file. The tell is a dataset called anonymous that carries a stable per-row identifier. Removing names reads as anonymising; Section 3 refutes it, moving the same file from 266 unique records to 11,31,335 on one added date column.

Six: privacy UX is measured by what users change, not what they read. The tell is a settings page with excellent comprehension scores and 99 per cent of accounts still on the default. A clear explanation does not discharge the duty: the default is the decision, and the explanation only decides who feels informed.

Seven: deletion has a fan-out and a latency, and the latency is the honest number. The tell is an erasure commitment quoted without mention of backups. Ilavenil's floor is thirty-five days, the rolling backup window, because nothing is deleted until the last restorable copy ages out.

Eight: the cheapest win is a default, not a feature. The tell is a roadmap carrying a three-sprint privacy epic and not one changed default. Privacy is assumed to need investment; often the best change is one switch — precise location to coarse — which earns no credit.

7. How this changes across product types and company stages

In consumer products the binding constraint is attention: what matters is the default, because the consent screen is read by almost nobody. In B2B and enterprise the constraint is contract — minimisation is negotiated in a processing addendum and buyers audit sub-processor lists, so a privacy claim becomes a procurement asset, the clearest setting in which it has a purchaser. In platforms and marketplaces the hard problem is a third party's collection, so the lever is API scope and app review. In hardware it is the bill of materials; in AI products, the ingestion boundary and the prompt log.

Two claimed differences are not real. Enterprise products are not inherently more privacy-respecting: they hold more sensitive data under weaker UX scrutiny, and their subjects are employees who cannot decline. And B2B does not escape privacy law by selling to a company.

By stage the change is one of cost, not kind. Pre-product-market-fit the register costs an afternoon, and the answer is to collect less than seems prudent because there is no model to feed. At Series B, retrofitting purpose tags across a live schema with three processors attached costs weeks of migration. At scale the impact assessment, the data-protection officer and the audit become mandatory under Section 10. That curve is the most practical argument for doing this early.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Ilavenil's holdout. Bandlamudi claimed the five convenience fields lifted first-claim-to-renewal from 61.0 to 64.2 per cent. Buddharaju already had a test: a holdout opened on Monday 1 December 2025, reading renewal as the monthly cover renewal falling due after a first claim — a thirty-day event, not an annual anniversary — so the answer was in hand by late February. Across 46,000 new signups over the six weeks to Sunday 11 January 2026, 4,600 were enrolled without the five fields and 41,400 with them; renewal came in at 63.1 per cent against 64.2, a gap of 1.1 points. Pooled at (41,400 × 0.642 + 4,600 × 0.631) ÷ 46,000 = 0.6409, the standard error of the difference is √(0.6409 × 0.3591 × (1/41,400 + 1/4,600)) = 0.746 points, so 1.1 ± 1.96 × 0.746 runs from −0.36 to +2.56 points. The fields may be worth something — the interval reaches +2.56 — but the 3.2-point claim was never the experiment's effect.

Iravatham's on-device move. Bollineni's design cuts cloud retention from 180 days to 30: 37,80,000 fewer clips at 12 MB each, or 45.36 TB, at ₹1,900 per TB-month — ₹86,184 a month, ₹10.34 lakh a year. The inference-capable SoC adds ₹1,850 to a ₹14,200 bill of materials, 13.0 per cent, which is ₹77.7 lakh across 4,200 units, so payback on storage alone is 7.5 years at best — at best because 4,200 is the installed fleet, not a year's build, so the ₹77.7 lakh assumes every vehicle carries the new box from day one and the ₹10.34 lakh assumes the fleet is already at 30-day steady state. On a rollout from 6 July it is longer, and longer than the board's five-year life. Uplink runs on the customer's SIM, so Iravatham banks none of that either. The cost case does not close; it rests on tail risk and contract terms.

Inban Daily's over-correction. The Bengaluru grocery app, run by Roopesh Boyapati, deleted all order history at 90 days from Tuesday 1 July 2025. Refund abuse rose from 0.42 to 1.18 per cent of 2,30,000 monthly orders at ₹640 an abused order. The terminal run-rate is 1,748 extra orders a month, or ₹11.19 lakh — but the rate climbed through the window, so pricing seven months at the terminal gap overstates it. Taken as linear from July, which is when the gap opens because the policy deleted pre-existing history on day one, the mean excess is 0.38 points, 874 orders and ₹5.59 lakh a month: an estimated ₹39.16 lakh to January 2026, caught on Tuesday 3 February 2026. With no control cohort it is an association, not a demonstrated cost. The recovery kept a salted hash of device, payment token and delivery geohash for 24 months while still deleting name, address and phone at 90 days; abuse settled at 0.55 per cent, a residual 299 orders and ₹1.91 lakh a month.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Register drift. Early sign: the register's last-updated date precedes the last schema migration. Diagnostic: which column was added most recently, and is it in the register? Caught late, the assessment is rebuilt against a regulator's clock.

Deletion that does not fan out. Early sign: erasure tickets closed in minutes. Diagnostic: name every store the field reaches, and who ran the job in each. Caught late, the company has misstated its position to the Data Protection Board.

Minimisation sold as a cost saving. Early sign: a business case whose only benefit line is storage. Diagnostic: if storage were free, would we still do this? Caught late, the programme dies at the first budget review.

Over-minimisation. Early sign: fraud, dispute or support metrics drifting two quarters after a deletion policy ships. Diagnostic: which investigation can we no longer run? Inban's answer cost an estimated ₹39.16 lakh before anyone asked it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Guarantees against governance. The formal camp holds that only a bound counts, noting how often a dataset released as anonymous and later broken was governed by a policy. The governance camp answers that differential privacy's noise destroys utility exactly where products need it: small geographies and rare cohorts. The first fails if an honestly maintained register prevents the breaches that matter; the second fails if a bounded release keeps the utility a product consumes.

Consent as instrument. One side holds consent to be the only legitimating act, and the DPDP Act makes it the default basis, with narrow legitimate-use exceptions under Section 7. The other holds that notice-and-choice shifts an unpayable cognitive debt onto users, citing banner studies in which almost nobody reads and almost everybody accepts. It is weakest in B2B, where consent is negotiated between parties with counsel, and would be wrong if comprehension and switching rose with better notice design.

Whether it pays. The optimistic view reads the platform privacy changes of the early 2020s as evidence that restraint is a competitive asset. The sceptical view notes who gained: holders of first-party data at scale. On that reading, minimisation duties raise fixed compliance cost and entrench incumbents — an argument for the principle, against its enforcement. It would be wrong if small entrants cleared these duties proportionately cheaper.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this writes a policy and asks for a review. Someone who has internalised it changes the artefacts. They ask what the default does before asking what the screen says, and for the copy census rather than the policy. They write purposes narrowly on purpose, because a purpose is a refusal device. And they say early that the case rests on tail risk, not storage cost, because that is the claim that survives a budget review.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Buddharaju dropped all eight purposeless fields before the 29 May assessment and kept the five conveniences out on an interval straddling zero — a judgement about what the test could show, not a finding that the fields are worthless. She rewrote the actuarial extract to carry month rather than exact date of first claim, accepting 79.27 per cent uniqueness over 99.24 because the actuaries could defend seasonality and nobody could defend the day. Botcha spent the ₹1,850 on the SoC, shipped 30-day cloud retention, and offered Bellamkonda a contractual option to hold flagged collision clips for 365 days — an option priced after the 180-to-30-day saving, and one that hands part of it back.

Three questions. First: Iravatham's buyers pay for the camera and its drivers do not, so whose willingness to pay should set the retention window, and what would you measure? Second: the jump from 0.02 to 99.24 per cent assumed an adversary already holding all four quasi-identifiers — which is cheapest to acquire in India, and what does that imply for the three she kept beyond the date? Third: Inban kept a 24-month hashed fingerprint while deleting names at 90 days; is that minimisation or relabelled retention, and what test would settle it?

13. Going deeper

Data, consent and the DPDP Act turns these levers into statutory duties and unlocks consent-manager design; GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes explains why one register must satisfy several regulators. Data privacy in LLM products is where purpose limitation and erasure break, and privacy-preserving architecture supplies the techniques behind Bollineni's design. Personalisation vs surveillance gives contextual integrity its product form; consent flows and cookie UX is where defaults are won. Security compliance: SOC 2, ISO 27001 addresses the probability term minimisation never touched, terms of service, SLAs and contracts is how Botcha's option gets written, and IP, patents and trademarks for PMs with open-source licences cover the remaining law a PM reads without a lawyer.
