Lekhapath: What the Inbox Should Tell Us

A teaching case on privacy by design

1. Opening

At 8:30 on the evening of Thursday 15 October 2026, Vaishnavi Enayet, chief product officer of Lekhapath, opened a video call from her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru. In Berlin it was 5:00 pm; in Toronto, 11:00 am. By Friday 23 October she had to tell engineering which way the company's new Spend Insights feature would read its users' money. Marketing wanted it live on Monday 2 November, six days before Diwali on Sunday 8 November.

2. Company background

Lekhapath, founded in Bengaluru in 2021, is a personal-finance app for salaried Indians in their twenties and thirties. In September 2026 it had 42 lakh monthly active users, about 78 per cent of them on Android. Users track bills, credit-card due dates and credit scores; the company earns referral fees when they take a card or a loan through the app, an average of ₹150 per monthly active user over FY26 (April 2025 to March 2026).

The company began as a bill-reminder tool built by three friends who had worked at Infosys and Flipkart, and added credit-score tracking in 2023, when a first wave of UPI-native users arrived. Its 310 employees sit mainly in Bengaluru and Pune, with product and data specialists spread across Berlin and Toronto, and a small sales team in New Jersey that sells anonymised category insights to banks. Competitors range from CRED and Walnut to the money tabs inside PhonePe, Paytm and Groww. Many of them categorise spending automatically. Users now expect it, and the habit is spreading beyond metros to Lucknow, Indore and Coimbatore, and Lekhapath's own survey of 1,800 users found automatic categorisation to be the most requested missing feature.

3. The situation

Spend Insights would sort a user's spending into rent, food, travel and similar heads. A September prototype did this by reading the Android SMS inbox, where banks and UPI apps send a message for every debit. The prototype worked well, and the data science team wanted to keep it. It also sat uneasily with a promise made on the sign-up page, that Lekhapath "only looks at what you add".

Vaishnavi was uneasy. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, requires consent that is specific to a purpose, and its rules, notified in November 2025, phase in their duties over eighteen months. She asked a team of twelve volunteer employees to hand over their 200 most recent messages each, between 5 and 9 October, and had them classified (Exhibit 1).

Vaishnavi also had two consent tests from 14 to 27 September, each on a separate random 20,000 Android users, showing a consent screen only. A screen asking for the full inbox was accepted by 12,400; a screen describing on-device reading of bank messages alone was accepted by 11,600. A pilot of the RBI-regulated Account Aggregator route, with 5,000 users invited in September, ended with 900 completing consent.

Viewed from Berlin, the designer Vikas Eshanullah saw the consent screen as the product's real interface. In Toronto, Vidya Ehtesham, the data scientist, saw a model that improved with every message. In Pune, Vivek Ekram saw a festival window. In New Jersey, the sales team wanted to know how any new data would be described to the banks that buy its anonymised category insights, and a client in Dubai had asked the same question about where the data was stored.

4. The people

Vaishnavi Enayet, chief product officer, Bengaluru. Joined in 2023; accountable to the board for the launch and for any complaint to the Data Protection Board of India.

Vivek Ekram, head of growth, Pune. Wants the feature live for the Diwali spending peak, when Indian households spend most on gifts, gold and appliances, when installs and referrals are highest, and has promised the board an activation figure for the third quarter of FY27, which the choice of option will move. He is not indifferent to privacy; he points out that users who feel watched uninstall.

Vidya Ehtesham, senior data scientist, Toronto. Wants the richest data to train categorisation and, later, a credit-health score. She has argued that she cannot know today which messages will matter.

Vikas Eshanullah, lead designer, Berlin. Wants a consent screen a user can understand in one reading, and has said he will not design one that hides what is taken.

5. The numbers behind the options

Exhibit 2 puts the three routes on one base: a launch cohort of 10,00,000 invited users, of whom 7,80,000 (78 per cent) are on Android. Account Aggregator works on both platforms; SMS reading works only on Android.

Exhibit 3 places those launch dates against the decision deadline and Diwali.

6. The options

Option A: ingest the full inbox. Ship the prototype on 2 November. The app requests SMS access and uploads every message to Lekhapath's cloud, where the models separate transactions from the rest. It reaches Android users only, retains messages for as long as the account stays open unless a rule is added, and leaves the model team free to use any message later. It costs ₹12 lakh to launch, and it needs a retention rule and a fresh consent for any new purpose.

Option B: use Account Aggregator. Integrate as a financial-information user on the RBI-regulated framework. A user approves a consent artefact naming the accounts, the data, the purpose and the duration, and Lekhapath receives only that. It works on iPhones and Androids, costs ₹95 lakh, and launches on 18 January 2027, after Diwali and the festival-season peak.

Option C: read on the device. A model on the phone reads only messages from registered bank and UPI sender IDs, categorises them locally, and sends up monthly category totals. Raw messages never leave the handset. It costs ₹65 lakh, launches on 7 December, and offers nothing to iPhone users and gives the model team no message text to learn from.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, which parts of an inbox does Spend Insights need, and which of the rest could harm a user if exposed or misused?
  2. What do the consent rates and activated users in Exhibit 2 measure, and what do they leave out?
  3. For each option, what must Lekhapath be able to say to a user, and to the Data Protection Board, about purpose, quantity held and duration?
  4. If you were Vaishnavi, which option would you take to the Friday meeting, and how would you answer Vivek and Vidya?

8. A note for the learner

Privacy by design asks three things before launch: collect only what the stated purpose needs, keep it only as long as that purpose lasts, and explain both in words the user can follow. Each is easier to build in at the start than to retrofit, because the data model, the consent screen and the retention clock all harden once users arrive. Weigh the options on what each takes, keeps and tells, as well as on revenue, and keep your comparisons on a common base, as Exhibit 2 does.

One defensible path is Option C. It holds the purpose to the 612 transaction messages in Exhibit 1 and holds only totals on Lekhapath's servers, which leaves little to retain, breach or repurpose. The price is real: against Option A it activates 31,200 fewer users (4,83,600 less 4,52,400) and earns ₹46.8 lakh less a year (31,200 × ₹150), costs ₹53 lakh more to build, and arrives five weeks after 2 November. Vaishnavi could set against that a launch message about what stays on the phone, and a request to Vidya to design the credit-health work around Account Aggregator consent, which iPhone users could also use once B is built. Vivek's Diwali commitment would have to be reset with the board. Another reader might weigh the festival window more heavily; the test of an answer is whether it names what the feature needs, what it keeps and what it costs.
exp20v2-legal.privacy.principles:
Privacy by Design

How a product collects less, keeps less and explains more, by construction rather than by apology.

1. Sixteen fields and fifty-six days

On Monday 9 February 2026, Parvathi Anbazhagan, head of product at Hamsadhwani Care, opened a spreadsheet that her engineering lead, Prithviraj Appasamy, had assembled over a weekend. Hamsadhwani, a Chennai company, books physiotherapists to treat patients at home. The spreadsheet listed every field its sign-up flow collected: sixteen. The company held 6,40,000 registered users, and the app was due to launch in Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Pune on Monday 6 April, 56 days away.

Her growth lead, Pichumani Adusumilli, wanted the form left alone, because each field fed a targeting model he credited with repeat bookings. The company's counsel, Padmavathi Annadurai, could not name a purpose for four of the sixteen. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (the DPDP Act) was phasing in under rules notified in November 2025, and she expected a regulator to ask exactly that question.

A redesign would cost three two-week sprints, 42 days of engineering, leaving 14 days before launch. Skipping it meant carrying 6.4 lakh people's records into three new cities unchanged. Parvathi had to decide which risk to buy.

2. The idea

Privacy by design is the practice of building privacy protection into a product's structure, defaults and workflows from the first specification, instead of adding it after launch through policy text or a consent banner. Its problem is a familiar one: once a company has collected a field, every later team finds a use for it, and the cost of that accumulation (breach exposure, legal duties, user distrust) is borne long after the convenience was enjoyed.

Ann Cavoukian, then Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, framed the idea in the 1990s with Dutch regulators working on privacy-enhancing technologies, and published seven foundational principles around 2009. They include being proactive rather than reactive, making privacy the default setting, and keeping the system transparent. Europe made a version binding: Article 25 of the General Data Protection Regulation, in force from May 2018, requires "data protection by design and by default".

Three working levers follow. Data minimisation means collecting only what a stated purpose needs. Purpose limitation means using data only for the purpose given when it was collected. Retention limits mean deleting data when that purpose ends. The idea is also cheaper early than late: a field never collected needs no consent screen, no deletion job and no breach notice. Parvathi's sentence for the meeting: "Every field we hold must name its purpose and its expiry date, and if it cannot, we do not ask for it."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in five steps. First, inventory every personal data field, meaning any information that identifies or can be tied to a living person. Prithviraj's spreadsheet was this step. Second, attach a purpose to each field, written as a sentence a user would accept: "your address lets the therapist find you". Third, test necessity: could the purpose be met without the field, with a coarser version of it, or later?

Fourth, choose a moment of collection. This is the step practitioners leave implicit. A field needed only for one feature should be asked at the point that feature is used, with its reason beside it, and not at sign-up where it is a toll on everyone. Fifth, set retention: a date or event after which the field is deleted or anonymised, enforced by a scheduled job rather than a policy document.

Two further steps are routinely skipped. Defaults must favour the user: optional fields start empty, sharing starts off. And deletion must be real, reaching backups, analytics copies and vendors, or the retention rule describes a wish. For Hamsadhwani, the practical test was whether a data field could be named in three places: the form, the purpose register and the deletion job.

4. A worked example, line by line

Parvathi's team ran the five steps on all sixteen fields. The table records the verdicts.

FieldVerdict
Name, mobile, home addressKeep at sign-up (3)
Device identifierKeep, pseudonymous, for fraud checks (1)
Age band, medical history, live location, insurance number, emergency contactDefer to the point of need (5)
Email, gender, photoOptional, empty by default (3)
Aadhaar number, phone contacts, employer, income bandDrop (4)
Total fields16

Read the table as a negotiation record. Only the drop group was uncontroversial; Pichumani contested the optional group, and the compromise was that email, gender and photo stay but start empty and carry their own reason beside the field. Mandatory fields at sign-up fall from 16 to 4, a cut of 75 per cent. Now the stock already held. Of 6,40,000 users, 4,48,000 (70 per cent) had given an Aadhaar number, 3,20,000 (50 per cent) a medical history and 2,56,000 (40 per cent) their contacts: 10,24,000 high-risk records. Finance's planning figure for one exposed record of this kind is ₹1,500; this is an assumption, not a measurement.

High-risk records heldTodayPass 1: drops + 24-month rulePass 2: 36-month rule
Aadhaar numbers4,48,00000
Medical histories3,20,0001,40,0001,68,000
Phone contact lists2,56,00000
Total records10,24,0001,40,0001,68,000
Exposure at ₹1,500 (₹ crore)153.621.025.2

Pass 1 keeps a medical history only for users with a completed visit in the last 24 months (1,40,000 of the 1,92,000 who have ever had one). Exposure is records times ₹1,500; 10,24,000 × 1,500 = ₹153.6 crore.

Pass 1 cuts exposure from ₹153.6 crore to ₹21.0 crore, a fall of ₹132.6 crore or 86.3 per cent. Most of that comes from the drops: Aadhaar and contacts account for 7,04,000 of the 8,84,000 records removed (79.6 per cent), and the 24-month rule only the medical difference. Pass 2 changes one input, the retention window, from 24 to 36 months, which keeps 1,68,000 histories. Exposure rises to ₹25.2 crore, ₹4.2 crore (20 per cent) more. The extra 28,000 users in the 24 to 36 month band return at about 5 per cent a year, 1,400 people, each saved an 11-minute intake: about 257 hours in total. That is ₹30,000 of added if-breached exposure per returner (₹4.2 crore ÷ 1,400) set against eleven minutes saved, which tipped the argument towards 24 months.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Minimisation is not secrecy

Encrypting a field protects it; minimising removes it. A breach of encrypted data you did not need is still a breach of data you did not need, and an obligation to explain why you held it.

Consent does not cure over-collection

Many teams believe a ticked box licenses any field. Under the DPDP Act, consent must be tied to a specified purpose and limited to data necessary for it, so the box covers only what the purpose requires.

Anonymised is not pseudonymised

A pseudonym, such as a device hash, can be linked back to a person by someone holding the key or a second dataset. Genuinely anonymised data cannot. Treat pseudonymous data as personal until you can show re-linking is impractical.

Retention has a floor as well as a ceiling

Sectoral rules, tax law and clinical record norms may require keeping something for years. Deletion schedules are set with counsel, and where a statute demands longer, the statute wins. The principle forbids holding data for no reason, not holding it for a legal one.

Purpose limitation constrains reuse

A booking address collected to dispatch a therapist cannot quietly feed a marketing model. A new purpose needs a new justification, and often a new notice.

Privacy by design cannot tell you the right trade-off

It forces the question and the evidence. It does not say how much growth a field is worth. Pichumani's targeting lift was real and measurable, and the framework has no verdict on it; leadership does. A thoughtful newcomer should ask: who bears the cost if this fails, and can they see the choice being made?

Defaults are decisions

Most users never change a setting. A pre-ticked marketing box therefore collects a choice nobody made, and regulators increasingly treat it that way. Whoever sets the default is the real decision-maker.

Explaining more can be done badly

A notice is also a design surface. Forty lines of legal text, or a button that makes refusal harder than acceptance, is privacy theatre. Test explanations the way you test checkout: ask five users what they believe you hold and why, and compare it to the register.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

The principle is constant; the first move differs with who the data belongs to and who decides its use.

Product typeWhose dataFirst design move
ConsumerThe user's ownShrink sign-up; explain at point of ask
B2BCustomer's end usersAct as a processor; honour the customer's purposes
MarketplaceTwo sides, each with the other's dataReveal the minimum across the match

In B2B, the buyer decides the purposes, so the vendor's design work is limiting its own reuse. In a marketplace like Hamsadhwani, where therapists see patients' addresses, the question is how late a counterparty receives data: the exact address after a confirmed booking, a pin code before.

Scale changes the mechanism, not the duty. Early on, the risk is that nobody has written the purposes down at all; later, it is that fifty teams have each added one field. A seed-stage team can fix this with a spreadsheet and a weekend; a large company needs a data-owner for every field, review gates in the launch process, and automated retention jobs, because no single person remembers what was collected.

7. Common mistakes

The policy-page fix

Symptom: a long privacy policy beside a form that is unchanged. Misunderstanding: that disclosure equals design. Diagnostic: ask engineering to delete one user's data and time it; if the answer is "we would need a ticket per system", nothing was designed.

Minimising the form but not the pipeline

Symptom: a short sign-up, but analytics events still carry full addresses. Misunderstanding: that the form is the only entry. Diagnostic: sample one day of event logs and count personal fields nobody can justify.

Retention as a number nobody runs

Symptom: a stated two-year period and a database with seven-year-old rows. Misunderstanding: that a policy deletes data. Diagnostic: query the oldest record per field and compare it to the stated limit.

Copies nobody counted

Symptom: a user deletes their account and later receives a reminder. Misunderstanding: that the production database is the only copy. Diagnostic: trace one test user through exports, the email vendor, the data warehouse and backups, and list every place that still holds them.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled Hamsadhwani asks three things at sign-up, records one pseudonymous device identifier, and tells the user why each is needed. Medical history appears on the day of the first assessment, beside a sentence saying it is shared only with the treating therapist. A purpose register lists every field with an owner and an expiry date, and a nightly job enforces it. Growth keeps a targeting model, but on fields that passed the test, and any proposal for a new field arrives with a purpose, an owner and a deletion date. The launch review checks the register, not a promise. When Padmavathi asks of any field why it exists, the answer takes one sentence, and when a user asks the same question the app answers it in two taps.

9. Closing

Parvathi chose the redesign, with the 24-month rule and a cut-line: if the three sprints slipped past 23 March, the cities would launch with the new four-field form and the deferred collection screens would follow. Her reasoning had three parts. The form change cut 75 per cent of mandatory fields. The drops and the 24-month rule together removed 8,84,000 of the 10,24,000 high-risk records, leaving 1,40,000, a cut of 86.3 per cent. And the 14 days after 23 March were reserved for launch testing, so a sprint overrun would trigger the cut-line instead of eating the slack. Pichumani kept his model on the retained fields and was asked to prove the lift on them.

Next, read the DPDP Act and its consent mechanics, then the GDPR and CCPA comparison, then privacy in LLM products, where "delete" is hardest. Each applies this page's logic to a harder surface.

Two questions to sit with. Which field in a product you know would fail the purpose test, and who would object to dropping it? If a user asked what you hold about them and why, how long would a truthful answer take?
case40v1-legal.gdpr:
Indian School of Business · Case 40 · Ethics, Trust & Compliance

Indriya Systems: What Ijssel Asked For

Pune, Sunday 15 November 2026: a privacy addendum, four options, nineteen weeks.

1. The night before

At twenty to midnight on Sunday 15 November 2026, Rupam Borthakur sat on the floor of her flat in Baner with four options on a single sheet of A4 and the Diwali lights still up on the balcony opposite. She had printed it on Friday and not changed a word since. At 9.30 next morning the leadership team would meet in Pune to pick one; at 7 pm, 8.30 am for the board's lead investor in New Jersey, she had twelve minutes on the agenda.

Rupam had been Chief Product Officer at Indriya Systems Private Limited for five and a half years. In that time Indriya Vista had gone from a session-analytics library inside eleven Indian shopping apps to a customer-experience platform inside 271 of them across five regions. She had signed off on most of the design decisions that now constrained her. The sheet was headed, in her own hand, EU.

What had arrived on Friday 9 October was eleven pages of addendum from the procurement office of Ijssel Retail Groep in Utrecht, Indriya's largest customer, worth ₹9.80 crore of annual recurring revenue against group ARR of ₹88.00 crore. It had to be signed by Monday 30 November, failing which the renewal due on 31 January 2027 would not be processed. Nothing in it was unusual. That was the difficulty.

2. How Indriya got here

Indriya was founded in Pune in March 2019 by Riya Bagchi and Rituraj Bezbaruah, who had met building fraud models at a payments firm. By June 2021 Vista v1 replayed what a shopper did in an app by capturing the full document object model of each recorded session: the screen as the user saw it, including whatever was on it.

The decision that shaped everything after it came in the spring of 2022, when Ijssel, then a prospect, would sign only if European data stayed in Europe. Indriya was nineteen people. Romit Bhattacharjee, newly hired to run engineering from Bengaluru, proposed thin residency: a read-only replica in Frankfurt for Ijssel's dashboards and aggregates, with the write path, the replay blob store and the support tooling all remaining on the Mumbai primary. Blobs were keyed by hashed device identifier, and the table mapping a hash back to a person kept thirty days. Retention was defaulted to four hundred days, because a large Indian client wanted year-on-year festive comparisons. Ijssel signed on Monday 14 March 2022 and went live on 1 July 2022; standard contractual clauses followed in January 2023.

Each choice was defensible then and each is load-bearing now: thin residency is why Pune and Bengaluru read European sessions, the device-hash key is why deleting one person's replays after thirty days is a search rather than a lookup, and the four-hundred-day default is why there is so much to search.

3. The industry

Indriya sells into the market Freshworks, Zoho and Postman have taught Indian investors to recognise: engineering in India, revenue in hard currency, a product bought on a credit card and later audited by procurement. The Indian book is the quick-commerce and lending apps UPI and ONDC made possible; Indian clients pay least, Europeans pay most and send questionnaires.

The regulatory weather has changed twice in three years. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the rules under it brought consent managers, notice obligations and breach reporting into a market that had treated privacy as a contract clause. In Europe the General Data Protection Regulation has been in force since 2018, but what bites a vendor like Indriya is the transfer chapter: India has no adequacy decision, so every flow rests on standard contractual clauses plus an assessment of the far end, and remote access from Pune counts as a flow. In California the Consumer Privacy Act as amended by the Privacy Rights Act gives consumers deletion and opt-out rights that clients pass down to vendors in writing. Exhibit 1 shows what each jurisdiction is worth.

4. The situation in detail: what was recorded, and when

Exhibit 2 lists the record in order. It reads as a set of pairs: some statements Indriya made came before the documents that bear on them, some after.

Four pairs matter. First, lawful basis. Indriya's position since 2022 is that it is a processor: the client consents and sets the purpose, Indriya holds the data on instruction. On Wednesday 22 April 2026 Rahul Banerjee returned the auditor's processor questionnaire with the answer that Vista performed no cross-client processing. The release note for SDK v4.2, dated Wednesday 11 February 2026, says v4.2 enables “benchmark intelligence” by default: an intent model trained on support transcripts and replay event streams pooled across clients. The impact assessment delivered on Friday 18 September 2026 by Riddhi Bandyopadhyay, with counsel in Amsterdam, records that for training that model Indriya chooses both purpose and means, and that 62 of the 148 activities in the inventory — 41.9 per cent — carry no documented lawful basis.

Second, transfers: Frankfurt holds dashboard aggregates only, replay blobs live on the Mumbai primary, and the 14 October 2026 extract shows 41 support sessions touching EU replay data in the thirty days to 13 October, opened by seven people in Pune and Bengaluru. Third, requests, counted two ways in Exhibit 3. Fourth, erasure: the 11 September benchmark put a full pass over the store at ₹6.40 lakh and 31 hours, and the reverse-lookup table that would make a pass unnecessary holds thirty days.

Exhibit 4 shows where the data sits.

5. The people

Rupam Borthakur, 36, Chief Product Officer, Pune, since April 2021; paid on net revenue retention. Holds that the addendum describes what Indriya told Ijssel it already did. Has not told the team that she approved the v4.2 default herself, in a two-line Slack reply in January 2026, without reading the design doc.

Riya Bagchi, 41, co-founder and chief executive, Pune; paid on enterprise value. Wants the addendum signed, and calls privacy work “a cost of selling to Europe, not a product”. Has not told anyone outside the board that a US buyer opened talks on 28 October 2026, with a diligence list of 6 November asking for the DPIA.

Romit Bhattacharjee, 39, VP Engineering, Bengaluru, since January 2022; author of thin residency, measured on uptime and release predictability. Argues the problem is access control, not geography. Has not said that two of his four SDK engineers resigned on 6 November, last day 11 December.

Rituraj Bezbaruah, 44, co-founder and head of data science, Toronto since 2023; largest employee shareholder. Holds that the intent model stores parameters, not people, and is the only moat. Has not said that its nine-point lift in the March 2026 board deck came from one client's November 2025 test and was never reproduced.

Riddhi Bandyopadhyay, 33, senior counsel and data protection officer, Pune, part-time since November 2024; personally the named DPO. Wants the inventory fixed before anything is signed. Has not told Rupam that her 10 September DPIA draft recommended suspending cross-client training, and that the sentence left the final after a call with Riya.

Rahul Banerjee, 37, director of customer success, Singapore; three-quarters of his variable pay is gross renewal rate. Answered the April questionnaire from the platform documentation, which did not mention the SDK default, and told Utrecht the addendum is signable — a call he has not said preceded Rupam's sight of it.

Ranjan Bhaduri, 48, senior vice-president of sales, Jersey City; carries a 2027 US number built on replay as sold today. Argues California is contractual and that Indriya sells nothing. Has not said what the attestation he promised Ironvale Outdoor Co., ₹2.10 crore of the US row, will say about sale or sharing.

Rohinton Baishya, 34, principal designer, Berlin since September 2021, the only colleague in the EEA; reviewed on feature adoption. Argues masking is a product change to be designed, not defaulted. Ran an unapproved masked build with a client's QA team in October: three of eleven playback flows broke, which is nowhere in writing.

6. What the store holds

Exhibit 5 sets out one month of capture and the stock behind it. Sampling is uneven because it was sold, not engineered.

7. Voices

“Ninety free person-weeks is ninety free person-weeks. Pick one of the four and I will staff it on Monday.”

Romit Bhattacharjee, #eng-leads, 10 November 2026

“The model keeps weights, not sessions. Weights are not personal data, and I will tell the auditor so myself.”

Rituraj Bezbaruah, email from Toronto, 4.10 pm on 10 November, received in Pune at 2.40 am on the 11th

“I will not sign an attestation saying access is confined to the EEA while the support console says otherwise. I will sign one that describes what we actually do.”

Riddhi Bandyopadhyay, note to Rupam, 12 November 2026

“Nobody in California is buying ‘we are only a processor’. Ironvale's counsel wants a signature on the twentieth, and I have said yes.”

Ranjan Bhaduri, email, 13 November 2026

“We masked everything in a client's QA build last month. Three of eleven playback flows stopped working. The thing clients bought is the thing we would switch off.”

Rohinton Baishya, design review, 9.30 am Berlin, 2 pm Pune, 12 November 2026

8. The options as Rupam has written them

All four are costed over the twelve months to 31 October 2027 at October 2026 volumes — 21.0 crore sessions and 107.70 lakh replays a month, 271 clients, nine in the EU — with no growth.

A. Stand up a European plane. Replay storage, compute and a support console inside Frankfurt, operated by EEA-resident staff, with the Indian console cut off from EU replay. The EU share of October inflow is 6.91 of 21.63 TB, which allocates 85.6 TB of the 268 TB stock; the plan does not say whether those blobs then leave Mumbai. At Frankfurt's ₹61,000 per TB-year that is ₹52.22 lakh, plus ₹24.00 lakh of quoted compute and two EEA support engineers at ₹68.00 lakh each fully loaded: ₹212.22 lakh, or ₹2.12 crore of cash. Engineering 52 person-weeks, 14 in the SDK squad. It leaves in place the Mumbai primary for the other four regions, Iqaama's UAE copy, and the retention and training defaults.

B. Minimise at capture. SDK v5 masks all text nodes by default, stops capturing raw DOM and drops retention from four hundred days to ninety. At October inflow, ninety days holds 3 × 21.63 = 64.89 TB; at Mumbai's ₹47,000 per TB-year, ₹30.50 lakh a year against ₹125.96 lakh for the 268 TB stock at the same quoted price, a reduction of ₹95.46 lakh if inflow stays flat. Engineering 44 person-weeks, 31 in the SDK squad, plus ₹14.00 lakh of QA and re-integration. Ijssel's order form of 14 March 2022 names “unmasked DOM replay” as a deliverable; Ilsedorf's names “session replay” unqualified. It leaves untouched the device-hash index, the reverse lookup, where data is stored and training.

C. Control the access, sign the paper. A just-in-time access-approval layer, quoted on 6 November at ₹18.00 lakh a year, with an EEA-resident approver on retainer at ₹22.00 lakh; eleven person-weeks, four of them SRE. The thirty-day erasure undertaking is met by a scan pass of 31 hours on the last working day of each month, twelve passes at ₹6.40 lakh, or ₹76.80 lakh: total cash ₹116.80 lakh. It leaves untouched where data is stored, retention, capture fidelity and training.

D. Re-paper the European book. A Utrecht operating partner becomes counterparty to the EU clients and runs the European plane, licensing Vista from Indriya. Its term sheet of 3 November asks 22 per cent of EU contract value: on the EU ARR of ₹24.60 crore in Exhibit 1, ₹5.41 crore a year of revenue forgone, plus ₹35.00 lakh of legal and transition cost and 24 person-weeks, nine of them platform. Transition runs past 30 November. It leaves untouched the intent model and the Indian and US books.

The sheet is headed EU. The California attestation Ranjan promised on 30 October, the 62 undocumented activities, and the question whether the intent model should train on client data appear on none of the four.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Ijssel's addendum requires, by Monday 30 November 2026: that its customers' personal data be processed and stored only inside the EEA, with no access from outside; erasure certified within thirty days of a verified request; no use of Ijssel data to train models serving other customers; and audit on ten working days' notice. The ₹9.80 crore renewal falls due on 31 January 2027; Ironvale wants its attestation by Friday 20 November; Iqaama Retail Group of Dubai has a 2024 contract requiring a copy inside the UAE. Indriya held ₹31.0 crore of cash at 31 October 2026 against net burn of ₹1.90 crore a month over the preceding six months, or 16.3 months. The festive-peak change freeze runs to 15 January 2027. Riya has approved one senior hire, unfilled.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 5, state what Indriya holds on 31 October 2026, for whom and where. The two are measured seven months apart: which comparisons hold?
  2. Exhibit 3 counts privacy requests two ways over five months. What is each column's denominator, when was it measured, and what can and cannot be concluded from the relationship between columns 1 and 2?
  3. Take the questionnaire answer of 22 April 2026 with the release note of 11 February and the DPIA of 18 September. What would Indriya have to establish for the April answer to stand, who was positioned to know, and what follows?
  4. Exhibit 6 shows 90 uncommitted person-weeks to 26 March 2027. Price each option in Section 8 against that exhibit and its footnote: which fit inside the window, and on what assumption about the freeze?
  5. Each of the seven people around Rupam holds a fact or a judgement the others do not. One at a time: which changes the choice of option, which changes only the order she acts in, and which must go to the board whatever she chooses?
  6. What should Rupam do on Monday morning, and what should she say at the 7 pm board call — one sentence on the addendum, one on the intent model, one naming what she needs from the board and does not have? If these are not the right four options, say what you would put in their place and what you would give up for it.

 

At ten past one she gave up on the sheet and opened the support console. The audit log filtered by data-subject region, and she worked backwards through the forty-one sessions until she found one of her own: 21 September 2026, 11.52 pm, opened to reproduce a basket bug for Ilsedorf. She remembered the bug, and could not remember whether she had looked at a shopper's screen in Hamburg or at a synthetic replay from the test harness. No field in the log would tell her.

Outside, the lights opposite went off on their timer. She had eight hours, four options, and a question she had not written down: what she would have put in the April questionnaire herself.
case20v1-legal.gdpr:
Hooghly Desk and the Erasure Request

A teaching case on GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes

1. Opening

On Wednesday 21 October 2026, at 9.30 pm, Parna Acharjee, vice-president of product at Hooghly Desk, sat in her Kolkata office with a letter she had read four times. It was dated Monday 5 October and came from Philipp Adler, data protection officer at Nordlicht Versand, a Hamburg online retailer and Hooghly's largest German customer. Nordlicht's contract, worth ₹3.1 crore a year, renewed on Tuesday 15 December. The letter set three conditions for renewal. Parna had until Friday 30 October, when the first-half 2027 roadmap froze, to decide what Hooghly would build: for Nordlicht alone, for Europe, or for every customer on the platform.

2. Company background

Hooghly Desk was founded in Kolkata in 2017 by two former Infosys engineers. It sells a support and messaging platform that puts email, chat and WhatsApp conversations into one agent inbox, and its newest feature suggests replies to agents. It competes with Freshworks and Zoho Desk on the helpdesk side and with Gupshup and Yellow.ai on messaging. Its Indian customers sit in the direct-to-consumer segment that brands such as Nykaa, Lenskart and boAt anchor. Engineering is in Kolkata and Pune, design in Berlin, data science in Toronto, customer success in Singapore and North American sales in New Jersey.

At 30 September 2026 Hooghly had 1,040 paying accounts and ₹200 crore of annual recurring revenue (ARR). Exhibit 1 shows that 62 per cent of that ARR now comes from outside India. Every shopper conversation a customer's agents handle is stored on Hooghly's servers in Mumbai.

3. The situation

Nordlicht's letter asked for three things: a tested process to export or erase any shopper's data within 72 hours of a request, evidenced by a live test on 15 December; self-service automation of that process by 30 June 2027; and storage of Nordlicht's data inside the EU by 30 September 2027. Patrick Aldous, who runs North American sales from New Jersey, added that 16 other accounts, 9 in Europe and 7 in North America, had sent similar questionnaires since July. A Dubai retail group, the largest Gulf account at ₹6.4 crore, had asked about in-country hosting.

The pressure was already visible inside the company. When a shopper asks a customer to delete her data, the customer forwards the request, and Hooghly's support engineers search conversations, attachments, search indexes and analytics tables by hand. Hooghly's standard data processing agreement promises a response within 10 calendar days, leaving the customer time to meet its own one-month limit under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Exhibit 2 shows how that promise has held while monthly volume more than doubled, from 18 requests in April to 38 in August. Each late response left a customer with less than the remaining twenty days of its own month to reply to a shopper, and Patrick's questionnaires suggested more requests would follow.

The second problem was subtler. Prerna Ahmed, the Toronto data scientist, had trained the reply-suggestion model on transcripts pooled across customers, and agents liked it. Pushpita Aich, Hooghly's counsel, doubted that a company handling transcripts on its customers' instructions could reuse them for its own product. California's CCPA, as amended by CPRA, restricts a service provider in much the same way, and 54 California accounts were exposed. India's own Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 was phasing in its duties through 2027.

From Berlin, designer Pauline Amann reported that German shoppers expected a delete button, not an email address. From Singapore, customer-success lead Pei Ling Ang, awake at midnight for the call, said Southeast Asian prospects were starting to ask the same questions.

4. The people

Prabir Adak, head of engineering in Pune, wants a plan that does not stall the WhatsApp channel launch; he can free nine engineers only by pausing it. Pushpita Aich, in Kolkata, wants Hooghly to stop reusing customer transcripts without a documented basis and a contract that matches practice. Patrick Aldous, in New Jersey, wants Nordlicht renewed and the 16 questionnaires answered without promising what engineering cannot ship. Prerna Ahmed, in Toronto, wants to keep the data that makes the suggestion model good.

6. The options

Parna knew the board would see the frozen roadmap in November, and that engineering capacity, not money, was the scarcer resource. Whatever she chose, something already promised to customers would move.

Parna asked Prabir to price three courses over one window, 1 November 2026 to 31 October 2027, at one planning volume: 60 requests a month, 720 in all. Exhibit 3 gives the costs and Figure 1 the dates.

Option A, a platform privacy layer. Nine engineers work six months from Monday 2 November. They build a map of every store a conversation touches, purpose tags on every record, automated export and erasure through one interface with a self-service portal, and per-customer region pinning. It reaches all 1,040 accounts and can restrict pooled training to customers who opt in. It costs ₹185.40 lakh, pauses the WhatsApp launch, and leaves six months of manual handling.

Option B, Europe first. Five engineers work four months to stand up a separate Frankfurt stack for EU and UK tenants, with automated erasure and export for them only. It goes live at the end of February 2027 and costs ₹123.28 lakh. The other 892 accounts, including California, stay on manual handling, and Hooghly operates a second stack.

Option C, process before product. Two privacy-operations specialists at ₹18 lakh a year each, a counsel retainer and a 72-hour runbook start on 1 November. It costs ₹64.20 lakh and diverts engineers for 1.5 hours a request. It ships no automation or EU hosting, and pooled training continues as now.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, how large is Hooghly's privacy workload today, and what else would you want to know about September's 46 requests before trusting a planning figure of 60 a month?
  2. Which of Hooghly's current behaviours (manual erasure, pooled transcripts, Mumbai-only storage) would Philipp Adler or a regulator find hardest to defend, and why?
  3. Using Exhibit 3 and Figure 1, what does each option cost, which of Nordlicht's conditions does each meet and when, and who does each leave exposed?
  4. What would you commit to on 30 October, what would you ask Prabir and Patrick to do before then, and what evidence would make you change course?

8. A note for the learner

Privacy law changes a product through four questions: what role the company plays for the data, what purposes it may use it for, what rights people can exercise against it, and where the data sits. A policy page answers none of them; a data map, a purpose tag, an erasure job and a storage region do. A well-reasoned answer prices every option at the same volume, checks each against the dates it must meet, and names who each leaves exposed.

One defensible path is Option A, with a manual interim. Its extra cost over B is ₹62.12 lakh (₹185.40 lakh less ₹123.28 lakh), and that buys coverage of 892 more accounts, a control on pooled training, and one system rather than two. Total spend is under 1 per cent of ₹200 crore ARR. Parna would commit on 30 October to a priority manual lane that passes Nordlicht's 15 December test, and to a dated milestone on 28 February so that Philipp Adler sees progress early. She would revisit if the first two months showed the build running behind the 30 April plan, since the 30 June automation condition leaves little slack. This is one path, not the only one.
exp40v2-legal.gdpr:
GDPR, CCPA and global privacy regimes

What the statutes change about the product, not the policy page: two companies deciding in October 2026.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On Thursday 8 October 2026 Lakshana Thirumaran had the same slide on screen for the fifth month. Thirumaran ran product at Dhyana Health, a Bengaluru company whose sleep-and-anxiety app had 4.10 million monthly users: 29.5 lakh in India, 6.20 lakh in the European Economic Area, 3.80 lakh in the United States, 1.50 lakh elsewhere. Revenue to 31 March 2026 was ₹188 crore. The slide proposed shipping to Europe the engine Lingesh Tadimalla's team had run in India since February, reading nightly sleep-stage and mood logs to rewrite each programme.

Lavanthika Thanikachalam, Dhyana's data protection officer, had written in May: the question is not whether consent or legitimate interest is better, it is that for this data only one of them exists. Sleep and mood logs are data concerning health, and Article 9 of the General Data Protection Regulation forbids processing them unless one of ten narrow conditions applies; for a wellness product only explicit consent is live. A legitimate-interest assessment, however well written, does not reach Article 9 data.

Five days later Latchumanan Tallapaneni faced the same problem from the other side. Tallapaneni had co-founded Dastak Intelligence, a Pune firm selling conversation analytics to contact centres: ₹214 crore of annual recurring revenue, 34 EEA customers, a pooled corpus of 41.2 million utterances under a 24-month retention ceiling. Engineering wanted one shared quality-assurance model across all tenants; 11 of the 34 EU customers (32.4 per cent) had a clause forbidding that. A Dutch insurer's ₹14.2 crore renewal, due 15 December, was conditional on no transcript being readable outside the EEA. It was the largest of seven EEA customers asking the same, together ₹61.4 crore of recurring revenue; meeting them meant moving an 18-person support pod out of Hyderabad.

2. The idea, and who disagrees

European data protection law is a prohibition with exceptions: personal data may not be processed unless the controller names a lawful basis from Article 6, binds it to a purpose, and keeps it no longer than the purpose requires. The American tradition inverts the default, intervening at disclosure, opt-out and demonstrated harm.

The history runs mostly through Germany. Warren and Brandeis named a right to be let alone in 1890; Westin's Privacy and Freedom (1967) reframed it as control over information about oneself. Hesse passed the first data protection act in 1970, and in 1983 the German Constitutional Court, striking down a census, named informational self-determination. That concept, not privacy as secrecy, is what the OECD guidelines of 1980 and Regulation 2016/679 encode. The United States took the sectoral road; California's 2018 statute, rebuilt in 2020, is notice-and-opt-out in European clothes.

Four schools divide the field. The rights school signs a company may not process data merely because it is useful and refuses harm is the test of lawfulness; the harm school signs the second and refuses the first. The structural school signs an opt-in rate measures interface design, not preference; the fiduciary school, the duty of care runs to the user whatever the user clicked.

3. Mechanics

Expert practice has four parts, and teams collapse the first two. First the purpose: a documented statement of what the processing is for, written before the field exists. Second the basis, chosen per purpose, not per product; special-category data needs an Article 6 basis and an Article 9 condition, which is where Dhyana's five months went. Third the enforcement point: a consent record is worthless unless something refuses to serve the data when the record says no; experts enforce at read, because collection-time enforcement cannot be revoked. Fourth the evidence, each document dated before the launch it blesses.

Enforcing at read reshapes the backlog: if the predicate excluding a non-consenting user lives in the query, every downstream consumer must carry the purpose tag. That is a lineage project, which is why privacy work appears on data-platform roadmaps.

Between 15 and 28 June 2026 Dhyana randomised 33,000 EEA users: 24,000 shown the explicit-consent prompt, 9,000 left untouched. Of those prompted, 14,880 consented, 62.0 per cent, and were personalised; 9,120 refused. Twenty-eight-day outcomes closed on 26 July, read out on 7 August.

Consenters retained at 41.8 per cent against the control's 34.6 per cent, a 7.2-point gap a careless deck would call the value of personalisation. The deck cannot know whether it is right, because consenters chose themselves. The intention-to-treat contrast, prompted cell against control, is 38.9 against 34.6 per cent, a lift of 4.3 points; at those rates on 24,000 and 9,000 users the standard error of the difference is 0.59 points, so the effect is 7.3 standard errors. Refusers in the prompted cell retained at 34.2 per cent, 0.4 points from control against a standard error of 0.71: inside noise, so refusers behave like untreated users. Scaling the 4.3 points by the 0.620 consent rate puts 6.9 on a consenting user, so selection explains only 0.3 of the naive 7.2. The gap happened to be close; only the contrast could show it.

Conversion behaves identically. 2,592 of the 24,000 prompted users converted, 10.80 per cent, against 846 of the 9,000 controls, 9.40 per cent. That 1.40-point intention-to-treat lift already embeds the 62.0 per cent consent rate, so the lift on a user who actually receives personalisation is 1.40 / 0.620 = 2.26 points. Every modelled row of Exhibit 1 is that number attenuated.

Option C is the expert move. It earns ₹6.33 crore of the ₹7.65 crore the unlawful option would, 83 per cent, because it stops treating refusal of the health layer as refusal of everything. Option A, the instinctive compliant answer, withholds behavioural personalisation from 2.36 lakh refusers and pays ₹1.59 crore a year for tidiness. And the consent rate is an interface measurement: ten points either way moves A by 0.23 points of conversion, about ₹0.8 crore.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: the binding regime is the one whose thresholds you cross, not the one your customers discuss. Dhyana's board had been briefed on California, whose revenue threshold runs on the preceding calendar year, so an April-to-March figure must be recut: calendar 2025 was ₹171 crore, $19.4 million at ₹88 to the dollar, under the $25 million gate. The other gate is 100,000 consumers whose data is sold or shared; 92,000 of Dhyana's 3,80,000 American users are Californian, 24.2 per cent, rising 4,100 a month, so it crosses in two months. Washington's My Health My Data Act has no threshold, covers consumer health data exactly, and is privately enforced: the binding regime was never California. Dastak answers differently: a processor under Article 28 for its 34 EU customers, a controller only for its own training.

Claim two: where special-category data is processed, the consent-versus-legitimate-interest argument is moot. True for Dhyana and load-bearing. For Dastak it holds weakly: a caller mentioning a diagnosis puts Article 9 data into a transcript collected for another purpose, the law's least settled corner.

Claim three: a transfer is about access, not geography. A Hyderabad engineer reading a European transcript is a transfer under Chapter V whether or not a byte is copied, as Dastak's insurer found. Dhyana fails it too: its Bengaluru on-call rota reads European records.

It misleads in two places. Where data is genuinely anonymous the apparatus switches off, but the bar is impossibility of singling out an individual, which a device-keyed table does not meet. And consumer consent logic imported into business-to-business work is nonsense: an employee's consent to her employer is rarely freely given.

5. Edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product companies break on identity, not policy: one account across four products means one identity graph, and purpose limitation dies in the join when a field collected for fraud scoring becomes a recommender feature. Marketplaces break on Article 26, where platform and seller are joint controllers for part of the processing and independent for the rest; what settles it is who determines the purpose (C-40/17). Somebody must answer the access request, and the contract rarely says who.

Regulated products collide erasure with retention mandates. A payments business holding records under Reserve Bank of India directions is obeying a legal obligation: real, narrow and overclaimed whenever convenient. Hardware is worse: a ring buffer in a customer's home is personal data no backend command reaches, and the retailer who handled the warranty is a second controller nobody mapped. AI-native products are hardest: a user exercising Article 17 leaves the next training run, but weights already trained on her cannot be unpicked, and the working answer, exclusion plus disproportionate effort, has never been tested.

At the seam the failure is structural, not moral: the impact assessment comes from a function that cannot move the launch date. What mature companies do, as against what their trust pages say, is move the control into the build: default-deny on new fields at schema review, a required purpose column, and a quarterly reconciliation of processing records against the live schema.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One. A consent rate measures an interface. The tell is an opt-in rate that moves ten points on a copy change, as Dhyana's did in pilot. Reading 62.0 per cent as what Europeans want treats a design artefact as a preference.

Two. Legitimate interest is the expensive path. It carries a balancing test producible on demand, an absolute Article 21 right to object, and a habit of evaporating when data turns out to be special-category. The tell is a team that chose it to dodge a consent flow and built neither.

Three. "Anonymous" is a legal conclusion engineers are asked to assert. The tell is a dataset called anonymised that still carries a join key to the production table: the identifiers left the columns, not the system.

Four. Remote access is the transfer everyone forgets. The tell is a transfer assessment listing three cloud regions and no human beings: no support rota, no on-call engineer, no contractor. The paperwork is about where data can be read; screens are where it is read.

Five. The deadline that breaks a request programme is not the statutory one. Article 12 gives a month, extendable by two; identity verification consumes it. The tell is a queue with a healthy median and a 95th percentile at 29 days.

Six. Erasure is a distributed-systems problem with a statutory clock. The tell is a deletion endpoint with no acknowledgement ledger: the primary store confirms, and nothing records whether the warehouse, the vendor's system and two analytics copies did.

Seven. The consent plane and the opt-out plane are different machines. Europe needs a signal gating processing before it happens; America one that stops a sale or cross-context disclosure after collection, arriving as a Global Privacy Control header. The tell is a banner that respects it while the server-side bid request, which the banner never sees, does not.

Eight. The fine is not the exposure; the order is. Article 83's ceiling is the higher of €20 million and 4 per cent of worldwide turnover, so for Dhyana the higher of ₹192 crore at ₹96 to the euro and ₹7.52 crore: above its whole annual revenue. But the enforcement record is mostly reprimands and Article 58 orders rather than headline fines, and an order to stop processing or delete a model ends a product. The tell is a risk register with a fine number and no line for being told to stop.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products the consent rate is a product metric and the request queue a volume business. In business-to-business products the regime arrives through the processing agreement, not the statute; consent is largely unavailable and real enforcement comes from the buyer's security questionnaire. Enterprise buyers turn residency and the transfer assessment into procurement questions. Here the difference stops being real: purpose tags, the enforcement predicate and the deletion ledger are the same build for a consumer app and an enterprise platform, and only the deadlines and the audience change. Platforms differ genuinely, because joint controllership must be allocated before anyone answers a request; hardware, because firmware and the retail channel sit outside the backend; AI, because erasure cannot reach weights.

Stage matters more than founders expect. At seed the programme is a data map and a purpose column, three engineer-weeks. At the first enterprise contract it is an impact assessment and an agreement whose notice windows someone has read. At Dhyana's stage the self-serve machinery stops being optional; at scale it is reconciliation.

8. Three worked examples

The lawful basis. Exhibit 1's lesson is severability: the ₹1.59 crore between C and A exists because C refuses to bundle. But C's ₹38.15 crore rests on a measured 2.26-point lift and an unmeasured transfer of it.

The request queue. Exhibit 2 prices it from the cost side, and the denominator is the trap. Dhyana's EEA base opened that year at 4.56 lakh and closed at 6.20 lakh, where it still stood in October, so the mean was 5.38 lakh. Planners read 1,934 requests over twelve months as 161 a month and divided by the closing base, giving 2.60 per 10,000 users; on the mean base the rate is 3.00, and 3.00 against 6.20 lakh is 186 a month. They had planned for two quarters against a number 13 per cent below the right one.

The failure. Dhanishta Devices, a Coimbatore maker of connected treadmills and a sleep ring, sunset a product line in June 2024 and emailed 1.9 million European owners. The notice generated an erasure wave: 41,800 requests between July 2024 and January 2026, one per account after dedupe, about twelve per 10,000 owners a month, driven by Dhanishta's own email and an order of magnitude above Dhyana's organic 0.95 erasures per 10,000 of its mean base a month. All were honoured in the primary store. A reconciliation in February 2026, run against the erasure request ledger rather than a log, found 11,240 of the 41,800 subjects (26.9 per cent) still in at least one of 14 downstream systems: 9,180 in the analytics warehouse alone, 1,610 in a vendor's CRM alone, 450 in both, the warehouse copies called pseudonymous but joined to production on a device identifier. Lakshmipriya Theerthagiri, who ran engineering, went to the regulator unasked; the August 2026 outcome was a reprimand and an order, no fine. Remediation took seven engineer-months at ₹8.9 lakh each plus a ₹38 lakh audit; the ledger she built after, 14 endpoints with median propagation 4.2 days and a p95 of 26 days, cost ₹53.4 lakh. Built first it would have cost ₹53.4 lakh; found late, ₹153.7 lakh, a shade under three times. With a p95 of 26 days and a p99 of 41 against a one-month duty, between 1 and 5 per cent land late: at least 418 requests, perhaps 2,090.

9. Failure modes and early warnings

Consent recorded but never enforced. Early sign: a consent table with no foreign key in any production query path. Diagnostic: show me the query that reads mood logs and the predicate excluding a non-consenting user. Caught late it costs Dhanishta's multiple, three times building it first.

Purpose creep through a new feature on an old field. Early sign: a specification reusing a column without naming its purpose. Diagnostic: which notice told this user about this use. Caught late the remedy is re-consent, which costs you everyone who does not answer.

Transfer paperwork covering machines and not people. Early sign: an inventory of cloud regions with no named human access path. Diagnostic: list every screen a European record appears on, and where the body before it sits.

Treating a processor's incident as not yours. Early sign: an agreement giving you 72 hours to notify under Article 33 and your vendor five business days, which can be 168 hours against your 72. Diagnostic: my deadline minus my vendor's window. Caught late, the late notification is itself an infringement.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether consented personalisation is worth anything. The optimist's case is Dhyana's own: a 1.40-point intention-to-treat lift on a 9.40 per cent base is 14.9 per cent more paying users, measured against an untouched control rather than self-selected consenters. The sceptic's case is that a 28-day window measures novelty, and that sceptics re-running these tests at six months find the lift halved. The optimist is wrong if a six-month re-test decays; the sceptic, if month-six cohorts separate as cleanly as day 28.

Whether legitimate interest can carry personalisation at all. One camp reads the Court of Justice's October 2024 judgment on a sports federation's commercial interest (C-621/22) as settling that a commercial interest can be legitimate, so a documented balancing test plus a working objection path suffices. The other reads the European Data Protection Board's 2024 opinion on consent-or-pay as evidence that regulators will narrow it until only consent survives. The first is wrong if an authority defeats a documented assessment on balancing alone; the second if that test holds in litigation.

Whether fragmentation converges. The Brussels-effect camp holds that building to the strictest regime satisfies the rest, pointing at twenty-odd American state statutes with recognisably European vocabulary. The divergence camp points at Maryland's minimisation ban, India's negative-list transfers under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and China's localisation rules. Convergence fails the moment two regimes make incompatible demands rather than merely different ones; divergence, if the engineering is one data map with different switch positions.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks what the purpose is before what the data is: the purpose determines everything downstream, the data nothing. She prices the order, not the fine. She says unprompted which numbers are measured and which modelled: Thirumaran knows 2.26 points is measured and 55 per cent an ablation. She can show the threshold arithmetic for every regime she is not complying with, and she builds the ledger before the first request arrives.

12. What they decided

Thirumaran took Option C to the 22 October board, staged: Ireland and the Netherlands first, the behavioural layer on legitimate interest with a documented assessment and an objection path, consent gating only the sleep-and-mood layer, and an EEA re-run of the June ablation. She funded the self-serve build on the volume-shock argument, not the payback.

Tallapaneni split his problems apart. The shared model he declined on evidence: the fit implies honouring all 11 clauses costs 0.009 of F1, while its own 0.850 target needs 198 million utterances, 4.8 times the full corpus and more if returns diminish, so the clause was never what stood between Dastak and its goal. The pod he moved: 18 people at €48,000 loaded in Kraków is ₹8.29 crore at ₹96 to the euro, against ₹2.61 crore for 18 at ₹14.5 lakh in Hyderabad, so ₹5.68 crore a year to protect ₹61.4 crore. What worries him is in the plan: a Kraków rota does not close the seam while Pune engineers debug production.

Discussion questions.

1. Option C rests on a modelled 55 per cent attenuation from an ablation on Indian users. Design the EEA experiment that would test it, and say what you ship if it comes back at 20 per cent.

2. Dastak spends ₹5.68 crore a year to protect ₹61.4 crore of recurring revenue. At what level of protected revenue would you reverse that, and how would you price the residual exposure the pod does not remove?

3. Both companies treat a reprimand and a fine as different in kind. Build the case for treating them as one risk priced differently, and say what that changes about staffing a privacy programme.

13. Going deeper

  • Privacy by design: these principles before they were law.
  • Consent flows and cookie UX: where the 62.0 per cent is won.
  • Children's privacy and age assurance: consent replaced by prohibition.
  • AI regulation: the layer above Article 22.
  • Export controls and data residency: architecture goes regional.
  • Security incidents and breach response: the 72-hour clock.
  • Data governance and lineage: the purpose tag enforcement needs.
  • Compliance across jurisdictions: one engine, not twenty.
  • Data, consent and the DPDP Act: consent plus legitimate uses.
  • Personalisation vs surveillance: the argument under Exhibit 1.

GDPR, CCPA and Global Privacy Regimes

What the laws change about the product, not just the policy page.

1. A Monday in March

On Monday 9 March 2026, Kumaran Subramaniam, head of product at Cadambari Fit in Chennai, opened two emails before his first meeting. The first came from a user in Berlin, who asked for a copy of everything the app held about her and cited Article 15 of the General Data Protection Regulation. The second came from a user in San Diego, who wrote one line: stop selling my data.

Cadambari Fit logs meals, workouts, sleep and heart rate for 2.4 million registered users. Its worldwide turnover is ₹210 crore. In six weeks, on Monday 20 April, it planned to launch Cadambari Coach, a paid feature that reads sleep and heart-rate trends and sends daily advice. The plan sent raw heart-rate readings to a United States analytics vendor.

Kanimozhi Srirangam, the company's lawyer, did not ask whether the emails were annoying. She asked whether anyone could say where each user's data went, and by what right. Nobody could. Table 1 shows who the users are.

Table 1. Cadambari Fit registered users, 9 March 2026. Shares are of 2,400,000.

The exposed groups are 16 per cent of users, 384,000 people, but the law follows the person, not the company's address, and a launch that sends health readings abroad without a lawful footing could be stopped by a regulator after it had been built.

2. The idea

A privacy regime is a law that gives individuals rights over information about them and puts duties on whoever decides why and how it is used. Three terms carry most of the weight. Personal data is any information relating to an identifiable person. A controller is the party deciding the purposes and means of processing. A processor handles data only on the controller's instructions.

The problem was bargaining power. By the 2010s, firms could collect, combine and resell personal data at a scale no individual could see. The European Union answered with the GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, adopted in April 2016 and enforceable from 25 May 2018, replacing a 1995 directive. California answered with the California Consumer Privacy Act, passed in 2018 and in force from 1 January 2020, strengthened by the California Privacy Rights Act from 1 January 2023. India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in 2023, with its provisions switching on in phases.

Kumaran's meeting sentence: we hold users' data on conditions, and the conditions are product features. Table 2 sets the two main regimes beside each other.

Table 2. GDPR and CCPA/CPRA compared on five points.
PointGDPRCCPA/CPRA
Who is coveredAnyone offering services to people in the EU, or monitoring themBusinesses over a size threshold dealing with California residents
DefaultCollection needs a lawful basis chosen in advanceCollection allowed; people may opt out of sale or sharing
Response clockOne month, extendable by two45 days, extendable by 45
Penalty frameUp to €20 million or 4% of worldwide turnover, whichever is higherPer-violation fines, higher where intentional or involving minors
EnforcerNational authorities, such as Ireland'sCalifornia Privacy Protection Agency and Attorney General

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 traces Cadambari's data. Treat it as a sequence of questions, each of which becomes a piece of product work.

Arrow A comes first. Before collecting anything, Cadambari must pick a lawful basis for each purpose, not each data field. The GDPR lists six: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task and legitimate interests. It must also tell the user, in plain words, what is happening. Kanimozhi's inventory found 31 purposes in use; nothing downstream can be answered without that inventory.

Heart rate is health data, a special category under Article 9, which is barred unless a narrower condition applies. For Coach, that condition is explicit consent. Arrow B is the rights flow: a user may ask for access, correction, deletion or portability, and the clock starts when the request arrives.

Arrow C is a transfer: sending personal data outside the European Economic Area. It needs a recognised tool, such as an adequacy decision (the EU-US Data Privacy Framework since July 2023, covering certified firms) or standard contractual clauses signed with the vendor. Arrow D is Article 28, which requires a written contract with each processor. Finally, Article 35 demands a data protection impact assessment, a written risk review done before launch, when processing is likely high risk, as large-scale health data is.

4. A worked example: the cost of the rights flow

Kanimozhi asked what the rights flow would cost. Cadambari will give one flow to both EU and California users, because California's 100,000-consumer threshold is near (see the nuances below). The planning assumption is that 0.15 per cent of those 384,000 users make a request in a year. A manual request takes 3.5 staff hours at ₹1,200 an hour loaded, or ₹4,200. Two analysts supply 130 productive hours each per month, which is 260.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Consent is one basis of six, and often the wrong one

Consent can be withdrawn at any moment, which makes it fragile for anything the service needs in order to work. Fraud screening may rest on legitimate interests. Consent fits optional extras such as Coach's health analysis.

Necessary is stricter than useful

The contract basis covers what is objectively needed to deliver the service the user signed up for. Advice personalised by heart rate is useful to Cadambari's business model; it is not necessary to log a meal.

Opt-in against opt-out

The GDPR demands a basis before collection. California lets collection proceed and gives a right to stop sale or sharing. Honour browser signals such as Global Privacy Control where California applies.

Applicability is a calculation, not an assumption

Cadambari earns ₹210 crore. At an assumed ₹88 to the dollar that is about $23.9 million, below the $25 million statutory base figure for the revenue test, which is adjusted upward for inflation; even unadjusted, a rate of ₹84 or stronger would meet it. California users number 96,000, under the 100,000-consumer test. Only about 4,000 more registered users, a 4.2 per cent rise, would reach 100,000, and the statute also counts households and non-registered visitors. The third test, half of revenue from selling or sharing data, does not apply. Counsel decides; the product lead must know the question is live.

Personal data is wider than names

A device identifier, an advertising ID or a pseudonymous user number is still personal data if it can be linked to a person. Only truly anonymous data leaves the law, and the bar is high.

A transfer is about onward flow, not server location

Server location is not the test; a recipient outside the EEA is. The US vendor and the Mumbai store are both transfers needing a tool. The Court of Justice of the EU struck down the EU-US Privacy Shield in July 2020 (the Schrems II judgment), so tools are checked. The European Data Protection Board's view is that a user sending data directly to a non-EU controller is itself not a transfer, a point where reasonable lawyers still argue.

A ceiling is not a forecast

The GDPR's top tier is the higher of €20 million or 4 per cent of worldwide turnover. At ₹100 to the euro, 4 per cent of ₹210 crore is ₹8.4 crore, while €20 million is ₹200 crore, so the flat sum applies. That is nearly a year's revenue. Actual fines turn on factors in Article 83(2): gravity, duration, cooperation.

What no regime can tell you

The law does not say whether Coach is good for users, which regime wins in a conflict, or how a deletion request squares with tax-record duties. Judgement about harm stays with the product team.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

Table 5. How the same law lands on three product types.
Product typeCadambari's roleWhat changes in the product
ConsumerControllerConsent screens, rights flow, privacy by default settings
B2BOften processor for the employerData processing agreements, instruction logs, sub-processor lists, audit support
MarketplaceJoint or separate controller with sellersRoles per data flow, seller obligations, visible data-sharing rules

If Cadambari sold Coach to employers as a wellness benefit, it would process staff data for the employer, who decides purposes. The rights request would route to the employer first. In a marketplace of trainers and members, both sides decide something, so roles must be written down for each flow.

Size matters too. An early-stage firm needs a data map, one vendor register and a rights email that works. A large company adds a data protection officer, mandatory under Article 37 for large-scale special-category processing.

7. Common mistakes

Table 6. Three mistakes, how they look from outside, and the cheapest test.
MistakeSymptomMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Fixing the policy page onlyNew policy text, but trackers fire at first launchLaw governs behaviour, not wordingInstall on a clean phone behind a proxy and list calls made before any tap
Rights requests in a shared inboxReplies land on day 29 or 30The clock starts on receipt, not on triageFile a dummy request and time it to the last export
Consent as universal coverA feature that quietly stops working for those who decline, or consent rates near 100%Consent must be free and specificAsk what happens to the user who says no

Each treats a legal requirement as a communications task. The tests measure the product, not the document.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Kumaran has one page showing 31 purposes, each with a basis, a retention period and an owner. Heart-rate readings stay inside Cadambari's own Mumbai storage; the vendor receives counts without the raw readings. Coach asks for explicit consent on a separate screen that can be declined without losing the app. The assessment was signed before 10 April. Both emails were answered within the clock, the San Diego one without waiting to learn whether the law bound the company.

9. The decision

Kumaran kept 20 April. He shipped Coach with explicit consent, the vendor limited to aggregate counts, and signed contracts with all three processors. He approved the ₹38 lakh rights flow, reasoning that the cheaper path cost him a missed deadline in the stress case and, in the planning case, paid back inside the 24 months Finance uses for tooling. He kept one flow for everyone rather than per region because California was 4,000 users from its threshold.

Learn next: consent flows and cookie UX, because that is where this law meets the screen, and then security incidents and breach response, since the 72-hour notification clock is the sharpest deadline the GDPR sets.

Two questions to sit with. First, which of your product's purposes would survive if the lawful basis had to be written beside each one tomorrow? Second, if a regulator asked for the one number that proves your rights process works, which would you offer, and who in your company measures it?
